type:LABEL: collection
name: Itihāsa (the epics)
summary: The Sanskrit category itihāsa (“thus indeed it was”) designates the two great epics, the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata, which present themselves as accounts of the past and as authoritative teaching on dharma.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
summary: The Sanskrit epic of Rāma attributed to the sage Vālmīki, in seven books (kāṇḍas); in the Baroda Critical Edition 606 sargas and c. 18,760 verses. Most scholars regard Books 2–6 as the older core and the Bālakāṇḍa and Uttarakāṇḍa as later.

type:LABEL: text
name: Mahābhārata
summary: The Sanskrit epic of the Bhārata war between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas, attributed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa; in the Pune Critical Edition 18 parvans, 1,995 adhyāyas and c. 74,000 verses, with the Harivaṃśa as its supplement (khila).

type:LABEL: text
name: Bhagavad Gītā
subtype: philosophical dialogue embedded in the epic
summary: Kṛṣṇa’s 700-verse teaching to Arjuna on the eve of battle, embedded in the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata: MBh (CE) 6.23–40 (= chapters 25–42 of the Bhīṣmaparvan in the vulgate numbering).

type:LABEL: text
name: Harivaṃśa
summary: The “Genealogy of Hari”, transmitted as the khila (supplement) of the Mahābhārata, narrating the Yādava genealogy and Kṛṣṇa’s life from birth among the cowherds to his rule in Dvārakā. Critical Edition by P. L. Vaidya (BORI 1969–71): 118 adhyāyas, c. 6,000 verses — about a third of the vulgate.

type:LABEL: text
name: Rāmopākhyāna (Mahābhārata)
summary: The Mahābhārata’s own telling of the Rāma story, narrated by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya to Yudhiṣṭhira after Jayadratha’s attempt to abduct Draupadī: MBh (CE) 3.257–275, Āraṇyakaparvan.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bālakāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 1)
summary: The “Book of Youth”: the frame (Nārada’s summary to Vālmīki, the krauñca curse and the invention of the śloka, the teaching of Lava and Kuśa), the sacrifice for sons, Viṣṇu’s decision to be born, the births of the four princes, Viśvāmitra’s expedition, Ahalyā, the breaking of Śiva’s bow and the marriages, and the encounter with Paraśurāma.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ayodhyākāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 2)
summary: The “Book of Ayodhyā”: the planned consecration, Kaikeyī’s two boons, Rāma’s exile with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, Daśaratha’s death, Bharata’s refusal and the sandals.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Araṇyakāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 3)
summary: The “Book of the Forest”: life among the sages of the Daṇḍaka, Śūrpaṇakhā’s mutilation, the war with Khara, the golden deer, Sītā’s abduction, Jaṭāyu’s death, Kabandha and Śabarī.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 4)
summary: The “Book of Kiṣkindhā”: Hanumān’s meeting with Rāma, the alliance with Sugrīva, the killing of Vālin and the search for Sītā.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Sundarakāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 5)
summary: The “Beautiful Book”: Hanumān’s leap to Laṅkā, his search, his meeting with Sītā in the aśoka grove, the token ring, and the burning of the city.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Yuddhakāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 6)
summary: The “Book of the War”: Vibhīṣaṇa’s defection, the causeway built by Nala, the war, the deaths of Kumbhakarṇa, Indrajit and Rāvaṇa, Sītā’s fire ordeal and Brahmā’s hymn, and the return and consecration in Ayodhyā.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Uttarakāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 7)
summary: The “Last Book”: Rāvaṇa’s origins and earlier conquests, Hanumān’s childhood, the banishment of Sītā, the birth of Lava and Kuśa in Vālmīki’s hermitage, the Śambūka episode, the recitation of the poem by the twins, Sītā’s return into the earth and Rāma’s return to Viṣṇu’s form.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ādiparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 1)
summary: The “First Book”: the frame narratives, the snake sacrifice, the origins of the Bhārata line (Śakuntalā, Śantanu, Bhīṣma’s vow), the births and youth of the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas, the house of lac, Draupadī’s svayaṃvara and marriage, Indraprastha and the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Sabhāparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 2)
summary: The “Book of the Assembly Hall”: the hall built by Maya, the killing of Jarāsandha, the rājasūya and the killing of Śiśupāla, the dice game, Draupadī’s humiliation and the second game that sends the Pāṇḍavas into exile.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Āraṇyakaparvan (Vanaparvan) (Mahābhārata, Book 3)
summary: The “Book of the Forest”: twelve years of exile, Arjuna’s acquisition of weapons (Kirāta), pilgrimages, and many embedded tales — Nala and Damayantī, the Rāmopākhyāna, Sāvitrī — ending with the theft of Karṇa’s earrings and the Yakṣa’s questions.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Virāṭaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 4)
summary: The “Book of Virāṭa”: the thirteenth year in disguise at the Matsya court, the killing of Kīcaka, the cattle raid and Uttarā’s marriage to Abhimanyu.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Udyogaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 5)
summary: The “Book of the Effort”: embassies and preparations for war, Vidura’s and Sanatsujāta’s counsels, Kṛṣṇa’s embassy and theophany at the Kaurava court, Kṛṣṇa’s and Kuntī’s approaches to Karṇa, and the story of Ambā/Śikhaṇḍin.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhīṣmaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 6)
summary: The “Book of Bhīṣma”: the first ten days of battle under Bhīṣma’s command, containing the Bhagavad Gītā (6.23–40), ending with Bhīṣma’s fall onto a bed of arrows (6.114).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Droṇaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 7)
summary: The “Book of Droṇa”: the battle under Droṇa, the deaths of Abhimanyu, Jayadratha and Ghaṭotkaca, and Droṇa’s death after the report of “Aśvatthāman’s” death.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Karṇaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 8)
summary: The “Book of Karṇa”: Karṇa’s command, Śalya as his charioteer, Bhīma’s killing of Duḥśāsana, and Arjuna’s killing of Karṇa (8.67).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Śalyaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 9)
summary: The “Book of Śalya”: Śalya’s command and death, Balarāma’s pilgrimage along the Sarasvatī, and the mace duel in which Bhīma breaks Duryodhana’s thighs (9.57).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Sauptikaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 10)
summary: The “Book of the Sleepers”: Aśvatthāman’s night massacre of the Pāñcālas and Draupadī’s sons, and Kṛṣṇa’s curse on Aśvatthāman.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Strīparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 11)
summary: The “Book of the Women”: lament on the battlefield, Gāndhārī’s curse on Kṛṣṇa, and Kuntī’s revelation that Karṇa was her son.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Śāntiparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 12)
summary: The “Book of Peace”: Bhīṣma’s instruction of Yudhiṣṭhira from the bed of arrows — Rājadharma (12.1–128), Āpaddharma (129–167) and Mokṣadharma (168–353), including the Nārāyaṇīya (321–339).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Anuśāsanaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 13)
summary: The “Book of Instruction”: further teaching by Bhīṣma (including the Viṣṇusahasranāma, 13.135) and his death at the winter solstice (13.154).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Āśvamedhikaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 14)
summary: The “Book of the Horse Sacrifice”: the Anugītā (14.16–50), the revival of the still-born Parīkṣit by Kṛṣṇa, and Yudhiṣṭhira’s horse sacrifice.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Āśramavāsikaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 15)
summary: The “Book of the Hermitage”: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī, Kuntī and Vidura retire to the forest; Vyāsa shows the dead warriors to the living; the elders die in a forest fire.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Mausalaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 16)
summary: The “Book of the Clubs”: the self-destruction of the Yādavas at Prabhāsa, Balarāma’s and Kṛṣṇa’s deaths, and the submergence of Dvārakā.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Mahāprasthānikaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 17)
summary: The “Book of the Great Departure”: the Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī walk towards the Himālaya; all fall except Yudhiṣṭhira, who refuses to abandon the dog that follows him.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Svargārohaṇaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 18)
summary: The “Book of the Ascent to Heaven”: Yudhiṣṭhira’s vision of hell and heaven, the final state of the heroes, and the close of the recitation.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Harivaṃśaparvan (Harivaṃśa)
summary: Book 1 of the Harivaṃśa (CE): cosmogony, the solar and lunar dynasties and the genealogy of the Yādavas down to Kṛṣṇa.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇuparvan (Harivaṃśa)
summary: Book 2 of the Harivaṃśa (CE): the life of Kṛṣṇa from the gods’ plan and his birth to Devakī (HV 48) through his childhood in Vraja, the killing of Kaṃsa (76), the move to Dvārakā (85–86) and later wars and marriages.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhaviṣyaparvan (Harivaṃśa)
summary: Book 3 of the Harivaṃśa (CE): a short concluding section on the future and the close of Janamejaya’s line.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Nalopākhyāna (MBh 3.50–78)
summary: The story of Nala and Damayantī, told by the sage Bṛhadaśva to Yudhiṣṭhira during the forest exile (MBh (CE) 3.49 frame; 3.50–78 story).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Pativratāmāhātmya / Sāvitrī-upākhyāna (MBh 3.277–283)
summary: The story of Sāvitrī, who wins back her husband Satyavān from Yama, told by Mārkaṇḍeya to Yudhiṣṭhira (MBh (CE) 3.277–283).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Śakuntalopākhyāna (MBh 1.62–69)
summary: The story of King Duḥṣanta and Śakuntalā and the birth of Bharata, eponym of the Bhāratas (MBh (CE) 1.62–69).

type:LABEL: passage
name: The churning of the ocean (MBh 1.15–17)
summary: The Mahābhārata’s account of the churning of the ocean for amṛta, told by Ugraśravas to explain the horse Uccaiḥśravas (MBh (CE) 1.15–17; 1.18.1 closes “thus I have told you how the amṛta was churned”).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Aṃśāvataraṇa: the partial incarnations (MBh 1.61)
summary: The catalogue of which gods, demons and others were born as the epic’s characters — e.g. Kṛṣṇa as a portion of Nārāyaṇa, Balarāma of Śeṣa, Karṇa of the Sun, Draupadī of Śrī, Duryodhana of Kali (MBh (CE) 1.61.63–99).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Pañcendropākhyāna: the five Indras (MBh 1.189)
summary: Vyāsa’s account to Drupada of five former Indras born as the Pāṇḍavas with Śrī as their common wife, followed by the tale of the sage’s daughter who asked Śiva five times for a husband (MBh (CE) 1.189.1–49).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Dyūtaparvan: the dice game (MBh 2.43–65)
summary: The sub-book of the first dice game, from Duryodhana’s envy at Indraprastha to Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s boons to Draupadī and the Pāṇḍavas’ release (MBh (CE) 2.43–65); the return match follows in 2.66–72.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ambopākhyāna (MBh 5.170–193)
summary: Bhīṣma’s narration of Ambā’s abduction, her rejection, his duel with Paraśurāma, her rebirth as Śikhaṇḍinī and the sex-exchange with the yakṣa Sthūṇa (MBh (CE) 5.170–193).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Kuṇḍalāharaṇa: the theft of Karṇa’s earrings (MBh 3.284–294)
summary: Sūrya warns Karṇa that Indra will beg his armour and earrings; the narrative of Kuntī’s boon, Karṇa’s birth and abandonment in a basket on the Aśvanadī, and his rescue by Adhiratha and Rādhā; Indra receives the armour and gives the spear (MBh (CE) 3.284–294).

type:LABEL: passage
name: The Yakṣa’s questions (MBh 3.297–298)
summary: At the poisoned lake the yakṣa — the god Dharma — questions Yudhiṣṭhira and restores his brothers (MBh (CE) 3.297–298).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viduranīti / Prajāgara (MBh 5.33–40)
summary: Vidura’s night-long counsel on policy and conduct to the sleepless Dhṛtarāṣṭra (MBh (CE) 5.33–40).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Sanatsujātīya (MBh 5.42–45)
summary: The sage Sanatsujāta’s teaching to Dhṛtarāṣṭra on death and liberation (MBh (CE) 5.42–45).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhagavadyāna: Kṛṣṇa’s embassy (MBh 5.70–137)
summary: Kṛṣṇa’s peace mission to Hāstinapura, including his theophany when the Kauravas plan to seize him (5.129) (MBh (CE) 5.70–137).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Rājadharma (MBh 12.1–128)
summary: Bhīṣma’s instruction on the duties of kings (MBh (CE) 12.1–128).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Āpaddharma (MBh 12.129–167)
summary: Bhīṣma’s instruction on conduct in emergencies (MBh (CE) 12.129–167).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Mokṣadharma (MBh 12.168–353)
summary: Bhīṣma’s instruction on liberation, incorporating Sāṃkhya, Yoga and Nārāyaṇa theology (MBh (CE) 12.168–353).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Nārāyaṇīya (MBh 12.321–339)
summary: The Nārāyaṇīya section of the Mokṣadharma, an early Pāñcarātra-related account of Nārāyaṇa worship, Nārada’s visit to Śvetadvīpa and the vyūha doctrine (MBh (CE) 12.321–339).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇusahasranāma (MBh 13.135)
summary: The thousand names of Viṣṇu, taught by Bhīṣma to Yudhiṣṭhira (MBh (CE) 13.135).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Anugītā (MBh 14.16–50)
summary: After the war Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa to repeat the Gītā; Kṛṣṇa says he cannot and teaches anew (MBh (CE) 14.16–50).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Āstīkaparvan (MBh 1.13–53)
summary: The story of Jaratkāru, Āstīka and Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice, which forms the outer frame of Vaiśampāyana’s recitation (MBh (CE) 1.13–53).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Saṃkṣepa Rāmāyaṇa: Nārada’s summary (VR 1.1)
summary: The opening sarga in which Vālmīki asks Nārada who is the most virtuous man living and Nārada summarises Rāma’s story (VR (CE) 1.1).

type:LABEL: passage
name: The krauñca episode and the first śloka (VR 1.2)
summary: Vālmīki’s grief at a hunter killing one of a pair of krauñca birds turns into the first śloka, “mā niṣāda …” (VR (CE) 1.2.14).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Brahmā’s hymn to Rāma (VR 6.105)
summary: After Sītā’s fire ordeal Brahmā tells Rāma that he is Nārāyaṇa and that Sītā is Lakṣmī (VR (CE) 6.105.12, 25).

type:LABEL: character
name: Rāma
summary: Prince of Ayodhyā, eldest son of Daśaratha and Kausalyā and hero of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; exiled for fourteen years, he recovers his wife Sītā from Rāvaṇa and rules as the model righteous king. Vaiṣṇava tradition regards him as an avatāra of Viṣṇu.
earliest_material: second half of the 5th century CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Sītā
summary: Daughter of King Janaka of Videha — found in a ploughed furrow — and wife of Rāma; abducted by Rāvaṇa, she is vindicated by an ordeal of fire but later banished, and finally returns into the earth. Brahmā’s hymn in the Yuddhakāṇḍa identifies her with Lakṣmī.
earliest_material: second half of the 5th century CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Lakṣmaṇa
summary: Son of Daśaratha and Sumitrā, twin of Śatrughna, who accompanies Rāma and Sītā into exile and fights beside Rāma; he mutilates Śūrpaṇakhā, kills Indrajit, and in the Uttarakāṇḍa leaves Sītā in the forest at Rāma’s command.
earliest_material: second half of the 5th century CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Bharata (brother of Rāma)
summary: Son of Daśaratha and Kaikeyī, for whom Kaikeyī demands the throne; he refuses it, seeks Rāma in the forest, and rules from Nandigrāma as regent with Rāma’s sandals on the throne.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śatrughna
summary: Youngest son of Daśaratha, Lakṣmaṇa’s twin by Sumitrā and companion of Bharata; in the Uttarakāṇḍa he kills the demon Lavaṇa and founds Madhurā (Mathurā).

type:LABEL: character
name: Hanumān
summary: Vānara minister of Sugrīva, son of the wind god Vāyu and Añjanā (wife of the vānara Kesarin), who leaps the ocean to find Sītā in Laṅkā and becomes Rāma’s foremost devotee and messenger.

type:LABEL: character
name: Rāvaṇa
summary: Ten-headed rākṣasa king of Laṅkā, son of the sage Viśravas and the rākṣasī Kaikasī, made invulnerable to gods and demons by Brahmā’s boon; he abducts Sītā and is killed by Rāma.
earliest_material: second half of the 5th century CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Vibhīṣaṇa
summary: Righteous younger brother of Rāvaṇa who urges him to return Sītā, defects to Rāma, and is installed as king of Laṅkā after the war.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sugrīva
summary: Vānara prince of Kiṣkindhā, son of the Sun, exiled by his brother Vālin; he allies with Rāma, who kills Vālin and restores him, and in return sends the vānara armies in search of Sītā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vālin
summary: Vānara king of Kiṣkindhā, son of Indra and elder brother of Sugrīva, whom he had driven out; he is killed by Rāma’s arrow during his duel with Sugrīva and is succeeded by his son Aṅgada as heir.
earliest_material: second half of the 5th century CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Jaṭāyu
summary: King of the vultures and friend of Daśaratha, who tries to stop Rāvaṇa carrying off Sītā, is mortally wounded, and tells Rāma what happened before dying.

type:LABEL: character
name: Daśaratha
summary: Ikṣvāku king of Ayodhyā, father of Rāma, Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna; bound by two boons promised to Kaikeyī, he exiles Rāma and dies of grief.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kaikeyī
summary: Princess of Kekaya, wife of Daśaratha and mother of Bharata, who, prompted by the servant Mantharā, claims her two boons: Bharata’s consecration and Rāma’s fourteen-year exile.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kausalyā
summary: Chief queen of Daśaratha and mother of Rāma.

type:LABEL: character
name: Janaka (father of Sītā)
summary: King of Videha at Mithilā (Sīradhvaja Janaka in the Rāmāyaṇa) who found Sītā in a furrow while ploughing and set the stringing of Śiva’s bow as the condition for her marriage.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vālmīki
summary: Sage to whom the Rāmāyaṇa is attributed: he hears the story from Nārada, invents the śloka metre in grief at a krauñca bird’s death, composes the poem and teaches it to Rāma’s sons Lava and Kuśa, at whose hermitage Sītā lives after her banishment.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kumbhakarṇa
summary: Gigantic brother of Rāvaṇa who sleeps for long periods; roused for the war, he devastates the vānara army before Rāma kills him.

type:LABEL: character
name: Indrajit
summary: Son of Rāvaṇa and Mandodarī, born as Meghanāda and called Indrajit (“conqueror of Indra”) after capturing Indra; a master of illusion who twice binds Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with serpent-arrows and is finally killed by Lakṣmaṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śūrpaṇakhā
summary: Sister of Rāvaṇa who propositions Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa in the Pañcavaṭī forest; Lakṣmaṇa cuts off her nose and ears, provoking the war with Khara and then Rāvaṇa’s abduction of Sītā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ahalyā
summary: Wife of the sage Gautama, seduced by Indra and cursed by her husband to do penance unseen in the hermitage until Rāma’s arrival restores her.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śabarī
summary: Female ascetic of the Śabara community living at the Pampā lake, who receives Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa and then ascends to heaven.

type:LABEL: character
name: Lava
summary: One of the twin sons of Rāma and Sītā (the younger), born in Vālmīki’s hermitage, named by Vālmīki and taught by him to sing the Rāmāyaṇa, which they perform before Rāma.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kuśa
summary: One of the twin sons of Rāma and Sītā (the elder), born in Vālmīki’s hermitage, named by Vālmīki and taught by him to sing the Rāmāyaṇa, which they perform before Rāma.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sumitrā
summary: Wife of Daśaratha and mother of the twins Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ūrmilā
summary: Daughter of Janaka and younger sister of Sītā, married to Lakṣmaṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Māṇḍavī
summary: Daughter of Kuśadhvaja (Janaka’s brother) married to Bharata.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śrutakīrti
summary: Daughter of Kuśadhvaja married to Śatrughna.

type:LABEL: character
name: Mandodarī
summary: Chief queen of Rāvaṇa, daughter of the dānava architect Maya and the apsaras Hemā, and mother of Indrajit.

type:LABEL: character
name: Aṅgada
summary: Son of Vālin and Tārā, made heir-apparent of Kiṣkindhā under Sugrīva; leads the southern search party and serves as Rāma’s envoy to Rāvaṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Tārā
summary: Wife of Vālin and mother of Aṅgada, whose lament over Vālin and counsel to Sugrīva are prominent in the Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Mantharā
summary: Hunchbacked servant of Kaikeyī who persuades her to claim her boons; in the Mahābhārata’s Rāmopākhyāna she is the gandharvī Dundubhī born on earth at Brahmā’s command.
earliest_textual: within the epic’s growth, c. 3rd century BCE – 3rd century CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Mārīca
summary: Rākṣasa, son of Tāṭakā, who at Rāvaṇa’s command takes the form of a golden deer to lure Rāma away from Sītā and is killed by him.

type:LABEL: character
name: Tāṭakā
summary: Yakṣī turned demoness who ravages the forest near the Gaṅgā; Rāma kills her at Viśvāmitra’s instruction.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kabandha
summary: Headless monster of the forest, freed from a curse when Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa cut off his arms and cremate him; he directs them to Sugrīva.

type:LABEL: character
name: Saṃpāti
summary: Elder brother of Jaṭāyu, a vulture with burnt wings who tells the searching vānaras that Sītā is in Laṅkā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Trijaṭā
summary: Rākṣasī guard of Sītā in the aśoka grove who dreams of Rāvaṇa’s ruin and befriends Sītā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kesarin
summary: Vānara chief, husband of Añjanā, in whose “field” Hanumān is born; Hanumān is thus his kṣetraja son while being Vāyu’s own son.

type:LABEL: character
name: Añjanā
summary: Apsaras Puñjikasthalā living as a vānarī, wife of Kesarin and mother of Hanumān by the wind god.

type:LABEL: character
name: Viśravas
summary: Sage, son of Pulastya, father of Kubera (Vaiśravaṇa) and, by Kaikasī, of Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā and Vibhīṣaṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kaikasī
summary: Daughter of the rākṣasa Sumālin, who at her father’s bidding chooses the sage Viśravas and becomes the mother of Rāvaṇa and his siblings.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kubera (Vaiśravaṇa)
summary: Son of Viśravas, lord of wealth and guardian of a direction, first ruler of Laṅkā, who is driven out by his half-brother Rāvaṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vedavatī
summary: Daughter of the sage Kuśadhvaja (son of Bṛhaspati) who, molested by Rāvaṇa, enters the fire vowing to be reborn for his destruction; the Uttarakāṇḍa identifies her with Sītā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śambūka
summary: Śūdra ascetic performing austerities, whom Rāma beheads in the Uttarakāṇḍa after a brahmin’s son dies prematurely; the episode is a focus of modern criticism.

type:LABEL: character
name: Gautama (husband of Ahalyā)
summary: Sage of Mithilā’s forest whose wife Ahalyā is seduced by Indra; he curses both and later receives her back purified.

type:LABEL: character
name: Guha
summary: Niṣāda chief of Śṛṅgaverapura on the Gaṅgā, Rāma’s friend, who hosts the exiles and ferries them across the river.

type:LABEL: character
name: Jāmbavān
summary: King of the bears (ṛkṣas) in Rāma’s army, eldest counsellor of the search party, who reminds Hanumān of his parentage and powers before the leap.

type:LABEL: character
name: Nala (vānara engineer)
summary: Vānara son of Viśvakarman who builds the causeway (setu) across the ocean to Laṅkā — distinct from King Nala of Niṣadha (char:nala).

type:LABEL: character
name: Ṛśyaśṛṅga
summary: Sage, son of Vibhāṇḍaka, brought to Daśaratha’s court on Sumantra’s advice to perform the sacrifice that produces the four princes; married to Śāntā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bharadvāja
summary: Sage whose hermitage at Prayāga hosts Rāma and later Bharata in the Rāmāyaṇa; in the Mahābhārata he is the father of Droṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kṛṣṇa
summary: Vṛṣṇi prince, son of Vasudeva and Devakī, cousin and ally of the Pāṇḍavas, Arjuna’s charioteer and the teacher of the Bhagavad Gītā; the Mahābhārata calls him a portion of Nārāyaṇa, the Harivaṃśa and Purāṇas narrate his cowherd childhood, and Vaiṣṇava traditions worship him as Viṣṇu’s avatāra or, for some schools, the supreme Lord himself.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vyāsa
summary: Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, the island-born son of the sage Parāśara and Satyavatī, credited with arranging the Vedas and composing the Mahābhārata; he fathers Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu and Vidura by niyoga and repeatedly intervenes in the story he authors.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bhīṣma
summary: Devavrata, son of King Śantanu and the river goddess Gaṅgā, who renounces the throne and marriage so that his father may marry Satyavatī; grand-uncle of both Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas, he commands the Kaurava army for ten days, falls to Arjuna and Śikhaṇḍin, and instructs Yudhiṣṭhira from his bed of arrows.

type:LABEL: character
name: Yudhiṣṭhira
summary: Eldest Pāṇḍava, son of Kuntī by the god Dharma and legal son of Pāṇḍu; the “Dharma king” who loses his kingdom, brothers and wife at dice, endures exile, wins the war and rules, and is tested to the end by Dharma himself.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bhīma
summary: Second Pāṇḍava, son of Kuntī by the wind god Vāyu, of enormous strength and appetite; he kills Hiḍimba, Baka, Jarāsandha, Kīcaka, Duḥśāsana and the Kaurava brothers, and breaks Duryodhana’s thighs.

type:LABEL: character
name: Arjuna
summary: Third Pāṇḍava, son of Kuntī by Indra, the supreme archer who wins Draupadī, marries Ulūpī, Citrāṅgadā and Subhadrā, obtains divine weapons from Śiva and Indra, and receives the Bhagavad Gītā from Kṛṣṇa, his charioteer and friend.
earliest_textual: c. 5th – mid-4th c. BCE (not later than the early-to-mid 4th c. BCE)

type:LABEL: character
name: Nakula
summary: One of the twin Pāṇḍavas (with Sahadeva), sons of Mādrī by the Aśvins and legal sons of Pāṇḍu.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sahadeva
summary: One of the twin Pāṇḍavas (with Nakula), sons of Mādrī by the Aśvins and legal sons of Pāṇḍu.

type:LABEL: character
name: Draupadī
summary: Daughter of King Drupada, born from the sacrificial altar, won by Arjuna at her svayaṃvara and married to all five Pāṇḍavas; staked and dragged into the assembly hall at the dice game, her question whether Yudhiṣṭhira could stake her after losing himself and her humiliation drive the epic’s conflict.

type:LABEL: character
name: Karṇa
summary: Son of Kuntī by the Sun god, born before her marriage with innate armour and earrings, set adrift and raised by the charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Rādhā; made king of Aṅga by Duryodhana, he remains loyal to the Kauravas even after learning he is the eldest Pāṇḍava, and is killed by Arjuna.

type:LABEL: character
name: Duryodhana
summary: Eldest of the hundred sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī, rival of the Pāṇḍavas, who contrives the house of lac and the dice game, refuses any settlement and dies after Bhīma breaks his thighs.

type:LABEL: character
name: Duḥśāsana
summary: Second Kaurava, who drags Draupadī into the assembly hall and pulls at her garment; Bhīma kills him in battle and drinks his blood, fulfilling a vow.

type:LABEL: character
name: Droṇa
summary: Brahmin teacher of arms to the Kuru princes, son of the sage Bharadvāja born from a vessel (droṇa), who demands Ekalavya’s thumb, takes half of Drupada’s kingdom, commands the Kaurava army after Bhīṣma, and is killed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna after being told that “Aśvatthāman” is dead.

type:LABEL: character
name: Aśvatthāman
summary: Son of Droṇa and Kṛpī, born of the combined portions of Mahādeva, Antaka, Kāma and Krodha; after the war he massacres the sleeping Pāñcālas and Draupadī’s sons and is cursed by Kṛṣṇa to wander for three thousand years.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vidura
summary: Son of Vyāsa by a servant woman of Ambikā, wise counsellor of the Kurus and uncle of the Pāṇḍavas, an incarnation of Dharma owing to the sage Māṇḍavya’s curse.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kuntī
summary: Pṛthā, daughter of the Yādava Śūra and sister of Vasudeva, given in adoption to King Kuntibhoja; with Durvāsas’s mantra she bears Karṇa by the Sun before marriage and, as Pāṇḍu’s wife, Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma and Arjuna by Dharma, Vāyu and Indra.

type:LABEL: character
name: Gāndhārī
summary: Princess of Gandhāra, daughter of Subala and sister of Śakuni, who blindfolds herself on marrying the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra, bears the hundred Kauravas and a daughter, and after the war curses Kṛṣṇa with the destruction of his clan.

type:LABEL: character
name: Dhṛtarāṣṭra
summary: Blind king of the Kurus, son of Vyāsa and Ambikā by niyoga, husband of Gāndhārī and father of the hundred Kauravas; his indulgence of Duryodhana allows the dice game and the war, which Sañjaya narrates to him.

type:LABEL: character
name: Pāṇḍu
summary: King of the Kurus, son of Vyāsa and Ambālikā by niyoga, cursed to die if he approaches a woman; he authorises Kuntī and Mādrī to bear sons by gods and is the legal father of the five Pāṇḍavas.

type:LABEL: character
name: Mādrī
summary: Princess of Madra, second wife of Pāṇḍu, who bears the twins Nakula and Sahadeva by the Aśvins and joins Pāṇḍu on his funeral pyre.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śakuni
summary: Prince of Gandhāra, son of Subala and brother of Gāndhārī, the expert dicer who wins for Duryodhana against Yudhiṣṭhira; an incarnation of the Dvāpara age.

type:LABEL: character
name: Balarāma
summary: Elder brother of Kṛṣṇa, son of Vasudeva and Rohiṇī, wielder of the plough and club, teacher of Duryodhana and Bhīma in mace fighting, who stays neutral in the war; the Mahābhārata calls him a portion of the serpent Śeṣa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Abhimanyu
summary: Son of Arjuna and Subhadrā, married to Uttarā, who breaks into Droṇa’s circular array on the thirteenth day and is killed after being surrounded; father of the posthumously born Parīkṣit.

type:LABEL: character
name: Subhadrā
summary: Sister of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, abducted with Kṛṣṇa’s approval by Arjuna and married to him; mother of Abhimanyu.
earliest_material: begun under Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga, early–mid 12th c.; completion given as 1161 in Wikipedia’s infobox

type:LABEL: character
name: Śantanu
summary: Kuru king, husband of Gaṅgā (mother of Bhīṣma) and then of Satyavatī (mother of Citrāṅgada and Vicitravīrya).

type:LABEL: character
name: Satyavatī
summary: Fisherman’s daughter (born from a fish, raised by the chief of fishermen) who bears Vyāsa to Parāśara and then marries Śantanu on condition that her son inherit, prompting Bhīṣma’s vow; matriarch of the Kuru line.

type:LABEL: character
name: Drupada
summary: King of Pañcāla, Droṇa’s estranged boyhood friend, who sacrifices for a son to kill Droṇa and receives Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Draupadī from the fire; father also of Śikhaṇḍin.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śikhaṇḍin
summary: Child of Drupada born female (Śikhaṇḍinī), the reborn Ambā, who becomes male through an exchange with the yakṣa Sthūṇa; Bhīṣma refuses to fight him, and Arjuna shoots Bhīṣma from behind him.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ekalavya
summary: Niṣāda prince, son of Hiraṇyadhanus, who learns archery before a clay image of Droṇa after being refused as a pupil; when his skill surpasses Arjuna’s, Droṇa demands his right thumb as teacher’s fee, and Ekalavya gives it.

type:LABEL: character
name: Jarāsandha
summary: King of Magadha, born in two halves joined by the demoness Jarā, enemy of Kṛṣṇa and the Yādavas, killed by Bhīma in a wrestling match before the rājasūya.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śiśupāla
summary: King of Cedi and cousin of Kṛṣṇa who objects to Kṛṣṇa’s receiving the first honour at Yudhiṣṭhira’s rājasūya and is beheaded by Kṛṣṇa’s discus.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sañjaya
summary: Charioteer and minister of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, given divine sight by Vyāsa to narrate the battle — including the Bhagavad Gītā — to the blind king.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ghaṭotkaca
summary: Son of Bhīma and the rākṣasī Hiḍimbā, who fights for the Pāṇḍavas and is killed at night by Karṇa with the spear Indra had given him — the weapon Karṇa had reserved for Arjuna.

type:LABEL: character
name: Parīkṣit
summary: Son of Abhimanyu and Uttarā, born still-born after Aśvatthāman’s weapon and revived by Kṛṣṇa; he succeeds Yudhiṣṭhira and dies of the bite of the serpent Takṣaka, which prompts his son Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice.

type:LABEL: character
name: Janamejaya
summary: Kuru king, son of Parīkṣit, at whose snake sacrifice Vaiśampāyana recites the Mahābhārata; his questions punctuate the narrative.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: character
name: Vaiśampāyana
summary: Disciple of Vyāsa who, at his teacher’s instruction, recites the Mahābhārata to King Janamejaya during the snake sacrifice.

type:LABEL: character
name: Devakī
summary: Wife of Vasudeva and mother of Kṛṣṇa, whose earlier children are killed by her cousin Kaṃsa; Kṛṣṇa is born to her in captivity and exchanged with Yaśodā’s daughter.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vasudeva (father of Kṛṣṇa)
summary: Yādava (Vṛṣṇi) noble, son of Śūra, brother of Kuntī and husband of Devakī and Rohiṇī; father of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma. Kept distinct from the deity Vāsudeva.

type:LABEL: character
name: Nanda
summary: Chief of the cowherds of Vraja who, with his wife Yaśodā, fosters Kṛṣṇa (and Balarāma) after Vasudeva brings the infant from Mathurā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Yaśodā
summary: Wife of Nanda and foster mother of Kṛṣṇa; she gives birth to a daughter at the same time as Devakī bears Kṛṣṇa, and the children are exchanged.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kaṃsa
summary: King of Mathurā, son of Ugrasena and cousin of Devakī, who kills her children fearing a prophecy and is killed by Kṛṣṇa in the wrestling arena.

type:LABEL: character
name: Rukmiṇī
summary: Princess of Vidarbha, daughter of Bhīṣmaka, abducted by Kṛṣṇa before her intended marriage to Śiśupāla; Kṛṣṇa’s chief queen and mother of Pradyumna. Later tradition identifies her with Lakṣmī.

type:LABEL: character
name: Pradyumna
summary: Son of Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī, carried off as an infant by the demon Śambara and later kills him; the Mahābhārata calls him an incarnation of Sanatkumāra.

type:LABEL: character
name: Nala
summary: King of Niṣadha, son of Vīrasena, whose love for Damayantī, loss of his kingdom at dice under the influence of Kali, and eventual restoration form the Nalopākhyāna (MBh 3.50–78) — distinct from the vānara engineer Nala (char:nala-vanara).

type:LABEL: character
name: Damayantī
summary: Princess of Vidarbha who chooses Nala over the gods at her svayaṃvara, is abandoned by him in the forest, and through her resourcefulness recovers him.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sāvitrī
summary: Daughter of King Aśvapati of Madra who chooses the exiled prince Satyavān knowing he will die within a year, follows Yama when he takes Satyavān’s life, and wins back her husband by her eloquence and boons.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śakuntalā
summary: Daughter of the sage Viśvāmitra and the apsaras Menakā, raised by the sage Kaṇva, who marries King Duḥṣanta by gāndharva rite and, when he later disowns her, compels his recognition of their son Bharata.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: character
name: Rohiṇī (wife of Vasudeva)
summary: Wife of Vasudeva and mother of Balarāma; in Vyāsa’s account Nārāyaṇa’s white hair enters her womb, while in the Harivaṃśa Devakī’s seventh embryo is transferred to her.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ambā
summary: Eldest princess of Kāśī, abducted by Bhīṣma for Vicitravīrya, rejected by her chosen suitor Śālva and by Bhīṣma; she does austerities for Bhīṣma’s death and is reborn as Śikhaṇḍinī, daughter of Drupada.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ambikā
summary: Second princess of Kāśī, wife of Vicitravīrya, who by niyoga with Vyāsa bears the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ambālikā
summary: Youngest princess of Kāśī, wife of Vicitravīrya, who by niyoga with Vyāsa bears Pāṇḍu.

type:LABEL: character
name: Parāśara
summary: Sage, grandson of Vasiṣṭha, who fathers Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa on Satyavatī during a pilgrimage and restores her virginity.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vicitravīrya
summary: Younger son of Śantanu and Satyavatī, married to Ambikā and Ambālikā, who dies childless, occasioning the niyoga with Vyāsa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Citrāṅgada (son of Śantanu)
summary: Elder son of Śantanu and Satyavatī, installed by Bhīṣma and killed young by a gandharva of the same name — distinct from Citrāṅgadā of Maṇipūra.

type:LABEL: character
name: Uttarā
summary: Daughter of King Virāṭa of Matsya, taught dance by the disguised Arjuna, whom Arjuna accepts as daughter-in-law for Abhimanyu; mother of Parīkṣit.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ulūpī
summary: Nāga princess who takes Arjuna beneath the Gaṅgā during his exile and becomes his wife; mother of Irāvat.

type:LABEL: character
name: Citrāṅgadā (of Maṇipūra)
summary: Daughter of King Citravāhana of Maṇipūra, married to Arjuna on condition that their son continue her father’s line; mother of Babhruvāhana.

type:LABEL: character
name: Babhruvāhana
summary: Son of Arjuna and Citrāṅgadā, king of Maṇipūra, who fights and kills his father during the horse-sacrifice campaign; Arjuna is revived by Ulūpī’s jewel.

type:LABEL: character
name: Irāvat
summary: Son of Arjuna and the nāga Ulūpī, killed in the war; in South Indian traditions worshipped as Aravāṉ.

type:LABEL: character
name: Adhiratha
summary: Charioteer (sūta) of the Kurus, husband of Rādhā, who finds the infant Karṇa in a basket on the river and raises him as his son.

type:LABEL: character
name: Rādhā (foster mother of Karṇa)
summary: Wife of the charioteer Adhiratha, childless until she takes in the infant Karṇa found floating in a basket; Karṇa is called Rādheya after her. Distinct from Rādhā, Kṛṣṇa’s beloved (char:radha).

type:LABEL: character
name: Hiḍimbā
summary: Rākṣasī of the forest who falls in love with Bhīma after he kills her brother Hiḍimba; with Kuntī’s leave she lives with him and bears Ghaṭotkaca.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kṛpa
summary: Brahmin teacher of arms to the Kuru princes before Droṇa, son of the sage Śaradvat, adopted with his twin sister Kṛpī by Śantanu; one of the three Kaurava survivors.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kṛpī
summary: Twin sister of Kṛpa, wife of Droṇa and mother of Aśvatthāman.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śalya
summary: King of Madra and brother of Mādrī, maternal uncle of Nakula and Sahadeva, tricked by Duryodhana into fighting for the Kauravas; Karṇa’s charioteer and the last Kaurava commander, killed by Yudhiṣṭhira.

type:LABEL: character
name: Virāṭa
summary: King of the Matsyas at whose court the Pāṇḍavas spend the thirteenth year of exile in disguise; father of Uttarā and Uttara, ally of the Pāṇḍavas in the war.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kīcaka
summary: Commander of Virāṭa’s army and brother of Queen Sudeṣṇā, who harasses the disguised Draupadī and is killed at night by Bhīma.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bhīṣmaka
summary: King of Vidarbha (Kuṇḍina), father of Rukmiṇī and Rukmin, a vassal-ally of Jarāsandha.

type:LABEL: character
name: Satyabhāmā
summary: Beloved wife of Kṛṣṇa, daughter of Satrājit, who in the Āraṇyakaparvan asks Draupadī how she keeps five husbands devoted.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ugrasena
summary: King of the Vṛṣṇis/Andhakas at Mathurā, father of Kaṃsa, deposed by his son and restored by Kṛṣṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sāmba
summary: Son of Kṛṣṇa and Jāmbavatī whom the Yādava youths dress as a pregnant woman to mock visiting sages; the sages’ curse that he will bear an iron club brings about the Yādavas’ destruction.

type:LABEL: character
name: Jarā (the hunter)
summary: Hunter whose arrow, mistaking Kṛṣṇa’s foot for a deer, strikes the sole of Kṛṣṇa’s foot as he lies in yoga, causing his death.

type:LABEL: character
name: Dhṛṣṭadyumna
summary: Son of Drupada born from the sacrificial fire with Draupadī, destined to kill Droṇa; commander of the Pāṇḍava army, he beheads Droṇa and is killed in his sleep by Aśvatthāman.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sātyaki
summary: Vṛṣṇi warrior, pupil of Arjuna and loyal ally of the Pāṇḍavas; an incarnation of the Maruts.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kṛtavarman
summary: Vṛṣṇi/Bhoja warrior who fights for the Kauravas, one of the three survivors who join Aśvatthāman’s night raid.

type:LABEL: character
name: Jayadratha
summary: King of the Sindhus, husband of Duḥśalā, who tries to abduct Draupadī during the exile and is killed by Arjuna on the fourteenth day.

type:LABEL: character
name: Duḥśalā
summary: The only daughter of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī, married to Jayadratha.

type:LABEL: character
name: Yuyutsu
summary: Son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra by a vaiśya woman, who crosses over to the Pāṇḍavas before the battle and survives it.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kuntibhoja
summary: Childless king, friend of Śūra, who receives Śūra’s first daughter Pṛthā in adoption; she is therefore called Kuntī.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śūra (Yādava)
summary: Yādava chief, father of Vasudeva and of Pṛthā (Kuntī), whom he gives in adoption to Kuntibhoja.

type:LABEL: character
name: Subala
summary: King of Gandhāra, father of Gāndhārī and Śakuni.

type:LABEL: character
name: Duḥṣanta
summary: Paurava king who meets Śakuntalā while hunting, marries her by gāndharva rite and later acknowledges their son Bharata.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bharata (son of Śakuntalā)
summary: Son of Duḥṣanta and Śakuntalā, universal sovereign from whom the Bhārata lineage and the epic take their name — distinct from Rāma’s brother Bharata.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kaṇva
summary: Sage of the Kāśyapa line who raises Śakuntalā in his hermitage.

type:LABEL: character
name: Menakā
summary: Apsaras sent by Indra to distract Viśvāmitra; mother of Śakuntalā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Satyavān
summary: Son of the blind, exiled king Dyumatsena, chosen by Sāvitrī as husband though fated to die within a year.

type:LABEL: character
name: Aśvapati
summary: King of Madra, father of Sāvitrī, who obtains her by worshipping the goddess Sāvitrī.

type:LABEL: character
name: Dyumatsena
summary: Exiled, later blind king of the Śālvas, father of Satyavān, whose sight and kingdom are restored by Sāvitrī’s boons.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bṛhadaśva
summary: Sage who visits the exiled Pāṇḍavas and tells Yudhiṣṭhira the story of Nala and Damayantī.

type:LABEL: character
name: Māṇḍavya
summary: Sage (Aṇī-Māṇḍavya) wrongly impaled as a thief, who curses Dharma for punishing a childhood fault too severely; Dharma is therefore born as Vidura.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ugraśravas
summary: Bard (sūta, paurāṇika), son of Lomaharṣaṇa, who comes to Śaunaka’s twelve-year sacrifice in the Naimiṣa forest and recites the Mahābhārata as he heard it from Vaiśampāyana.

type:LABEL: character
name: Lomaharṣaṇa
summary: Bard (sūta), father of Ugraśravas, regarded in Purāṇic tradition as a disciple of Vyāsa who received the Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śaunaka
summary: Kulapati (head of a family of sages) of the Naimiṣa forest, at whose twelve-year sacrifice Ugraśravas recites the Mahābhārata.

type:LABEL: character
name: Takṣaka
summary: Serpent king whose bite kills Parīkṣit, provoking Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice.

type:LABEL: character
name: Āstīka
summary: Son of the sage Jaratkāru and the nāga woman Jaratkāru who halts Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice and saves Takṣaka.

type:LABEL: character
name: Maya (dānava architect)
summary: Dānava architect who builds the Pāṇḍavas’ assembly hall in gratitude for being spared in the Khāṇḍava fire; in the Rāmāyaṇa’s Uttarakāṇḍa he is the father of Mandodarī.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kāliya
summary: Many-headed serpent poisoning a pool of the Yamunā in Vraja, subdued by the boy Kṛṣṇa, who dances on his heads and banishes him to the ocean.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Dharma (the god)
summary: Dharma personified as a god in the Mahābhārata: the divine father of Yudhiṣṭhira, born as Vidura through Māṇḍavya’s curse, the yakṣa who questions Yudhiṣṭhira at the lake and the dog who follows him to heaven. The epic at times identifies him with Yama.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Dharma
summary: The central normative concept of the epics — right order, duty, law and virtue — whose subtlety (sūkṣmatā) the Mahābhārata repeatedly stresses, notably in Draupadī’s question, Yudhiṣṭhira’s dilemmas and Bhīṣma’s teachings.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Rāma’s exile
summary: Rāma’s fourteen-year banishment to the forest with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, imposed through Kaikeyī’s boons and accepted by Rāma to keep his father’s word.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The breaking of Śiva’s bow and Sītā’s marriage
summary: At Mithilā Rāma lifts and breaks the great bow of Śiva that Janaka had set as the test for Sītā’s hand; the four brothers are then married to Sītā, Ūrmilā, Māṇḍavī and Śrutakīrti.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The abduction of Sītā
summary: Rāvaṇa, having sent Mārīca as a golden deer to draw Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa away, carries Sītā off from the Pañcavaṭī hermitage through the sky to Laṅkā, mortally wounding Jaṭāyu who tries to stop him.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Hanumān’s leap and search in Laṅkā
summary: Hanumān leaps the ocean from the southern shore, searches Laṅkā by night, finds Sītā in the aśoka grove, gives her Rāma’s ring, is captured and has his tail set on fire, and burns the city before returning.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The building of the bridge to Laṅkā
summary: At the Ocean’s suggestion the vānara Nala, son of Viśvakarman, directs the vānaras in building a causeway across the sea to Laṅkā.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The war in Laṅkā and the death of Rāvaṇa
summary: The war between Rāma’s vānara army and Rāvaṇa’s rākṣasas, culminating in the deaths of Kumbhakarṇa, Indrajit and Rāvaṇa, whom Rāma kills with the Brahmā weapon given by Agastya.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Sītā’s ordeal by fire
summary: After Rāvaṇa’s death Rāma publicly refuses Sītā; she has Lakṣmaṇa build a pyre and enters the fire calling Agni to witness her fidelity; Agni returns her unharmed and the gods proclaim Rāma’s divinity.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The banishment of Sītā and her return to the earth
summary: Hearing that his subjects gossip about Sītā’s stay in Rāvaṇa’s house, Rāma has Lakṣmaṇa abandon the pregnant Sītā near Vālmīki’s hermitage; years later, asked to prove her purity again at the horse sacrifice, she calls upon the Earth, who receives her.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The krauñca bird and the first śloka
summary: Vālmīki sees a hunter kill one of a pair of mating krauñca birds; his grief (śoka) issues spontaneously as the first verse (śloka), and Brahmā bids him compose Rāma’s story in that metre.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The sacrifice for sons and the birth of the four princes
summary: Daśaratha’s sacrifice performed by Ṛśyaśṛṅga, the gods’ request that Viṣṇu be born as a man to kill Rāvaṇa, and the births of Rāma, Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna as portions of Viṣṇu.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Rāma kills Tāṭakā
summary: On Viśvāmitra’s instruction the young Rāma kills the demoness Tāṭakā, his first deed against the rākṣasas.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The release of Ahalyā
summary: Passing Gautama’s hermitage, Rāma ends the curse on Ahalyā, who had been seduced by Indra.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Rāma and Paraśurāma
summary: On the way back from Mithilā, Jāmadagnya Rāma (Paraśurāma) challenges Dāśarathi Rāma to string Viṣṇu’s bow; Rāma does so and Paraśurāma yields.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kaikeyī’s two boons
summary: Incited by Mantharā, Kaikeyī reminds Daśaratha of the two boons he granted when she saved him in battle and demands Bharata’s consecration and Rāma’s exile.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The death of Daśaratha
summary: Grieving for Rāma, Daśaratha recalls how he once killed an ascetic’s son and was cursed to die lamenting a son, and dies in the night.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Bharata and the sandals
summary: Bharata seeks Rāma at Citrakūṭa and begs him to return; Rāma refuses, and Bharata takes his gold-adorned sandals to rule in his name.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The mutilation of Śūrpaṇakhā
summary: Rāvaṇa’s sister Śūrpaṇakhā propositions Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa at Pañcavaṭī and attacks Sītā; Lakṣmaṇa cuts off her nose and ears, setting the war with the rākṣasas in motion.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The golden deer
summary: At Rāvaṇa’s command Mārīca takes the form of a jewelled golden deer near the hermitage; Sītā asks Rāma to catch it, and Mārīca, dying, cries out in Rāma’s voice to draw Lakṣmaṇa away.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Jaṭāyu’s fight with Rāvaṇa
summary: The vulture king Jaṭāyu attacks Rāvaṇa to free Sītā, is mortally wounded, and lives long enough to tell Rāma what happened.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The alliance of Rāma and Sugrīva
summary: Hanumān brings Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa to Sugrīva on Ṛśyamūka; they swear friendship before fire, Rāma promising to kill Vālin and Sugrīva to search for Sītā.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The killing of Vālin
summary: During Sugrīva’s second duel with Vālin, Rāma shoots Vālin from concealment; the dying Vālin reproaches him and Rāma defends the act.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Vibhīṣaṇa joins Rāma
summary: Rebuked by Rāvaṇa for urging Sītā’s return, Vibhīṣaṇa flies to Rāma’s camp; despite Sugrīva’s suspicion Rāma accepts him and promises him Laṅkā.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The death of Kumbhakarṇa
summary: Roused from sleep for the war, Kumbhakarṇa devastates the vānaras until he is killed — by Rāma in Vālmīki’s Yuddhakāṇḍa, by Lakṣmaṇa with the Brahmā weapon in the Mahābhārata’s Rāmopākhyāna.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The death of Indrajit
summary: Lakṣmaṇa kills Rāvaṇa’s son Indrajit after a long duel.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The return to Ayodhyā and Rāma’s consecration
summary: Rāma returns to Ayodhyā with Sītā and is consecrated king, as the gods consecrated Indra.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Rāvaṇa’s boon from Brahmā
summary: Through austerities Rāvaṇa obtains from Brahmā invulnerability to gods, demons, nāgas, yakṣas and other beings — but not to humans; Vibhīṣaṇa asks only for steadfastness in dharma.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Vedavatī’s curse
summary: The ascetic Vedavatī, molested by Rāvaṇa, enters the fire vowing to be reborn for his destruction; the Uttarakāṇḍa says she is reborn as Sītā.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Hanumān’s childhood leap at the sun
summary: The infant Hanumān leaps at the rising sun thinking it a fruit, is struck down by Indra’s thunderbolt; the wind god withdraws in grief until the gods restore the child and grant him boons.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The killing of Śambūka
summary: When a brahmin’s son dies prematurely, Rāma finds the śūdra Śambūka performing austerities and beheads him, after which the boy revives.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Lava and Kuśa sing the Rāmāyaṇa
summary: At Vālmīki’s instruction the twins sing the whole poem in Rāma’s presence during his horse sacrifice, leading to their recognition as his sons.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Rāma’s return to Viṣṇu’s form
summary: At the end of his reign Rāma, with his brothers, enters the Sarayū and, at Brahmā’s invitation, the radiance of Viṣṇu.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The dice game
summary: Duryodhana, envious of the Pāṇḍavas’ wealth, has Śakuni challenge Yudhiṣṭhira to dice in the new hall at Hāstinapura; Yudhiṣṭhira loses his wealth, kingdom, brothers, himself and Draupadī, and in the return match the Pāṇḍavas are condemned to twelve years’ exile and a thirteenth incognito.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The humiliation of Draupadī in the assembly hall
summary: Draupadī, staked and lost, is dragged by her hair into the hall in a single garment; she asks whether Yudhiṣṭhira lost himself before staking her; Duḥśāsana tries to strip her and her garment is miraculously renewed; Dhṛtarāṣṭra finally grants her boons.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Draupadī’s svayaṃvara
summary: At Drupada’s city the disguised Arjuna strings the great bow and hits the target to win Draupadī; Kuntī’s unwitting instruction to share leads to her marriage to all five Pāṇḍavas, justified in several ways in the text.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The house of lac
summary: Duryodhana has a house of lac built at Vāraṇāvata to burn the Pāṇḍavas and Kuntī; warned by Vidura, they escape through a tunnel and are thought dead.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The Kurukṣetra war
summary: The eighteen-day war between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas at Kurukṣetra, narrated in the Bhīṣma-, Droṇa-, Karṇa- and Śalyaparvans, which ends in the death of almost all the warriors on both sides.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kṛṣṇa’s discourse to Arjuna (the Gītā)
summary: On the battlefield, Arjuna, seeing his kinsmen and teachers arrayed against him, lays down his bow; Kṛṣṇa teaches him on duty, action without attachment, knowledge and devotion, and reveals his universal form.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The destruction of the Yādavas and Kṛṣṇa’s death
summary: Thirty-six years after the war, the Yādavas, cursed through Sāmba and fulfilling Gāndhārī’s curse, kill one another at Prabhāsa with clubs grown from erakā grass; Balarāma departs in yoga and Kṛṣṇa is shot in the foot by the hunter Jarā.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The birth of Kṛṣṇa
summary: Kṛṣṇa is born to Devakī and Vasudeva in Kaṃsa’s prison at Mathurā, after Kaṃsa has killed her earlier children; he is carried to Vraja and exchanged with the daughter born to Yaśodā at the same time.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kṛṣṇa lifts Mount Govardhana
summary: Kṛṣṇa persuades the cowherds to honour the mountain instead of Indra; when Indra sends a deluge he uproots Govardhana and holds it up for seven days to shelter Vraja, and Indra comes to honour him.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kṛṣṇa subdues the serpent Kāliya
summary: The boy Kṛṣṇa plunges into the pool of the Yamunā poisoned by Kāliya, subdues the serpent by dancing on its heads and sends it away to the ocean.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The killing of Kaṃsa
summary: Summoned to Mathurā for a wrestling festival, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma kill the wrestlers, and Kṛṣṇa drags Kaṃsa down by the hair and kills him, restoring Ugrasena.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Nala and Damayantī
summary: Damayantī chooses Nala over the gods; possessed by Kali, Nala loses his kingdom at dice to his brother Puṣkara and abandons her in the forest; after many trials, disguised as a charioteer, he is recognised and regains his kingdom.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Sāvitrī and Satyavān
summary: Sāvitrī marries Satyavān knowing he will die in a year; when Yama takes his life she follows and, winning boon after boon by her words, obtains his life back.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Ugraśravas’ recitation at Naimiṣa
summary: The outer frame of the Mahābhārata: the bard Ugraśravas arrives at Śaunaka’s twelve-year sacrifice in the Naimiṣa forest and recites the epic he heard at Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice
summary: To avenge his father Parīkṣit, killed by Takṣaka, Janamejaya performs a sacrifice that draws the serpents into the fire; Āstīka stops it. During its intervals Vaiśampāyana recites the Mahābhārata.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Bhīṣma’s vow
summary: To let his father Śantanu marry Satyavatī, whose father demands that her son inherit, Devavrata renounces the throne and vows lifelong celibacy, and is thenceforth called Bhīṣma.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Vyāsa’s niyoga: the births of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu and Vidura
summary: After Vicitravīrya dies childless, Satyavatī asks her son Vyāsa to raise offspring on his widows; Ambikā bears the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Ambālikā the pale Pāṇḍu, and a servant woman Vidura.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The birth and abandonment of Karṇa
summary: The unmarried Kuntī tests Durvāsas’s mantra on the Sun and bears Karṇa with armour and earrings; fearing disgrace she sets him adrift, and the charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Rādhā raise him.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The births of the Pāṇḍavas
summary: Cursed never to approach his wives, Pāṇḍu asks Kuntī to use her mantra: she bears Yudhiṣṭhira by Dharma, Bhīma by Vāyu and Arjuna by Indra; Mādrī bears the twins by the Aśvins.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Ekalavya’s thumb
summary: The niṣāda Ekalavya, refused by Droṇa, teaches himself archery before a clay image of him; when Arjuna sees his skill, Droṇa demands Ekalavya’s right thumb as fee, and Ekalavya cuts it off.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The tournament of the Kuru princes
summary: At the public display of the princes’ skill Karṇa enters and matches Arjuna; challenged on his birth, he is made king of Aṅga by Duryodhana, and Adhiratha’s arrival exposes him to Bhīma’s scorn as a sūta’s son.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Bhīma and Hiḍimbā
summary: After escaping the house of lac Bhīma kills the man-eater Hiḍimba and, with Kuntī’s consent, lives with his sister Hiḍimbā, who bears Ghaṭotkaca.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The burning of the Khāṇḍava forest
summary: Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna help the fire god Agni consume the Khāṇḍava forest against Indra’s rains; Agni gives Arjuna the bow Gāṇḍīva and Kṛṣṇa the discus, and the spared Maya later builds the Pāṇḍavas’ hall.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The killing of Jarāsandha
summary: Before the rājasūya, Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma and Arjuna enter Magadha disguised as brahmins and Bhīma kills Jarāsandha in a wrestling match.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The rājasūya and the killing of Śiśupāla
summary: At Yudhiṣṭhira’s royal consecration Bhīṣma proposes Kṛṣṇa for the first honour; Śiśupāla protests and insults Kṛṣṇa, who beheads him with his discus.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Arjuna and the Kirāta
summary: Seeking divine weapons in the Himālaya, Arjuna fights a hunter (kirāta) over a boar; the hunter is Śiva, who, pleased, gives him the Pāśupata weapon.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The Yakṣa’s questions
summary: At a lake whose water kills his brothers, Yudhiṣṭhira answers the questions of a yakṣa — the god Dharma — and wins back their lives.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The killing of Kīcaka
summary: At Virāṭa’s court the general Kīcaka harasses Draupadī (disguised as Sairandhrī); Bhīma meets him at night in the dancing hall and kills him.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kṛṣṇa’s embassy to the Kauravas
summary: Kṛṣṇa goes to Hāstinapura to seek peace; when Duryodhana plots to seize him he reveals his cosmic form, then leaves, taking Karṇa aside to reveal his birth.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Ambā’s revenge and Śikhaṇḍin
summary: Ambā, rejected after Bhīṣma’s abduction, seeks his death, is reborn as Drupada’s daughter Śikhaṇḍinī and becomes the man Śikhaṇḍin through an exchange of sex with the yakṣa Sthūṇa.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kuntī meets Karṇa
summary: Before the war Kuntī goes to Karṇa on the bank of the Gaṅgā and asks him to join his brothers; he refuses but promises to spare all but Arjuna, so that she will still have five sons.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The fall of Bhīṣma
summary: On the tenth day, with Śikhaṇḍin before him, Arjuna pierces Bhīṣma with arrows; Bhīṣma falls and lies on a bed of arrows awaiting the winter solstice.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The death of Abhimanyu
summary: On the thirteenth day Abhimanyu breaks into Droṇa’s circular array, is surrounded by several warriors and killed by Duḥśāsana’s son with a mace.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The death of Ghaṭotkaca
summary: In the night battle Karṇa uses Indra’s infallible spear, reserved for Arjuna, to kill Ghaṭotkaca.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The death of Droṇa
summary: Told that “Aśvatthāman” is dead — an elephant of that name killed by Bhīma, confirmed by Yudhiṣṭhira — Droṇa lays down his weapons and is beheaded by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The death of Karṇa
summary: On the seventeenth day Karṇa’s chariot wheel sinks into the earth; while he struggles to free it, Arjuna, urged by Kṛṣṇa, kills him.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The mace duel and the breaking of Duryodhana’s thighs
summary: In the final mace duel, prompted by Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, Bhīma strikes Duryodhana below the navel, breaking his thighs as he had vowed, to Balarāma’s anger.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The night massacre
summary: Aśvatthāman, with Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman, enters the Pāṇḍava camp by night and kills Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the Draupadeyas and the sleeping warriors.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Gāndhārī curses Kṛṣṇa
summary: Lamenting on the battlefield, Gāndhārī blames Kṛṣṇa for not preventing the slaughter and curses him and his clan to perish in thirty-six years.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Bhīṣma’s instruction from the bed of arrows
summary: At Kṛṣṇa’s urging, the dying Bhīṣma instructs Yudhiṣṭhira at length on kingship, emergencies, liberation and many other topics before dying at the winter solstice.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The great departure of the Pāṇḍavas
summary: Renouncing the kingdom, the Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī walk towards Mount Meru; one by one they fall, and only Yudhiṣṭhira, followed by a dog that proves to be Dharma, reaches Indra’s chariot.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Śakuntalā and Duḥṣanta
summary: King Duḥṣanta meets Śakuntalā in Kaṇva’s hermitage and marries her by gāndharva rite; when she later brings their son to court he denies her until a heavenly voice confirms her, and the boy Bharata becomes heir.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kṛṣṇa carries off Rukmiṇī
summary: Kṛṣṇa takes Rukmiṇī, daughter of Bhīṣmaka of Vidarbha, away from her intended marriage to Śiśupāla and defeats her brother Rukmin.

type:LABEL: place
name: Ayodhyā
summary: Capital of Kosala and of the Ikṣvāku kings in the Rāmāyaṇa, Rāma’s birthplace and royal seat; traditionally identified with Ayodhya on the Sarayū (Ghaghara) in Uttar Pradesh, and with ancient Sāketa.

type:LABEL: place
name: Mithilā
summary: Capital of Videha ruled by Janaka, where Rāma breaks Śiva’s bow and marries Sītā; traditionally identified with Janakpur in the Nepal Terai, within the wider Mithilā region of north Bihar and Nepal.

type:LABEL: place
name: Laṅkā (in the Rāmāyaṇa)
summary: Rāvaṇa’s island fortress-city beyond the southern ocean, earlier the seat of Kubera; widely identified in tradition with the island of Sri Lanka, though some scholars have proposed locations in central India.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kiṣkindhā
summary: Cave-city of the vānara kings Vālin and Sugrīva near the Pampā lake and Ṛśyamūka hill; traditionally identified with the Hampi–Anegundi area on the Tuṅgabhadrā in Karnataka.

type:LABEL: place
name: Citrakūṭa
summary: Hill in the forest south of the Yamunā where Rāma, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa first settle in exile on Bharadvāja’s advice, and where Bharata finds them; identified with Chitrakoot on the Uttar Pradesh–Madhya Pradesh border.

type:LABEL: place
name: Pañcavaṭī
summary: Forest spot on the Godāvarī recommended by Agastya, where Rāma builds his hermitage and from which Sītā is abducted; traditionally identified with Panchavati in Nashik, Maharashtra.

type:LABEL: place
name: Daṇḍaka forest
summary: The vast forest of the exile, peopled by sages and harassed by rākṣasas, stretching (in later understanding) between the Narmadā and the Godāvarī/Kṛṣṇā; the modern Dandakaranya region of central-eastern India takes its name from it.

type:LABEL: place
name: Hastināpura
summary: Capital of the Kuru kings and seat of the Kauravas; identified with Hastinapur in Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh, where B. B. Lal excavated Painted Grey Ware levels (1950–52).

type:LABEL: place
name: Indraprastha
summary: City founded by the Pāṇḍavas on the Yamunā after clearing the Khāṇḍava forest, seat of Yudhiṣṭhira’s rājasūya; traditionally identified with the area of the Purana Qila in Delhi.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kurukṣetra
summary: The “field of the Kurus” where the eighteen-day war is fought, also called Samantapañcaka and dharmakṣetra; identified with the Kurukshetra region in Haryana, an important pilgrimage area.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: place
name: Dvārakā
summary: Kṛṣṇa’s city by the western sea, to which the Yādavas move from Mathurā, and which the sea submerges after Kṛṣṇa’s death; identified with Dwarka in Gujarat (with Bet Dwarka island also associated).

type:LABEL: place
name: Mathurā
summary: City of the Śūrasenas on the Yamunā, ruled by Kaṃsa, where Kṛṣṇa is born and kills Kaṃsa; the modern city in Uttar Pradesh, an important early centre of Vāsudeva–Kṛṣṇa worship.

type:LABEL: place
name: Vṛndāvana
summary: Forest near the Yamunā to which the cowherds move from their first settlement and where Kṛṣṇa’s childhood feats and sports with the gopīs take place; identified with Vrindavan near Mathura.

type:LABEL: place
name: Naimiṣa forest
summary: Forest where Śaunaka holds his twelve-year sacrifice and Ugraśravas recites the Mahābhārata (and, in Purāṇic frames, the Purāṇas); identified with Nimsar (Neemsar) on the Gomatī in Sitapur district, Uttar Pradesh.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kāmpilya
summary: Capital of southern Pañcāla left to Drupada after Droṇa’s victory, the setting of Draupadī’s svayaṃvara in tradition; identified with Kampil in Farrukhabad district, Uttar Pradesh.

type:LABEL: place
name: Takṣaśilā
summary: City in Gandhāra from which Janamejaya returns to Hāstinapura after his snake sacrifice (MBh 18.5.29); identified with Taxila in Punjab, Pakistan.

type:LABEL: place
name: Virāṭanagara
summary: Capital of King Virāṭa of the Matsyas, where the Pāṇḍavas spend the thirteenth year in disguise; traditionally identified with Viratnagar (Bairat) in Jaipur district, Rajasthan.

type:LABEL: place
name: Prabhāsa
summary: Coastal tīrtha where the Yādavas gather and destroy one another in drunken strife; identified with Prabhas Patan (Somnath) in Gujarat.

type:LABEL: place
name: Pampā lake
summary: Lake near Ṛśyamūka on whose western shore Śabarī lives and near which Rāma meets Hanumān and Sugrīva; identified with Pampa Sarovar near Hampi, Karnataka.

type:LABEL: place
name: Śṛṅgaverapura
summary: Town of the niṣāda chief Guha on the Gaṅgā, where Rāma crosses the river at the start of the exile; identified with Shringverpur near Prayagraj.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The Kuru lineage
summary: The royal line descended from Kuru in the lunar dynasty, ruling from Hāstinapura, to which Śantanu, Bhīṣma, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu and both the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas belong.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The Pāṇḍavas
summary: The five legal sons of Pāṇḍu — Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma and Arjuna (by Kuntī) and Nakula and Sahadeva (by Mādrī), each fathered by a god — with their shared wife Draupadī and their descendants down to Parīkṣit and Janamejaya.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The Kauravas
summary: The hundred sons (and one daughter) of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī, led by Duryodhana; also, more broadly, the Kuru side in the war.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The Yādavas / Vṛṣṇis
summary: The descendants of Yadu, including the Vṛṣṇi, Andhaka and Bhoja clans of Mathurā and Dvārakā, to which Śūra, Vasudeva, Kuntī, Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma and Subhadrā belong; their genealogy fills the Harivaṃśa.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The Paulastyas (line of Pulastya)
summary: The descendants of the sage Pulastya through Viśravas: Kubera (Vaiśravaṇa) and the rākṣasa siblings Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā and Vibhīṣaṇa.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The vānaras of Kiṣkindhā
summary: The monkey people of Kiṣkindhā ruled by Vālin and Sugrīva, among them Hanumān, Aṅgada, Nala and Nīla, born — in the Rāmāyaṇa and Rāmopākhyāna — of gods to aid Viṣṇu’s descent.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The Pāñcālas (line of Drupada)
summary: The ruling house of Pañcāla: Drupada and his children Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin and Draupadī, allies of the Pāṇḍavas.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The Bhāratas (line of Bharata Dauḥṣanti)
summary: The lineage named after Bharata, son of Duḥṣanta and Śakuntalā, from which the Kurus descend and after which the epic (Bhārata, Mahābhārata) is named.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The identification of the Rāmāyaṇa’s Laṅkā with Sri Lanka
summary: The traditional and widely held view that Rāvaṇa’s island-city Laṅkā is the island of Sri Lanka, set against scholarly proposals that the epic’s Laṅkā lay elsewhere (notably in central India) or is a purely literary geography.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Vāsudeva (deity of early inscriptions)
subtype: deity attested in inscriptions and coins
summary: Vāsudeva is the deity named in the earliest Vaiṣṇava inscriptions of the 2nd–1st centuries BCE, such as the Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar, where he is called devadeva, “god of gods”. He was later identified with Kṛṣṇa and with Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa. The material record shows his worship centuries before the Purāṇic synthesis.
earliest_textual: c. 5th – mid-4th c. BCE (not later than the early-to-mid 4th c. BCE)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Saṅkarṣaṇa (deity of early inscriptions)
subtype: deity attested in inscriptions and coins
summary: Saṅkarṣaṇa is the deity invoked together with Vāsudeva in inscriptions of the 2nd–1st centuries BCE, and is usually named first. He is identified with Balarāma, Kṛṣṇa's elder brother, and later became the first emanation (vyūha) of Vāsudeva in Pāñcarātra theology.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Heliodorus pillar inscription, Besnagar
aliases: Garuda pillar|Khamba Baba|Garuḍa pillar|Besnagar pillar inscription
summary: Two Brāhmī inscriptions in Prakrit on a stone pillar at Besnagar (ancient Vidiśā) record that Heliodorus of Taxila set up a Garuḍa-standard (garuḍadhvaja) for Vāsudeva, “god of gods”. Heliodorus, son of Dion, calls himself a bhāgavata and was a Greek envoy of the Indo-Greek king Antialkidas to king Kāsīputra Bhāgabhadra. It is among the earliest dated pieces of evidence for Vāsudeva devotion.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions
summary: Three fragmentary Sanskrit inscriptions in Brāhmī script from Ghosuṇḍī and Hāthībāḍā near Nagari (ancient Madhyamikā), Rajasthan, dated to the 2nd–1st century BCE. They record that king Sarvatāta of the Gājāyana lineage, a devotee of Bhagavat and performer of an aśvamedha, built a stone enclosure for the worship of Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva, called Nārāyaṇa-vāṭikā. They are among the earliest Sanskrit (as opposed to Prakrit) inscriptions.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Nāṇeghāṭ inscription of Nāganikā
summary: A long Brāhmī cave inscription at the Nāṇeghāṭ pass (Maharashtra), commissioned by the Sātavāhana queen Nāganikā (Nāyanikā). It opens by invoking Dharma, Indra, Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva, the lunar line and the four Lokapālas (Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Vāsava), and lists Vedic sacrifices, including two horse sacrifices, with the fees paid for them. Most scholars date it to the 1st century BCE.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Mora well inscription (Mathurā)
summary: A fragmentary Sanskrit inscription on a stone slab from the Mora well near Mathurā, from the time of the Mahākṣatrapa Śoḍāsa, son of Rājuvula (c. 15 CE). It records the installation of images (pratimā) of the five Vṛṣṇi heroes (pañcavīra), called bhagavat, in a stone shrine linked to a woman named Toṣā. It is the earliest epigraphic reference to cult images of the Vṛṣṇi heroes.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Torso of a Vṛṣṇi hero from Mora
summary: A stone male torso of c. 15 CE found at Mora near Mathurā together with the Mora well inscription and a carved doorjamb. It is now in the Government Museum, Mathurā, and is probably one of the five Vṛṣṇi heroes whose images the inscription records. It is among the earliest surviving cult images associated with the Vāsudeva–Saṅkarṣaṇa group.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Vasu doorjamb inscription (Mathurā)
aliases: Mathura inscription of Śoḍāsa's time|Vasu inscription
summary: A twelve-line Sanskrit inscription in Brāhmī on the back of a red sandstone doorjamb found in an old well at Mathurā. It dates from the time of the Mahākṣatrapa Śoḍāsa (early 1st century CE) and records that a donor named Vasu set up a gateway (toraṇa) and railing (vedikā) at the great shrine of Bhagavat Vāsudeva. It is held in the Government Museum, Mathurā (GMM 13.367).

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Coins of Agathocles with Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva
summary: Six Indian-standard silver drachms of the Greco-Bactrian king Agathocles (c. 190–180 BCE), found in 1970 at Aï Khanoum (Afghanistan), each show two male deities. One holds a plough and a pestle or club, the other a conch and a wheel. They are usually identified as Saṅkarṣaṇa-Balarāma and Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa, and are often called the earliest unambiguous images of the Vṛṣṇi heroes.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Megasthenes’ “Herakles” of the Sourasenoi as Kṛṣṇa
subtype: identification of a deity in a Greek ethnography
summary: Megasthenes (c. 300 BCE), as excerpted by Arrian, Diodorus and Strabo, reported that an Indian people called the Sourasenoi especially honoured “Herakles”. They had two great cities, Methora and Kleisobora, and the navigable river Iobares ran through their land. Many scholars identify this Herakles with (Hari-)Kṛṣṇa, the Sourasenoi with the Śūrasenas, Methora with Mathurā and the Iobares with the Yamunā. Others propose Indra, Śiva or Balarāma, or doubt that the Greek label maps onto a single Indian deity.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Chāndogya’s Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra as the epic Kṛṣṇa
summary: The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (CU 3.17.6) names a Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra, “son of Devakī”, as a pupil of Ghora Āṅgirasa who learns a teaching that allegorises the sacrifice. Some scholars take him to be the epic and Purāṇic Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī, which would be the earliest textual reference to Kṛṣṇa. Others regard the shared name and matronymic as a coincidence, or the verse as an unrelated figure.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Heliodorus inscription B echoes a Mahābhārata verse
subtype: textual parallel claimed for an inscription
summary: Inscription B on the Heliodorus pillar lists three immortal steps: self-restraint, generosity and attentiveness (dama, cāga, apramāda). Since Raychaudhuri, scholars have compared this triad with a verse in the Mahābhārata's Strīparvan (MBh book 11). Some treat it as evidence that the epic, or its ethical verse tradition, was known in Vidiśā in the late 2nd century BCE.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: “Paśupati” seal, Mohenjo-daro
summary: A steatite stamp seal (c. 3.56 × 3.53 cm) excavated at Mohenjo-daro in 1928–29. It shows a horned, seated figure, possibly three-faced, in a yoga-like posture, surrounded by an elephant, a tiger, a water buffalo and a rhinoceros, with two deer or ibexes below and seven Indus signs above. John Marshall called it a “proto-Śiva” as Paśupati, lord of animals. The identification has been widely disputed since the 1960s. The seal is now in the National Museum, New Delhi.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The “proto-Śiva” interpretation of the Paśupati seal
subtype: identification of a prehistoric image with a later deity
summary: John Marshall (1928–29; Mohenjo-daro and the Indus Civilization, 1931) proposed that the seated horned figure on the Mohenjo-daro seal 420 is a prototype of Śiva as Paśupati (lord of animals) and Mahāyogin. His view was widely accepted for about two generations. Since the 1960s it has been contested on iconographic, methodological and chronological grounds. There is no scholarly consensus.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Gudimallam liṅga
summary: A stone liṅga about 1.5 m high in the Paraśurāmeśvara temple at Gudimallam, near Tirupati (Andhra Pradesh). It carries a standing two-armed figure in high relief, holding a ram or antelope and a water pot, with an axe on the shoulder, standing on a crouching dwarf or yakṣa. It is widely regarded as one of the earliest surviving liṅgas with a figural Śiva. Dates proposed range from the 3rd century BCE to the 3rd–4th century CE.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Gudimallam liṅga dates to the 2nd–1st century BCE
summary: Several art historians (e.g. Harle) date the Gudimallam liṅga to the 2nd–1st century BCE on stylistic grounds. If correct, it is the earliest surviving figural liṅga in worship. Other scholars prefer dates in the early centuries CE, partly because of finds from the 1973–74 excavation.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Oesho (OHÞO), deity of Kuṣāṇa coins
summary: Oesho (Bactrian ΟΗϷΟ) is the name of a deity on Kuṣāṇa coins from Kaniṣka I onward. On some issues he is shown with a bull, a trident and, from Huviṣka, several heads and four arms. Many numismatists identify him with Śiva. Others, notably Katsumi Tanabe and Helmut Humbach, read the name as the Iranian wind god Vāyu (Wēš), whose image took on Śaiva features.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Oesho on Kuṣāṇa coins is Śiva
summary: The traditional numismatic view holds that the Kuṣāṇa coin deity Oesho is Śiva, as his trident, bull and multiple heads and arms suggest. The alternative view holds that Oesho is the Bactrian form of the Iranian wind god Vāyu (Wēš). On this view the Śaiva iconography was borrowed and full syncretism with Śiva came later, as seen in Sogdian Weshparkar.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Gold coins of Wima Kadphises with a deity and bull
subtype: coin type (gold double stater, stater, quarter stater; copper)
summary: Gold and copper coins of the Kuṣāṇa king Wima (Vima) Kadphises show on the reverse a deity holding a long trident, sometimes with a bull and on some coppers ithyphallic, together with the triratna or nandipada symbol. The Kharoṣṭhī legend calls the king mahiśvara, read by many as “devotee of Maheśvara”. The deity is usually identified with Śiva. Wima was also the first Kuṣāṇa ruler to issue gold coins.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Kuṣāṇa coins naming OHÞO (Oesho)
summary: Gold and copper coin types of Kaniṣka I, Huviṣka and Vāsudeva I bear the Bactrian legend ΟΗϷΟ (Oesho) beside a deity with a trident, vajra, water pot and sometimes a bull. Under Huviṣka the deity has three heads and four arms. The type is central to the debate over whether Oesho is Śiva or the Iranian Vāyu.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Varāha relief, Udayagiri Cave 5
summary: A monumental rock-cut relief in the shallow niche called Cave 5 at Udayagiri near Vidiśā. It shows Viṣṇu as the boar-headed Varāha lifting the Earth goddess, who clings to his tusk, out of the cosmic ocean, watched by rows of gods and sages. It dates from the reign of the Gupta king Candragupta II (c. 401–412 CE) and is among the most studied reliefs of the Gupta period.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Udayagiri Cave 6 inscription of the time of Candragupta II (year 82)
aliases: Udayagiri Cave Inscription of Chandragupta II, Year 82
summary: A short Sanskrit inscription at the entrance of Udayagiri Cave 6, dated year 82 (Gupta era, 401/402 CE), on the 11th day of the bright half of Āṣāḍha. It records the pious gift (deyadharma) of a Sanakānīka mahārāja, son of Viṣṇudāsa and grandson of Chagalaga, who calls himself a devotee of the feet of the paramabhaṭṭāraka mahārājādhirāja Candragupta. It is the earliest dated record of Candragupta II.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Udayagiri Cave 8 inscription of Vīrasena
summary: A five-line Sanskrit verse inscription in Udayagiri Cave 8 (the Tawa cave). It records that Vīrasena of the Kautsa gotra, surnamed Śāba, a minister of Candragupta II, made the cave as a temple of Śambhu (Śiva) when he came to the place with the king. It is undated but falls within Candragupta II's reign.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Iron pillar inscription of Candra (Delhi)
aliases: Meharauli pillar inscription of Candra|Iron pillar of Delhi
summary: A Sanskrit verse inscription on the wrought-iron pillar now in the Qutb complex, Mehrauli, Delhi. It records that a king named Candra, a devotee of Viṣṇu, set up a standard (dhvaja) of Viṣṇu on a hill called Viṣṇupada. By script and style it dates to the late 4th or early 5th century CE, and Candra is generally identified with Candragupta II.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Colossal Varāha of Eran
summary: A free-standing red sandstone image of Varāha in full boar form, about 4.2 m long and 3.4 m high, standing in the open at Eran (ancient Airikiṇa).
