summary: The 'descent' of a deity, above all Viṣṇu, into a bodily form to restore dharma; the theory develops from the Bhagavad Gītā's 'yuge yuge' (4.7–8) and the Nārāyaṇīya's prādurbhāvas into the Purāṇic lists of ten, twenty-two or 'innumerable' avatāras.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Daśāvatāra (the ten avatāras)
summary: The conventional set of ten avatāras of Viṣṇu; the term occurs in the Agni Purāṇa (16.12; 49.1), and the set becomes canonical in medieval art and liturgy (e.g. Jayadeva's Gītagovinda), though the eighth and ninth places vary (Kṛṣṇa or Balarāma; Buddha).
earliest_textual: post-7th c.; a version existed by the 11th c.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Yuga
summary: One of the four ages — Kṛta (Satya), Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali — of declining dharma that together make a mahāyuga; Manusmṛti 1.68–71 gives 4,000, 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 years plus dawn and dusk, totalling 12,000 'a yuga of the gods'.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Kalpa
summary: A day of Brahmā, a thousand mahāyugas (Manu 1.72; ViP 1.3.15) containing fourteen manvantaras (ViP 1.3.16); the present kalpa is called Vārāha, the first of the second half (parārdha) of Brahmā's life (ViP 1.3.27–28).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Manvantara
summary: The period of a Manu, 'a little over seventy-one' mahāyugas (ViP 1.3.18; BhP 3.11.24; Manu 1.79), each with its own Indra, gods and seven sages; fourteen make a kalpa and the present is the seventh, of Vaivasvata Manu.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Mahāyuga (caturyuga)
summary: The cycle of the four yugas, 12,000 divine years (Manu 1.71; ViP 1.3.11; BhP 3.11.18), computed as 4,320,000 human years where a divine year is taken as 360 human years.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pralaya (dissolution)
summary: The dissolution of the worlds; the Bhāgavata distinguishes four kinds — occasional (naimittika, at the end of a day of Brahmā), elemental (prākṛtika), constant (nitya) and final (ātyantika) (12.7.17) — and Viṣṇu sleeps on the cosmic ocean in the interval.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pañcalakṣaṇa (five marks of a Purāṇa)
summary: The classical definition of a Purāṇa by five topics — sarga (creation), pratisarga (re-creation/dissolution), vaṃśa (genealogy), manvantara (ages of the Manus) and vaṃśānucarita (dynastic history) — stated in the Amarakośa and in several Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Trimūrti
summary: The triad of Brahmā (creation), Viṣṇu (preservation) and Śiva (destruction) as aspects of one reality; affirmed in non-sectarian and Smārta contexts, while sectarian Purāṇas subordinate two to the third.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Śakti pīṭha
summary: A seat of the Goddess, especially as derived from the parts of Satī's body; the number (4, 51, 108) and the derivation from a dismembered corpse vary — the Matsya instead has Satī herself name 108 tīrthas where she is to be worshipped (13.26–53).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Tīrtha
summary: A 'crossing-place' — a sacred ford, river-bank or site where pilgrimage and bathing are held to be efficacious; Purāṇic māhātmyas (glorifications) are the principal textual charters of tīrthas.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Jyotirliṅga
summary: The twelve 'liṅgas of light', self-manifest forms of Śiva at named sites (Somanātha, Mallikārjuna, Mahākāla, Kedāra, Viśveśvara and others), listed in the Śiva Purāṇa (Koṭirudra-saṃhitā) and in a widely recited stotra.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Vyūha
summary: The four 'emanations' of the Pāñcarātra theology — Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna and Aniruddha — set out in the Nārāyaṇīya (MBh CE 12.326.68–69), from Aniruddha of whom Brahmā arises.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The churning of the ocean
summary: Gods and asuras churn the ocean with Mount Mandara and the serpent Vāsuki to obtain amṛta; the versions differ on who supports the mountain, who takes the poison, what emerges and how the nectar is withheld from the asuras.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Varāha raises the Earth
summary: Viṣṇu as a cosmic boar dives into the waters and raises the submerged Earth on his tusk; in the Bhāgavata he also slays Hiraṇyākṣa.
earliest_material: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Narasiṃha and Prahlāda
summary: Hiraṇyakaśipu persecutes his devoted son Prahlāda; Viṣṇu bursts from a pillar as the man-lion and kills him at twilight on the threshold with his claws, honouring the letter of Brahmā's boon.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Vāmana and Bali
summary: Viṣṇu, born as the dwarf son of Aditi, asks the asura king Bali for three steps, grows to cosmic size as Trivikrama, recovers the worlds for Indra and sends Bali to the netherworld.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The destruction of Dakṣa's sacrifice
summary: Dakṣa excludes Śiva from his sacrifice; Satī gives up her body; Śiva's emanation Vīrabhadra and his hosts destroy the rite and Dakṣa is punished and restored.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The birth of Skanda
summary: Śiva's seed, too potent to bear, passes through Agni and Gaṅgā and is nursed by the six Kṛttikās; the child Skanda is made general of the gods and slays Tāraka. Versions differ on the bearers and the mother's role.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The Goddess slays Mahiṣāsura
summary: The gods, defeated by the buffalo-demon, emit their radiance which coalesces into the Goddess; armed with their weapons and riding Himavat's lion she destroys his army and kills him as he emerges from the buffalo (DM 2–3).
earliest_material: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The appearance of the fiery liṅga (Liṅgodbhava)
summary: Brahmā and Viṣṇu quarrel over supremacy; an endless pillar of fire appears; Brahmā as a swan flies up and Viṣṇu as a boar digs down, and neither finds its end; Śiva reveals himself within it.
earliest_material: c. 700 CE (reign of Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha, c. 690–728)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The liberation of Gajendra
summary: The king of elephants, seized by a crocodile in a lake on Mount Trikūṭa, prays to the supreme person; Hari comes on Garuḍa, kills the crocodile with his discus and frees him, and both are released from curses.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The story of Dhruva
summary: The child Dhruva, rejected from his father's lap, undertakes fierce austerity and is granted by Viṣṇu the highest immovable station, the Pole Star.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The descent of the Gaṅgā
summary: Sagara's sixty thousand sons, burned by Kapila, can be purified only by the Gaṅgā; after generations Bhagīratha's austerities bring her down, Śiva breaks her fall in his hair, and she flows over the ashes.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The Matsya avatāra and the flood
summary: A small fish begs Manu's protection, grows enormous, warns of a deluge and tows his boat, tied to its horn, to safety; in the Purāṇas the fish is Viṣṇu and the story is set at the end of a manvantara or kalpa.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Satī's body and the origin of the Śakti Pīṭhas
summary: After Satī's death Śiva wanders carrying her corpse; it is divided and its parts fall at places that become seats (pīṭhas) of the Goddess — a late, Śākta development of the Dakṣa story.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha
summary: During Viṣṇu's cosmic sleep two demons born from his ear-wax threaten Brahmā; Brahmā praises the Goddess as Yoganidrā, she releases Viṣṇu, and he slays them (DM 1).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The slaying of Śumbha and Niśumbha
summary: The asura brothers seek the Goddess in marriage; she destroys their generals Dhūmralocana, Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa and Raktabīja with Kālī and the Mothers, then Niśumbha and Śumbha (DM 5–10).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Sagara's sons and Kapila
summary: Sagara's sixty thousand sons dig through the earth in search of the sacrificial horse, find it near the sage Kapila, accuse him and are burned to ashes; Aṃśumat recovers the horse.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Yayāti and the exchange of old age
summary: Cursed by Śukra with premature old age, Yayāti asks his sons to take it; only Pūru agrees, and he becomes heir to the central realm while the others receive the peripheries.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Ilā/Sudyumna and the birth of Purūravas
summary: From a flawed rite of Manu a daughter Ilā is born, changed into a man (Sudyumna) and back; as Ilā she bears Purūravas to Budha, son of the Moon — the junction of the Solar and Lunar lines.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The advent of Kalki
summary: At the end of the Kali age Kalki is born at Śambhala to Viṣṇuyaśas, rides a swift horse given by the gods, destroys the dasyus posing as kings, and inaugurates a new Kṛta age.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Bhṛgu's curse and Viṣṇu's repeated births
summary: In the Matsya, Viṣṇu kills Bhṛgu's wife during a war of gods and asuras; Bhṛgu curses him to be born repeatedly among humans, which explains seven human manifestations after three divine ones (MatsP 47.235–251).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The Goddess formed from the gods' radiance
summary: The radiance (tejas) issuing from the angry Viṣṇu, Śiva, Brahmā, Indra and the other gods merges into a single female form whose body parts each derive from one god, and the gods arm her with copies of their weapons (DM 2 = MkP 82.8–31).

type:LABEL: lineage
name: Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśa / Ikṣvāku)
summary: The royal line descended from Vivasvat (the Sun) through Vaivasvata Manu and Ikṣvāku, ruling from Ayodhyā; it includes Māndhātṛ, Hariścandra, Sagara, Bhagīratha, Raghu, Aja, Daśaratha and Rāma. The sequence of kings differs markedly between the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa and the Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: Lunar dynasty (Candravaṃśa / Aila)
summary: The royal line descended from Soma (the Moon) through Budha and Ilā's son Purūravas (hence 'Aila'), then Āyu, Nahuṣa and Yayāti, whose sons Yadu and Pūru found the Yādava and Paurava–Kuru branches.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: Pauravas (descendants of Pūru)
summary: The branch of the Lunar line descended from Yayāti's son Pūru, including Bharata, Kuru and the Kurus of the Mahābhārata (ViP 4.19–20; BhP 9.20–22).

type:LABEL: lineage
name: Bhārgavas (descendants of Bhṛgu)
summary: The priestly clan of Bhṛgu, including Śukra (Kāvya), Ṛcīka, Jamadagni and Paraśurāma; Goldman traces their prominence in the Mahābhārata.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: Daityas (sons of Diti)
summary: The asuras descended from Kaśyapa and Diti — Hiraṇyakaśipu, Hiraṇyākṣa, Prahlāda, Virocana, Bali — perennial rivals of the gods (Ādityas, sons of Aditi).

type:LABEL: place
name: Kāśī (Vārāṇasī)
summary: The city on the Gaṅgā held to be Śiva's own (Avimukta, 'never forsaken'), where death brings liberation; glorified in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa and the subject of an early māhātmya in the original Skandapurāṇa.

type:LABEL: place
name: Prayāga
summary: The confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā (with the invisible Sarasvatī) at present Prayagraj, called 'king of tīrthas' in Purāṇic māhātmyas (e.g. Matsya Purāṇa, recall) and site of the Kumbha Melā.

type:LABEL: place
name: Mount Kailāsa
summary: Śiva's mountain abode in Purāṇic cosmography, traditionally identified with Mount Kailash (Gang Rinpoche) in western Tibet, sacred also to Buddhists, Jains and Bon.

type:LABEL: place
name: Gaṅgā river
summary: The Ganges, personified as the goddess Gaṅgā; Purāṇic geography traces her descent from Viṣṇu's foot through the heavens to Śiva's hair and the earth.

type:LABEL: place
name: Sarasvatī river (Vedic)
summary: The river praised in the Ṛgveda and remembered in later texts as disappearing in the desert (at Vinaśana) and flowing invisibly to join the Gaṅgā and Yamunā at Prayāga; its identification with the Ghaggar–Hakra is debated.

type:LABEL: place
name: Ocean of Milk (Kṣīrasāgara)
summary: The cosmic ocean of Purāṇic cosmography that is churned for the amṛta and on which Viṣṇu reclines; Mount Trikūṭa rises from it (BhP 8.2.1).

type:LABEL: place
name: Mount Mandara
summary: The mountain used as the churning-stick in the churning of the ocean; MBh (CE) 1.16.3 makes it 11,000 yojanas high. Tradition identifies a Mandar hill near Bhagalpur, Bihar.

type:LABEL: place
name: Mount Trikūṭa
summary: Three-peaked mountain in the Ocean of Milk, scene of Gajendra's rescue (BhP 8.2.1–2).

type:LABEL: place
name: Naubandhana peak (Himavat)
summary: The Himālayan peak where, in the Mahābhārata, the fish has the sages tie Manu's boat, 'still famous today' as Naubandhana (MBh CE 3.185.44–47); ŚB 1.8.1.6 has the 'northern mountain' (vedic domain).

type:LABEL: place
name: Malaya mountains
summary: The southern (Western Ghats) mountain range where, in the Matsya Purāṇa, King Manu performs austerities before meeting the fish (MatsP 1.12).

type:LABEL: place
name: Kṛtamālā river
summary: River in the Draviḍa country where Satyavrata catches the small fish (BhP 8.24.12); traditionally identified with the Vaigai at Madurai.

type:LABEL: place
name: Vindhya mountains
summary: The central Indian range on which the Harivaṃśa gives the goddess Nidrā/Kauśikī an eternal seat (HV CE 47.48); the shrine of Vindhyavāsinī near Mirzapur continues the tradition.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kāmarūpa
summary: Region of the lower Brahmaputra valley (Assam) glorified in the Kālikā Purāṇa as the most sacred land of the Goddess, where Satī's yoni fell at Nīlācala (Kāmākhyā).

type:LABEL: place
name: Śambhala (village of Kalki)
summary: The village where Kalki is to be born in the house of Viṣṇuyaśas (BhP 12.2.18); local traditions identify it with Sambhal (Uttar Pradesh), and it is distinct from the Buddhist Kālacakra Śambhala.

type:LABEL: place
name: Madhuvana
summary: Forest on the Yamunā near Mathurā where Dhruva performs austerities (BhP 4.8.42).

type:LABEL: place
name: Badarī (Viśālā)
summary: Himālayan hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa; in MBh (CE) 3.185.4 Manu performs austerities at Viśālā Badarī, and Nārada hastens there at the end of the Nārāyaṇīya (12.326.99).

type:LABEL: place
name: Kanakhala
summary: Place near Haridwar on the Gaṅgā identified in tradition and in several Purāṇic tellings (recall) as the site of Dakṣa's sacrifice.

type:LABEL: place
name: Gaṅgāsāgara
summary: The mouth of the Hooghly branch of the Gaṅgā (Sagar Island), where tradition places Kapila's hermitage and the ashes of Sagara's sons.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Vaiṣṇava traditions
summary: Traditions that worship Viṣṇu (with Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa, Rāma and other forms) as supreme; their Purāṇic canon centres on the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas and the avatāra doctrine.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Śaiva traditions
summary: Traditions that worship Śiva as supreme, from the Pāśupatas and the 'Śaiva age' of early medieval India (Sanderson) to Śaiva Siddhānta, Kashmir Śaivism and Vīraśaivism; their Purāṇas include the Liṅga, Śiva, Vāyu, Kūrma and Skanda.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Śākta traditions
summary: Traditions that worship the Goddess (Devī, Śakti) as supreme; the Devī Māhātmya (c. 5th–6th c.) is their first great Sanskrit text, followed by the Kālikā and Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇas and Tantric literature.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Smārta tradition
summary: Brahmanical orthopraxy based on the smṛti (Dharmaśāstra, Purāṇa), associated with the worship of five deities (pañcāyatana: Viṣṇu, Śiva, Devī, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa) and, since the medieval period, with Advaita monasteries.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Early Bhāgavata (Vāsudeva) devotion
summary: The early devotional cult of Vāsudeva (and Saṅkarṣaṇa) whose adherents called themselves bhāgavata; the Heliodorus pillar's donor styles himself 'bhāgavata' (late 2nd c. BCE), and the tradition flows into later Vaiṣṇavism.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Pāśupata Śaivism
summary: The earliest known Śaiva ascetic order, tracing itself to Lakulīśa (c. 2nd c. CE); its milieu shaped the Vāyu, Liṅga, Kūrma and the early Skandapurāṇa.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Saura (Sun) worship
summary: Worship of Sūrya as supreme, prominent in western and northern India between the Gupta and early medieval periods, with Maga priests from 'Śākadvīpa'; textual charters are the Sāmba and parts of the Bhaviṣya and Brahma Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Gāṇapatya
summary: Traditions that worship Gaṇeśa as supreme, crystallised in the Gaṇeśa and Mudgala Upapurāṇas (2nd millennium) and in Maharashtrian centres such as Morgaon and Chinchwad.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Kali age began in 3102 BCE
summary: The traditional Indian astronomical epoch of the Kali-yuga (midnight 17/18 February 3102 BCE, Ujjain, as computed in later siddhāntas), derived backwards from planetary models; Āryabhaṭa's 499 CE statement implies it, and the 634 CE Aihole inscription counts 3,735 years from the Bhārata war.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Devī Bhāgavata is the Mahāpurāṇa 'Bhāgavata'
summary: The Śākta position that the 'Bhāgavata' of the eighteen-lists is the Devī Bhāgavata, supported by the Matsya's description of the Bhāgavata as beginning with the Gāyatrī and containing the slaying of Vṛtra (MatsP 53.20–21); Vaiṣṇava tradition and most scholars hold it to be the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, with the Devī Bhāgavata an Upapurāṇa.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The term 'mahāpurāṇa' is late
summary: Rocher's observation that the term mahāpurāṇa occurs rarely in Purāṇic literature and is probably late; in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa critical edition the half-verse calling the eighteen 'mahāpurāṇas' is an insertion (3.6.23*8).

type:LABEL: claim
name: Vāsudeva was worshipped by self-styled bhāgavatas by the 2nd century BCE
summary: The scholarly conclusion, from the Heliodorus pillar (Besnagar), the Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī and Mora well inscriptions and the coins of Agathocles, that a devotional cult of Vāsudeva (and Saṅkarṣaṇa) existed in the last centuries BCE, long before the Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Śiva was worshipped in iconic and liṅga form by the early centuries CE
summary: The conclusion, from the Gudimallam liṅga and Kuṣāṇa coinage (Wima Kadphises' deity with bull), that Śiva worship in liṅga and anthropomorphic form predates the Śaiva Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Devī Māhātmya was in circulation by 608 CE
summary: A verse of the Devī Māhātmya's eleventh chapter is quoted in a dated inscription of 608 CE, giving a firm terminus ante quem for at least part of the text.

type:LABEL: person
name: Āryabhaṭa
summary: Indian astronomer-mathematician (b. 476 CE) whose Āryabhaṭīya (499 CE) states his age in the Kali era and adopts a mahāyuga of four equal quarters.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.3 (units of time, yugas, kalpa)
summary: Parāśara's account of time: nimeṣa to day, human and divine years (1.3.8–10), the caturyuga of 12,000 divine years (1.3.11–14), 1,000 caturyugas as Brahmā's day with fourteen Manus (1.3.15–16), a manvantara of a little over 71 caturyugas = 852,000 divine or 306,720,000 human years (1.3.18–21), and the present Vārāha kalpa (1.3.27–28).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.4 (Varāha raises the Earth)
summary: The boar form taken at the beginning of the present kalpa to raise the Earth from the waters, with the Earth's hymn.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.9 (Durvāsas' curse and the churning)
summary: Durvāsas' curse deprives Indra of Śrī; on Viṣṇu's advice gods and asuras churn the Ocean of Milk; Viṣṇu as tortoise; the nāgas take the poison; Śrī rises and goes to Hari's chest.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.11–12 (Dhruva)
summary: The story of Dhruva's austerity and his elevation to the pole.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.16–20 (Prahlāda)
summary: Prahlāda's devotion and persecution by Hiraṇyakaśipu; the father's death at Narasiṃha's hands is stated at 1.20.32.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.1 (the manvantaras)
summary: The six past Manus (Svāyambhuva, Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, Cākṣuṣa) and the present seventh, Vaivasvata, with its Indra Purandara, seven sages and Manu's sons (3.1.6–7, 30–34).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.6 (the eighteen Purāṇas and the five marks)
summary: Vyāsa's Purāṇa-saṃhitā given to Romaharṣaṇa; the list of eighteen purāṇas (3.6.20–23) and the five topics treated in all (3.6.24); the term 'mahāpurāṇa' only in insertion 3.6.23*8.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.4 (Sagara to Rāma)
summary: Sagara's sons and Kapila, Aṃśumat, Dilīpa and Bhagīratha (4.4.1–25); Khaṭvāṅga, Dīrghabāhu, Raghu, Aja, Daśaratha and the fourfold birth of Viṣṇu as Rāma and his brothers (4.4.47–49).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.10 (Yayāti)
summary: Nahuṣa's six sons; Yayāti's sons by Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā; Śukra's curse and the exchange of old age.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.24 (dynasties of the Kali age)
summary: The 'future' dynasties (Nandas, Mauryas, Śuṅgas … Guptas) and the onset of Kali when Kṛṣṇa departed; Kali lasts 360,000 human years (4.24.32–33, as the e-text reads).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.38 (after Kṛṣṇa's departure)
summary: Arjuna leads the Yādava women from Dvārakā; on the day Hari left the earth, Kali descended (5.38.8) and the sea flooded Dvārakā.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.3 (the twenty-two avatāras)
summary: The cosmic Person as seed of avatāras (1.3.1–5) and the numbered list of twenty-two descents (1.3.6–25), declared innumerable (1.3.26); 1.3.28 distinguishes partial descents from Kṛṣṇa, 'Bhagavān himself'.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.7 (Brahmā's catalogue of līlāvatāras)
summary: Brahmā tells Nārada of Viṣṇu's sportive descents — Varāha, Suyajña, Kapila, Datta, the Kumāras, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Pṛthu, Ṛṣabha, Hayaśīrṣa, Matsya, Kūrma, Nṛsiṃha, Hari (for Gajendra), Vāmana, Haṃsa, Manu, Dhanvantari, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa with Balarāma, Vyāsa, the deluder of the demons and the chastiser of Kali.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.11 (time and the yugas)
summary: Maitreya's account of the four yugas as 12,000 divine years (3.11.18–20), Brahmā's day of a thousand caturyugas and fourteen Manus (3.11.22–24).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.2–7 (Dakṣa's sacrifice)
summary: Dakṣa's enmity, Satī's death, Vīrabhadra's destruction of the sacrifice (4.5.2–3) and the restoration.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.8–12 (Dhruva)
summary: Dhruva's austerity at Madhuvana (4.8.42) and ascent to the viṣṇupada (4.12.25).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa book 7 (Prahlāda and Narasiṃha)
summary: Hiraṇyakaśipu's boon and persecution of Prahlāda; Narasiṃha's emergence from the pillar (7.8.17–19) and Prahlāda's hymn (7.9).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.2–4 (Gajendramokṣa)
summary: Mount Trikūṭa (8.2.1), the elephant's prayer (8.3), the rescue and the former births of the elephant (Indradyumna) and the crocodile (Hūhū) (8.4.3–11).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.5–12 (the churning and Mohinī)
summary: The churning with Viṣṇu as tortoise, Śiva drinking the hālāhala (8.7.43), Lakṣmī choosing Mukunda (8.8.24), Mohinī distributing the nectar (8.9) and Śiva's infatuation (8.12).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.13 (the present and future manvantaras)
summary: Vaivasvata (Śrāddhadeva) as the present seventh Manu, his ten sons, gods, Indra Purandara, seven sages, and Vāmana's birth in this period (8.13.1–6).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.15–23 (Bali and Vāmana)
summary: Bali's conquest, Aditi's vow and Vāmana's birth, the gift of three steps (8.19.20), Trivikrama's strides (8.20.34) and Bali's elevation to Sutala (8.22.35).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.24 (Matsya)
summary: The fish avatāra: Hayagrīva steals the Vedas (8.24.8); King Satyavrata of the Draviḍas catches the fish in the Kṛtamālā (8.24.10–13); the deluge, the boat, the teaching; Satyavrata becomes Vaivasvata Manu (8.24.58).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa book 9 (the royal dynasties)
summary: The Solar line from Manu's sons (Ikṣvāku, Sagara 9.8, Bhagīratha 9.9, Raghu–Aja–Daśaratha 9.10.1, Rāma 9.10–11) and the Lunar line (Purūravas 9.14, Paraśurāma 9.15–16, Yayāti 9.18–19, Pauravas and Yādavas 9.20–24).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa book 10 (Kṛṣṇa)
summary: The life of Kṛṣṇa from birth at Mathurā and childhood in Vraja to the killing of Kaṃsa and life at Dvārakā; the most influential Purāṇic book in Kṛṣṇa devotion.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.2 (Kali age and Kalki)
summary: The decline of the Kali age and the birth of Kalki in the house of Viṣṇuyaśas at Śambhala (12.2.16–20).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.7 (marks of a Purāṇa; list of eighteen)
summary: Ten characteristics of a Purāṇa, with the remark that some count five (12.7.9–10); the eighteen Purāṇas (12.7.23–24).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.13 (verse counts of the Purāṇas)
summary: Verse counts of the eighteen Purāṇas, totalling 400,000, the Bhāgavata having 18,000 (12.13.4–9).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Devī Māhātmya 1 (Madhu and Kaiṭabha) = MkP 81
summary: Frame story of Suratha, Samādhi and Medhas; Brahmā's hymn to Yoganidrā; the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Devī Māhātmya 2–4 (Mahiṣāsura) = MkP 82–84
summary: The gods' radiance becomes the Goddess and is armed (MkP 82.8–31); battle with Mahiṣa's army (82); his death (83); the gods' hymn (84).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Devī Māhātmya 5–10 (Śumbha and Niśumbha) = MkP 85–90
summary: Ambikā/Kauśikī emerges from Pārvatī (85.40–44); Dhūmralocana (86); Kālī and Cāmuṇḍā (87.5, 87.26); Raktabīja (88); Niśumbha (89); Śumbha (90).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Devī Māhātmya 7 (Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa; Kālī) = MkP 87
summary: Kālī springs from the angry Ambikā's brow (87.5), slays Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa and is named Cāmuṇḍā (87.26).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Devī Māhātmya 11 (Nārāyaṇī-stuti) = MkP 91
summary: The gods' hymn to the Goddess as Nārāyaṇī, including the verse 'sarvamaṅgalamāṅgalye…' (MkP 91.9) quoted in the 608 CE Dadhimatī-mātā inscription.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Manusmṛti 1.68–73 (lengths of the yugas)
summary: Kṛta 4,000 years with dawn and dusk of 400 each; the other three decreasing by a thousand and a hundred; the 12,000 'yuga of the gods'; a thousand such make Brahmā's day (cf. 1.64–67 time units; 1.79 manvantara of 71 divine yugas).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Matsya Purāṇa 1–2 (the fish and Manu)
summary: King Manu's austerity on the Malaya; the growing fish recognised as Keśava/Janārdana; the flood at the end of the Cākṣuṣa manvantara; the boat tied to the horn with a serpent rope.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Matsya Purāṇa 13 (Satī and the 108 tīrthas)
summary: At Dakṣa's sacrifice Satī announces she will abandon the body born of him, names 108 tīrthas with her names there (13.26–53) and burns herself; she is reborn as Pārvatī (13.59).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Matsya Purāṇa 47 (Bhṛgu's curse and Viṣṇu's manifestations)
summary: Twelve deva–asura wars (47.41–45); Bhṛgu's curse; three divine and seven human manifestations of Viṣṇu (47.235–251): Dattātreya, Māndhātṛ, Jāmadagnya, Rāma, Vedavyāsa, Buddha, Kalki.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Matsya Purāṇa 53 (the Purāṇas, their extent and marks)
summary: Descriptions, verse counts and gifts for the eighteen (53.12–58), the upabhedas (53.60–63), the five marks (53.65) and the guṇa correlation (53.68–69).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.1 (avatāra list)
summary: A list of twenty-two avatāras nearly verbatim with BhP 1.3.6–25 (1.1.14–33), Buddha called 'jinasuta' (1.1.32).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.86 (ten manifestations)
summary: Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nṛhari, Vāmana, Rāma (Bhārgava), Rāma Dāśarathi, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha and Kalki (1.86.10–11).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Agni Purāṇa 2–16 (the avatāras narrated)
summary: Matsya (2), Kūrma (3), Varāha to Paraśurāma (4), Rāma (5–11), Harivaṃśa (12), Mahābhārata (13–15), Buddha and Kalki (16), closing with 'viṣṇor daśāvatārākhyān' (16.12).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Agni Purāṇa 49 (iconography of the ten avatāras)
summary: Prescriptions for images of Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Balarāma (plough and pestle), Buddha and Kalki (49.1–9).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Liṅga Purāṇa 1.17 (Liṅgodbhava)
summary: Brahmā's account of the quarrel with Viṣṇu, the fiery liṅga, his swan form and Viṣṇu's boar form (1.17.31–45).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Liṅga Purāṇa 1.76 (image of the Liṅgodbhava)
summary: Prescription for an image with Candraśekhara within the flaming liṅga, Brahmā as swan above and Viṣṇu as boar below (1.76.60–61).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Śiva Purāṇa, Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā 5–9 (Liṅgodbhava and the ketakī)
summary: The pillar of fire between Brahmā and Viṣṇu; Brahmā's false witness, the ketakī flower (1.7.19–27).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Kūrma Purāṇa 1.1 (five marks and list of eighteen)
summary: The pañcalakṣaṇa (1.1.12) and a list of the Purāṇas that keeps Śaiva fourth and ends with the Vāyavīya and 'the eighteenth, called Brahmāṇḍa' (1.1.13–15).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.31–40 (Devī Gītā)
summary: The Goddess's teaching to Himālaya, transmitted separately as the Devī Gītā.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Caṅkam (Sangam) literature
summary: The earliest corpus of Tamil poetry — the Eight Anthologies (Eṭṭuttokai) and Ten Idylls (Pattuppāṭṭu) — together with the grammar Tolkāppiyam, composed roughly between the turn of the era and the 5th–6th century CE, with later layers such as the Paripāṭal and Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Tirumurai
summary: The twelve-book canon of Tamil Śaiva devotional literature: Tēvāram (1–7), Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvācakam and Tirukkōvaiyār (8), Tiruvicaippā and Tiruppallāṇṭu (9), Tirumūlar’s Tirumantiram (10), a miscellany including the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai (11) and Cēkkiḻār’s Periya Purāṇam (12).

type:LABEL: collection
name: Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās
summary: The scriptures of the Pāñcarātra tradition — traditionally 108, with over 200 known titles — including the Sāttvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya (“three gems”), the Ahirbudhnya, Pārameśvara, Īśvara and Lakṣmī Tantra.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Śaiva Āgamas (Siddhānta tantras)
summary: The Sanskrit scriptures of the Śaiva Siddhānta, traditionally twenty-eight Āgamas with subsidiary Upāgamas, beginning with the Kāmika; the earliest surviving tantra of the wider Mantramārga is the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Śākta Tantras
summary: Tantras centred on the Goddess and her retinue (yoginīs, Kālī, Tripurasundarī, Kubjikā), including the Brahmayāmala (Picumata) of the early Vidyāpīṭha, the Kaula texts and later Śrīvidyā literature.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Maṅgalkāvya
summary: Bengali narrative poems (c. 13th–18th c.) celebrating the power of local or Purāṇic deities — Manasā, Caṇḍī, Dharma Ṭhākur, Annadā — and the establishment of their worship among reluctant devotees.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Sthala-purāṇas (temple and place legends)
summary: Texts recounting the sacred history of a particular shrine or town — its deity’s manifestation, divine marriages, miracles and royal patrons — in Sanskrit (often as māhātmyas within Purāṇas) and in Tamil and other languages.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tolkāppiyam
summary: The oldest extant Tamil grammar and poetics, in three books (phonology, morphology, “subject-matter” — poruḷ). Its Akattiṇaiyiyal assigns presiding deities to the landscapes: Māyōṉ to the forest-pasture (mullai), Cēyōṉ to the hills (kuṟiñci), Vēntaṉ to farmland (marutam) and Varuṇaṉ to the shore (neytal).

type:LABEL: text
name: Paripāṭal
summary: A late Caṅkam anthology (fifth of the Eight Anthologies) of musical poems: of the 24 that survive complete, 7 are addressed to Tirumāl (Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa), 8 to Murukaṉ (Cevvēḷ) and 9 to the river Vaikai at Madurai.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai
summary: Nakkīrar’s poem “guiding [the devotee] to Murukaṉ,” the first of the Ten Idylls and also included in Tirumurai 11. It describes six places where Murukaṉ is present and blends Tamil and northern (Skanda) imagery.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tiruppāvai
summary: Āṇṭāḷ’s thirty Tamil verses in the voice of cowherd girls who rise before dawn in the month of Mārkaḻi to wake one another and Kṛṣṇa for a vow (nōṉpu). It is part of the Divya Prabandham and recited daily in Śrīvaiṣṇava worship.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nācciyār Tirumoḻi
summary: Āṇṭāḷ’s 143 Tamil verses of longing for union with Viṣṇu–Kṛṣṇa, including the celebrated dream of her wedding to him (vāraṇam āyiram), part of the Divya Prabandham.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tiruvāymoḻi
summary: Nammāḻvār’s 1,102-verse Tamil poem to Viṣṇu, in a hundred decads; Śrīvaiṣṇavas call it the Tamil (Drāviḍa) Veda and it was the subject of the first Śrīvaiṣṇava commentary, Piḷḷāṉ’s Āṟāyirappaṭi.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tiruvācakam
summary: Māṇikkavācakar’s Tamil hymns to Śiva, forming (with his Tirukkōvaiyār) Tirumurai book 8; intensely personal poems of grace, longing and Śiva as dancer at Tillai (Chidambaram).

type:LABEL: text
name: Tiruvempāvai
summary: Māṇikkavācakar’s twenty-verse pāvai poem within the Tiruvācakam, in which young women wake each other at dawn in Mārkaḻi to bathe and praise Śiva — a Śaiva counterpart of Āṇṭāḷ’s Tiruppāvai.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tirumantiram
summary: Tirumūlar’s Tamil verse treatise on Śaiva doctrine, yoga and tantra (c. 3,000 verses), Tirumurai book 10, regarded as the earliest Tamil statement of Śaiva Siddhānta ideas; its date is much disputed.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam
summary: The Tamil sthala-purāṇa of Madurai narrating the sixty-four “sacred sports” (tiruviḷaiyāṭal) of Śiva as Cuntarēcuvarar, including his marriage to the warrior-princess Taṭātakai (Mīnākṣī). The best-known version is by Parañcōti Muṉivar.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kanta Purāṇam
summary: Kacciyappa Civācāriyar’s Tamil Skanda Purāṇa, recounting Murukaṉ’s birth and his war against the asura Cūrapatmaṉ (Śūrapadma), traditionally first recited at the Kumarakōṭṭam shrine in Kanchipuram.

type:LABEL: text
name: Āndhra Mahābhāratamu
summary: The Telugu Mahābhārata of the “poet trinity” (kavitrayam): Nannaya began it under the Eastern Cāḷukya king Rājarāja Narēndra (11th c.), Tikkana wrote fifteen books from the Virāṭa onward (13th c.), and Errana completed the Araṇya book (14th c.).

type:LABEL: text
name: Raṅganātha Rāmāyaṇamu
summary: Telugu Rāmāyaṇa in dvipada couplets by Gona Budda Reddy (pen-name Raṅganātha), 13th–14th c. Its singable metre suited folk and puppet performance; it contains popular episodes absent from Vālmīki, such as the squirrel who helps build the bridge and Lakṣmaṇa drawing a protective line.

type:LABEL: text
name: Āndhra Mahābhāgavatamu (Pōtana)
summary: Bammera Pōtana’s 15th-century Telugu rendering of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, dedicated not to a king but to Rāma; much loved for its Gajendra-mokṣa and Kṛṣṇa narratives.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vikramārjuna Vijaya (Pampa Bhārata)
summary: The Kannada Mahābhārata in campū form by the Jain poet Pampa, completed c. 941 CE at the court of the Vēmulavāḍa Cāḷukya Arikēsari II; Pampa equates his patron with the hero Arjuna.

type:LABEL: text
name: Karṇāṭa Bhārata Kathāmañjarī (Gadugina Bhārata)
summary: Kumāravyāsa’s Kannada Mahābhārata (first ten books) in bhāminī ṣaṭpadi six-line stanzas, completed c. 1430 under the Vijayanagara king Dēvarāya II; it remains a living recitation text (gamaka) in Karnataka.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vacanas of Basavaṇṇa
summary: The free-verse Kannada sayings (vacana) attributed to Basava, addressed to Kūḍalasaṅgamadēva, criticising temple ritual and caste and exalting the devotee’s body as Śiva’s temple.

type:LABEL: text
name: Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇam Kiḷippāṭṭu
summary: Eḻuttacchaṉ’s 16th-century Malayalam rendering of the Sanskrit Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa in the “parrot-song” form, in which a parrot recites the story; it is read aloud in Kerala households during the month of Karkkaṭakam.

type:LABEL: text
name: Saptakāṇḍa Rāmāyaṇa (Assamese)
summary: Mādhava Kandali’s 14th-century Assamese rendering of Vālmīki, made for the Barāhī (Kachari) king Mahāmāṇikya — among the earliest renderings of a Sanskrit epic into a modern Indo-Aryan language. Its first and last books were lost and replaced in the 16th century by Mādhavadeva (Ādi) and Śaṅkaradeva (Uttara).

type:LABEL: text
name: Kīrtana Ghoṣā
summary: Śaṅkaradeva’s Assamese collection of devotional narrative songs, largely drawn from the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the core scripture recited in the nāmghars and sattras of Ekaśaraṇa Vaiṣṇavism.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śāraḷā Mahābhārata
summary: Śāraḷā Dāsa’s 15th-century Odia Mahābhārata, begun under the Gajapati Kapilendra Deva (r. 1435–1467). It follows the Bhārata outline but adds many episodes and Odia local colour, written in colloquial, unsanskritised Odia.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa
summary: Śāraḷā Dāsa’s Odia narrative of a war against a thousand-headed Rāvaṇa of the land of Vilaṅkā, after the defeat of the ten-headed one — a theme shared with the Sanskrit Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa’s Sahasra-Rāvaṇa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Odia Bhāgabata
summary: Jagannātha Dāsa’s Odia rendering of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (late 15th – early 16th c.), in a simple nine-syllable metre; it became the most widely read devotional book of Odisha and the basis of village Bhāgabata-ghara reading houses.

type:LABEL: text
name: Manasāmaṅgal
summary: Bengali Maṅgalkāvya narratives of the snake goddess Manasā, centred on the merchant Cā̃d Sadāgar’s refusal to worship her and the devotion of his daughter-in-law Behulā, who wins back her dead husband Lakhindar.

type:LABEL: text
name: Caitanya Caritāmṛta
summary: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja’s Bengali–Sanskrit biography and theology of Caitanya (early 17th c.), which the Gauḍīya tradition treats as definitive; it presents Caitanya as Kṛṣṇa who took on the emotion and complexion of Rādhā.

type:LABEL: text
name: Eknāthī Bhāgavata
summary: Eknāth’s Marathi ovī commentary on the eleventh book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (the Uddhava-gītā), 16th c.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tukārām Gāthā
summary: The collection of Marathi abhaṅgas attributed to Tukārām (traditionally c. 4,500), sung by Vārkarī pilgrims on the road to Pandharpur.

type:LABEL: text
name: Sūrsāgar
summary: The “Ocean of Sūr”: the corpus of Braj Bhāṣā songs attributed to Sūrdās, chiefly on Kṛṣṇa’s childhood and the love of Rādhā and the gopīs, arranged in later recensions in twelve books after the Bhāgavata. Most of the received corpus is later than Sūr; Hawley and Bryant reconstruct an early core from manuscripts.

type:LABEL: text
name: Hanumān Cālīsā
summary: Forty-verse Awadhi hymn to Hanumān, traditionally attributed to Tulsīdās and now the most widely recited Hindu devotional hymn in North India.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vākhs of Lal Ded
summary: Kashmiri four-line mystical sayings (vākh) attributed to the 14th-century yoginī Lal Ded (Lallā), venerated by Hindus as Lalleśvarī and by Muslims as Lal ʿĀrifa; they survived orally and were first written down systematically in the 20th century.

type:LABEL: text
name: Gāhā Sattasaī
summary: An anthology of 700 Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit love verses attributed to the Sātavāhana king Hāla; dated between the 1st and 7th centuries (before Bāṇa, 7th c.). One verse mentions Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā, the earliest known literary mention of her.

type:LABEL: text
name: Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa
summary: A Sanskrit Śākta-inflected Rāma narrative in 27 sargas framed as a secret telling by Vālmīki to Bharadvāja. Sītā is born to Mandodarī, and in the climax she takes the form of Mahākālī and destroys the thousand-headed Sahasra-Rāvaṇa after Rāma falls unconscious.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bhaṭṭikāvya (Rāvaṇavadha)
summary: Bhaṭṭi’s 6th–7th-century Sanskrit mahākāvya telling the Rāma story while illustrating the rules of Pāṇini’s grammar; it was the model for the first half of the Old Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Uttarapurāṇa of Guṇabhadra
summary: The 9th-century Digambara Jain Sanskrit universal history completing Jinasena’s Ādipurāṇa; its Rāma section follows a different Jain line from Vimalasūri, making Sītā the daughter of Rāvaṇa and Mandodarī, abandoned at birth because of a prophecy.

type:LABEL: text
name: Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra
summary: A Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra (c. 4th–5th c.) whose frame story has the Buddha visiting Laṅkā at the invitation of its king Rāvaṇa, who questions him on the dharma.

type:LABEL: text
name: Hikayat Seri Rama (Malay)
summary: The Malay prose Rāma narrative, put into its present form between the 13th and 17th centuries, with Islamic framing in some versions (Dasaratha as a descendant of the prophet Adam). Its oldest manuscript, in the Bodleian Library, was acquired by Archbishop Laud by 1633.

type:LABEL: text
name: Yama Zatdaw (Burmese)
summary: The Burmese Rāma tradition (Yamayana), known in Bagan-period terracottas as the Dasaratha Jātaka and in literature from a 1527 pyo poem; it was reshaped in the Konbaung period by Thai court drama brought back after the conquest of Ayutthaya.

type:LABEL: text
name: Phra Lak Phra Lam (Lao)
summary: The Lao Rāma epic, framed as a jātaka: Phra Lam is a previous birth of the Buddha, and Rāvaṇa (Hapmanasouane) is his cousin, compared with Devadatta or Māra. Versions were recorded on palm leaf from the 15th to the early 19th century.

type:LABEL: text
name: Jayākhya Saṃhitā
summary: One of the “three gems” of the Pāñcarātra canon, a ritual and theological saṃhitā edited in 1931; its date is disputed, from an early proposal of c. 5th c. to later scholarship placing it around the 8th–9th c.

type:LABEL: text
name: Sāttvata Saṃhitā
summary: Among the oldest and most authoritative Pāñcarātra saṃhitās (one of the “three gems”), with a commentary by Alaśiṅga Bhaṭṭa; date disputed.

type:LABEL: text
name: Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā
summary: Pāñcarātra saṃhitā known for its doctrine of the Sudarśana (Viṣṇu’s discus) and its cosmology; the subject of Schrader’s pioneering 1916 study, which placed it early, a dating later scholars question.

type:LABEL: text
name: Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā
summary: The earliest surviving tantra of the Śaiva Mantramārga, in five books; its editors date the oldest layer (Mūlasūtra) to c. 450–550 CE. It preserves an early stage of Śaiva Siddhānta ritual and the transition from the Atimārga.

type:LABEL: text
name: Brahmayāmala (Picumata)
summary: An early Vidyāpīṭha tantra of the Bhairava stream, centred on Kapālīśabhairava and the goddess Caṇḍā Kāpālinī with their yoginīs; studied by Hatley as a key source for early Śākta-Śaiva yoginī cults.

type:LABEL: text
name: Civañāṉapōtam (Śivajñānabodham)
summary: Meykaṇṭār’s 13th-century twelve-sūtra Tamil treatise that founded the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta school; tradition calls it a rendering of twelve Sanskrit verses from the Raurava Āgama, a claim scholars treat cautiously.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tantrāloka
summary: Abhinavagupta’s encyclopaedic Sanskrit exposition of Trika Śaiva ritual and doctrine (c. 1000 CE), in thirty-seven chapters, based above all on the Mālinīvijayottara Tantra.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nāthamuni
summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya (9th–10th c.) of Vīranārāyaṇapuram (Kāṭṭumaṉṉārkōyil), credited with collecting and arranging the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham and setting it to music; grandfather of Yāmuna.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi
summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-compiler of Tirunāraiyūr (10th–11th c.) who arranged the Tēvāram and other hymns into the first eleven books of the Tirumurai; tradition links his work to Rājarāja I.

type:LABEL: person
name: Māṇikkavācakar
summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint, author of the Tiruvācakam and Tirukkōvaiyār (Tirumurai 8); hagiography makes him a minister of a Pāṇḍya king who renounced office after meeting Śiva at Tirupperuntuṟai. Most scholars place him in the 9th century, though earlier dates are proposed.

type:LABEL: person
name: Cēkkiḻār
summary: Tamil poet and minister at the court of the Cōḻa king Kulōttuṅka II (12th c.), author of the Periya Purāṇam.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nakkīrar
summary: Tamil poet to whom the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai is attributed; tradition (including the Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam) makes him the president of the Madurai academy (caṅkam) who dared to challenge Śiva’s poem.

type:LABEL: person
name: Iḷaṅkō Aṭikaḷ
summary: The “venerable prince-ascetic,” brother of the Cēra king Ceṅkuṭṭuvaṉ according to the prologue of the Cilappatikāram, to whom the epic is attributed; the attribution rests on a later prologue and is doubted.

type:LABEL: person
name: Periyāḻvār
summary: Āḻvār of Śrīvilliputtūr (8th–9th c.), author of the Periyāḻvār Tirumoḻi with its celebrated poems of Kṛṣṇa’s infancy and of the Tiruppallāṇṭu; foster-father of Āṇṭāḷ.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nannaya
summary: Telugu poet (11th c.), “first poet” (ādikavi) of Telugu, who began the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu at the request of the Eastern Cāḷukya king Rājarāja Narēndra.

type:LABEL: person
name: Tikkana
summary: Telugu poet and minister (13th c.) who rendered fifteen books (Virāṭa to Svargārohaṇa) of the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu.

type:LABEL: person
name: Errana
summary: Telugu poet (14th c.) at the court of Prolaya Vēma Reḍḍi who completed the Araṇya book of the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu.

type:LABEL: person
name: Gona Budda Reddy (Raṅganātha)
summary: Telugu poet (13th–14th c.), author under the pen-name Raṅganātha of the dvipada Raṅganātha Rāmāyaṇamu.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bammera Pōtana
summary: Telugu poet (15th c.) of Bammera near Warangal, author of the Āndhra Mahābhāgavatamu, who according to tradition refused to dedicate his work to the king of Rācakoṇḍa and offered it to Rāma.

type:LABEL: person
name: Pampa (Ādikavi Pampa)
summary: Jain Kannada poet (902–c. 955) at the Vēmulavāḍa Cāḷukya court of Arikēsari II, author of the Ādipurāṇa (941) and the Vikramārjuna Vijaya.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kumāravyāsa
summary: Kannada poet (Nāraṇappa, early 15th c.) of Gadag, author of the Karṇāṭa Bhārata Kathāmañjarī, active under Dēvarāya II of Vijayanagara.

type:LABEL: person
name: Tuñcattu Rāmānujaṉ Eḻuttacchaṉ
summary: Malayalam poet (16th c.), called the father of modern Malayalam literature, author of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇam Kiḷippāṭṭu and a Mahābhāratam Kiḷippāṭṭu.

type:LABEL: person
name: Mādhava Kandali
summary: Assamese poet (14th c.) who rendered Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa into Assamese for the Barāhī king Mahāmāṇikya.

type:LABEL: person
name: Śrīmanta Śaṅkaradeva
summary: Assamese saint, poet, dramatist and founder of Ekaśaraṇa Vaiṣṇavism (1449–1568), author of the Kīrtana Ghoṣā, the Aṅkīyā Nāṭ one-act plays and the Bargīt songs, and of the Uttara kāṇḍa of the Assamese Rāmāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: person
name: Mādhavadeva
summary: Assamese poet and chief disciple of Śaṅkaradeva (16th c.), author of the Nām Ghoṣā and of the Ādi kāṇḍa of the Assamese Rāmāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: person
name: Śāraḷā Dāsa
summary: Odia poet (15th c.) of the reign of the Gajapati Kapilendra Deva, author of the Odia Mahābhārata, the Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa and the Caṇḍī Purāṇa; his name, “by the grace of Sāraḷā,” refers to his goddess.

type:LABEL: person
name: Jagannātha Dāsa
summary: Odia poet (late 15th – 16th c.) of Puri, one of the Pañcasakhā, author of the Odia Bhāgabata and founder of the Atibaḍī tradition.

type:LABEL: person
name: Eknāth
summary: Marathi poet-saint of Paiṭhaṇ (c. 1533–1599), author of the Eknāthī Bhāgavata and the Bhāvārtha Rāmāyaṇa, who produced a corrected text of the Jñāneśvarī in 1584.

type:LABEL: person
name: Tukārām
summary: Marathi poet-saint of Dehū (1608 or 1598 – 1649/1650), a grocer by caste whose abhaṅgas to Viṭṭhala are central to the Vārkarī pilgrimage.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nāmdev
summary: Marathi poet-saint (traditionally 1270–1350), a tailor of Pandharpur, devotee of Viṭṭhala and contemporary of Jñāneśvar; songs attributed to him are also in the Sikh Ādi Granth.

type:LABEL: person
name: Sūrdās
summary: Braj Bhāṣā poet-singer of the 16th century to whom the Sūrsāgar is attributed; hagiography makes him blind and a disciple of Vallabha, claims modern scholarship treats as later constructions.

type:LABEL: person
name: Lal Ded (Lalleśvarī)
summary: Kashmiri yoginī-poet of the 14th century, revered by Hindus as Lalleśvarī and by Muslims as Lal ʿĀrifa, to whom the vākhs are attributed.

type:LABEL: person
name: Narsinh Mehtā
summary: Gujarati poet-saint of Junagadh (c. 1414 – 1480s), honoured as the Ādi Kavi of Gujarati, devotee of Kṛṣṇa and author of the bhajan “Vaiṣṇava jana to.”

type:LABEL: person
name: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja
summary: Gauḍīya poet-theologian of Vṛndāvana (16th–17th c.), author of the Caitanya Caritāmṛta.

type:LABEL: person
name: Meykaṇṭār
summary: Tamil Śaiva theologian (13th c.) of Tiruveṇṇainallūr, author of the Civañāṉapōtam and founder of the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta lineage.

type:LABEL: person
name: Abhinavagupta
summary: Kashmirian Śaiva philosopher and aesthetician (fl. c. 975–1025), author of the Tantrāloka, of commentaries on Utpaladeva’s Pratyabhijñā and of the Abhinavabhāratī on the Nāṭyaśāstra.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rama I (Phutthayotfa Chulalok)
summary: First king of the Chakri dynasty of Siam (r. 1782–1809), founder of Bangkok, under whom the canonical Ramakien was compiled (1797–1807), partly by the king himself.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kulōttuṅka Cōḻa II
summary: Cōḻa king (r. 1133–1150) at whose court Cēkkiḻār composed the Periya Purāṇam; Śaiva tradition associates him with the expansion of the Chidambaram temple.

type:LABEL: person
name: Lakṣmaṇasena
summary: King of the Sena dynasty of Bengal (r. c. 1178–1206), at whose court tradition places Jayadeva together with the poets Umāpatidhara, Śaraṇa, Govardhana and Dhoyī.

type:LABEL: person
name: Arikēsari II
summary: Vēmulavāḍa Cāḷukya ruler (10th c.), a feudatory of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa Kṛṣṇa III, patron of Pampa, who equated him with Arjuna in the Vikramārjuna Vijaya.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Viṭṭhala (Viṭhobā) of Pandharpur
summary: The deity of Pandharpur in Maharashtra, standing with hands on hips upon a brick, worshipped by Vārkarīs as a form of Kṛṣṇa/Viṣṇu; scholars debate his origins (pastoral hero-stone, Jain, Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava elements).
earliest_material: 15th–16th c. CE, with major expansion under Kṛṣṇadevarāya (1509–1529)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Māyōṉ (Tamil)
summary: The “dark one,” presiding deity of the mullai (forest-pasture) landscape in the Tolkāppiyam, and in Caṅkam poetry a dark cowherd god (also called Māl, Tirumāl) later identified with Viṣṇu and Kṛṣṇa. Kept distinct from deity:vishnu and joined by IDENTIFIED_WITH.

type:LABEL: character
name: Nappiṉṉai (Piññai)
summary: The Tamil cowherd girl beloved of Kṛṣṇa (Māyavaṉ) in the Cilappatikāram’s round-dance of the cowherdesses and in the Āḻvārs’ hymns, where she is his consort; some scholars see her as a southern parallel or precursor of Rādhā, others identify her with Nīḷā Devī.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vaḷḷi
summary: Murukaṉ’s Tamil consort, a hunter (kuṟava) girl of the hills whom the god woos in disguise; she stands beside Teyvāṉai (Devasenā), daughter of Indra, in Tamil tradition.

type:LABEL: character
name: Suvannamaccha
summary: Mermaid princess, daughter of Thotsakan (Rāvaṇa), in Thai and other Southeast Asian Rāma tellings; sent to sabotage the causeway to Laṅkā, she falls in love with Hanumān and bears him a son, Macchanu.

type:LABEL: character
name: Macchanu
summary: Son of Hanumān and the mermaid Suvannamaccha in the Ramakien, half monkey and half fish, who later meets and fights his father before they recognise each other.

type:LABEL: character
name: Thotsakan
summary: The ten-faced king of Laṅkā in the Thai Ramakien — the counterpart of Rāvaṇa (the name renders Daśakaṇṭha) — who in this telling is the father of Sida, keeps his heart outside his body, and dies when Hanumān crushes it.

type:LABEL: character
name: Māyā-Sītā (the illusory Sītā)
summary: The illusory double or reflection of Sītā who, in the Kūrma Purāṇa, Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa and Tulsīdās’s Rāmcaritmānas, is the one Rāvaṇa abducts while the real Sītā is kept safe in Agni.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bhāmaṇḍala
summary: In Jain Rāma tellings (Vimalasūri’s Paumacariya and successors), Sītā’s twin brother, carried off at birth and raised as a vidyādhara prince, who falls in love with Sītā from her portrait and seeks her hand before learning that she is his twin sister.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sahasra-Rāvaṇa (the thousand-headed Rāvaṇa)
summary: A thousand-headed elder brother or double of Rāvaṇa who, in the Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa, is destroyed by Sītā in the form of Mahākālī after Rāma is struck down; a thousand-headed Rāvaṇa is also fought in Śāraḷā Dāsa’s Odia Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kaṇṇaki
summary: Heroine of the Cilappatikāram, who proves her executed husband Kōvalaṉ innocent before the Pāṇḍya king, burns Madurai with her curse and is deified as the chaste goddess Pattiṉi, worshipped in Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Sri Lanka.

type:LABEL: place
name: Pandharpur
summary: Town on the Bhīmā (Candrabhāgā) river in Maharashtra, seat of the Viṭṭhala temple and goal of the Vārkarī pilgrimages (vārī) of Āṣāḍha and Kārttika.

type:LABEL: place
name: Śrīvilliputtūr
summary: Temple town in Virudhunagar district, Tamil Nadu, home of Periyāḻvār and Āṇṭāḷ according to tradition, with twin shrines of Āṇṭāḷ and Vaṭapatrasāyī (Raṅganātha).

type:LABEL: place
name: Nevāsā
summary: Town on the Pravarā near its confluence with the Godāvarī (Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra), identified by tradition as the place where the Jñāneśvarī was composed, home of the Mohinīrāja (Mahālayā) temple named in the colophon.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Vārkarī
summary: The Marathi devotional tradition of Viṭṭhala of Pandharpur, carried by pilgrims (vārkarī) who walk to Pandharpur twice a year singing the abhaṅgas of Jñāneśvar, Nāmdev, Eknāth, Tukārām and other saints.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Ekaśaraṇa Dharma
summary: The Assamese Vaiṣṇava movement founded by Śaṅkaradeva (15th–16th c.): exclusive refuge in Kṛṣṇa through congregational singing and hearing of his name and deeds, organised in sattras and village nāmghars; Rādhā is not worshipped alongside Kṛṣṇa.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Puṣṭimārga
summary: The Kṛṣṇa tradition founded by Vallabha (16th c.), centred on Śrīnāthjī and the “eight seals” (aṣṭachāp) of poets, among whom it counts Sūrdās.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Rāmānandī
summary: The North Indian Vaiṣṇava ascetic order tracing itself to Rāmānanda, centred on Rāma and Sītā; it claims Tulsīdās and is traditionally associated with the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Rāmlīlā
summary: North Indian staged performance of the Rāma story based on Tulsīdās’s Rāmcaritmānas, held around Dussehra over ten to twelve days or (at Ramnagar, Varanasi) a month; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2005).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Kūṭiyāṭṭam
summary: Sanskrit theatre of Kerala performed by Cākyār and Nampyār families in temple theatres (kūttampalam), with long elaborations of single acts of Sanskrit plays (including Rāma plays); inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2001).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Yakṣagāna
summary: Dance-drama of coastal Karnataka, led by a singer-narrator (bhāgavata), performing episodes (prasaṅga) from the Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and Bhāgavata; an inscription of 1556 at Kurugodu records land given to performers.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Kathakaḷi
summary: Kerala dance-drama that crystallised in the 16th–17th centuries from Rāmanāṭṭam (attributed to the Kottarakkara Tampurāṉ) and Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam (of the Zamorin Mānavēdaṉ), performing Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and Bhāgavata stories.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Wayang
summary: Indonesian puppet and shadow theatre (wayang kulit and related forms) led by a dalang with gamelan, performing stories from the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa among others; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2003).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Khon
summary: Thai masked dance-drama performing episodes of the Ramakien, historically a court art; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2018 as “Khon, masked dance drama in Thailand.”

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Royal Ballet of Cambodia
aliases: Khmer classical dance|Robam Preah Reach Trop
summary: Khmer classical court dance, whose repertoire includes Reamker episodes; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2003).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Triyampawai–Trippawai ceremony
summary: Thai royal Brahman new-year ceremony (December–January) whose name comes from two Tamil devotional poems — Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvempāvai and Āṇṭāḷ’s Tiruppāvai — and during which hymns from these collections are chanted; it was historically linked to the Giant Swing in Bangkok.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Cāḷukyas of Vēmulavāḍa
summary: A 9th–10th-century dynasty in northern Telangana, feudatories of the Rāṣṭrakūṭas, patrons of the Kannada poet Pampa under Arikēsari II.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Rattanakosin Kingdom (Chakri dynasty)
summary: The Siamese kingdom ruled from Bangkok by the Chakri dynasty from 1782, under whose first kings the Ramakien was compiled and the Wat Phra Kaew murals painted.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Sena dynasty of Bengal
summary: Dynasty ruling Bengal in the 11th–13th centuries, whose king Lakṣmaṇasena is traditionally Jayadeva’s patron.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Prambanan Rāmāyaṇa reliefs illustrate the Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa
summary: The claim that the 9th-century Rāmāyaṇa reliefs on the Śiva and Brahmā temples at Prambanan follow the Old Javanese Kakawin. Since Stutterheim (1925) scholars have noted episodes that diverge from the Kakawin and suggest another, possibly oral, telling.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Sūrdās was a disciple of Vallabha
summary: The Puṣṭimārga hagiographic claim (Caurāsī Vaiṣṇavan kī Vārtā) that Sūrdās was initiated by Vallabha and became one of the aṣṭachāp poets; Hawley argues the connection is a later sectarian construction.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Basava founded the Vīraśaiva / Liṅgāyata tradition
summary: The traditional claim that Basava founded the Liṅgāyata community; modern scholars using Kalacuri-period inscriptions and the vacana corpus often see him as a reformer and organiser of an existing Śaiva milieu.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Dasaratha Jātaka preserves an older form of the Rāma story than Vālmīki
summary: Argued in the 19th century (notably by Albrecht Weber) because of the jātaka’s simpler plot and sibling-marriage motif; most later scholars regard it as a Buddhist reworking of a story already known in Rāmāyaṇa form, though its verses may be old.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Āgamas and Tantras
summary: The large body of post-Vedic scriptures (Āgama, Tantra, Saṃhitā) of the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra and Śākta traditions, which regulate initiation, mantra, temple building, image worship, festivals and yoga.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Devotional (bhakti) literature
summary: Devotional poetry, song and hagiography addressed to Śiva, Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa/Rāma, the Goddess and other deities in Tamil, Kannada, Telugu, Marathi, Hindi dialects, Bengali, Assamese, Odia, Gujarati, Kashmiri and other languages, from the Tamil saints of c. 6th–9th c. onward.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Regional and vernacular retellings
summary: Tellings of the Rāma and Bhārata narratives (and of Purāṇic material) in Indian languages, in later Sanskrit, and in Jain and Buddhist traditions. Each telling is recorded as a work with its own date, author and theology, not as a deviation from an original.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Southeast Asian adaptations
summary: Rāma and other Indic narratives as written, carved, recited and performed in Java, Bali, Cambodia, Thailand, Laos, Myanmar and the Malay world, from the Old Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa (late 9th–early 10th c.) to the Thai Ramakien of Rama I (1797–1807).

type:LABEL: text
name: Kamba Rāmāyaṇam (Irāmāvatāram)
summary: The Tamil Rāma epic of the poet Kampaṉ, in six kāṇṭams of viruttam verse (c. 10,500 stanzas in the standard edition), dated variously between the 9th and 12th centuries. It is the most celebrated Tamil telling and is shaped by Tamil poetics and Śrīvaiṣṇava devotion.

type:LABEL: text
name: Rāmcaritmānas
summary: Tulsīdās’s Awadhi Rāma epic in seven kāṇḍs of caupāī–dohā verse, begun at Ayodhyā in Saṃvat 1631 (1574 CE) according to the poem itself. It is the dominant Rāma text of North India and the basis of the Rāmlīlā.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kṛttivāsī Rāmāyaṇa
summary: The Bengali Rāma narrative (Śrīrām Pā̃cālī) attributed to Kṛttibās Ojhā, composed probably in the 15th century in the pā̃cālī form for recitation and singing, and the most widely read Rāmāyaṇa in Bengal.

type:LABEL: text
name: Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa
summary: A Sanskrit Rāma narrative in seven kāṇḍas presented as a Śiva–Pārvatī dialogue within the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, re-reading the story through Advaita Vedānta: Rāma is the supreme Brahman and events are his līlā. Dated to roughly the 13th–15th c.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tēvāram
summary: The Tamil Śaiva hymns (patikams) of Campantar, Appar and Cuntarar (7th–8th c.), forming the first seven books of the Tirumurai; about 796 hymns survive. The hymns praise Śiva at named temples, which tradition counts as the 275 Pāṭal Peṟṟa Talams.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nālāyira Divya Prabandham
summary: The “Four Thousand Sacred Compositions”: Tamil hymns of the twelve Āḻvārs (c. 6th–9th c.) praising Viṣṇu at named shrines, compiled by Nāthamuni in the 9th–10th century. Śrīvaiṣṇavas regard it as a Tamil Veda and recite it in temple worship.

type:LABEL: text
name: Periya Purāṇam
summary: Cēkkiḻār’s 12th-century Tamil hagiography of the sixty-three Śaiva saints (Nāyaṉmār), composed at the Cōḻa court of Kulōttuṅka II and placed as the twelfth and last book of the Tirumurai.

type:LABEL: text
name: Gītagovinda
summary: Jayadeva’s 12th-century Sanskrit lyrical poem in twelve cantos (24 songs, aṣṭapadī) on the love, separation and reunion of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. It is the first major Sanskrit work centred on Rādhā and is sung nightly in the Jagannātha temple, Puri.

type:LABEL: text
name: Jñāneśvarī
summary: Jñānadeva’s Marathi ovī commentary (Bhāvārthadīpikā) on the Bhagavad Gītā in eighteen chapters, completed in Śaka 1212 (1290 CE) according to its colophon. It is the foundational scripture of the Vārkarī tradition and among the earliest major works of Marathi literature.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa (Old Javanese)
summary: The Old Javanese Rāmāyaṇa in kakawin (Indic-metre court poetry), the longest kakawin of the Hindu-Buddhist period, composed in Central Java c. 856–930 CE. Its first half closely follows the Sanskrit Bhaṭṭikāvya rather than Vālmīki.

type:LABEL: text
name: Ramakien (Thai)
summary: The Thai national Rāma epic. Earlier Ayutthaya-period versions were largely lost in 1767; the canonical recension was compiled under King Rama I (Phutthayotfa Chulalok) in 1797–1807, partly written by the king, and a shorter version for dance-drama was made under Rama II.

type:LABEL: text
name: Reamker (Khmer)
summary: The Khmer Rāma epic (Rāmakerti, “Glory of Rāma”), whose surviving text dates from the 16th–17th c. (first part) and later centuries. It recasts the story in Theravāda Buddhist terms and is a mainstay of Cambodian court dance and Lkhon Khol masked theatre.

type:LABEL: text
name: Paumacariya of Vimalasūri (Jain)
summary: The earliest Jain telling of the Rāma story, in Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit, by Vimalasūri. Its own colophon dates it 530 (variant 520) years after Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa; scholars disagree on how to convert this and many place the work between the 1st and 5th centuries CE.

type:LABEL: text
name: Dasaratha Jātaka (Buddhist)
summary: Jātaka no. 461 of the Pali canon’s Jātaka collection: a birth-story in which Rāma-paṇḍita, the Bodhisatta, his brother Lakkhaṇa and their sister Sītā, children of King Dasaratha of Bārāṇasī, live twelve years in the Himalaya. There is no abduction and no Rāvaṇa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Cilappatikāram
summary: The Tamil epic of Kaṇṇaki and Kōvalaṉ attributed to Iḷaṅkō Aṭikaḷ, in three books set in the Cōḻa, Pāṇḍya and Cēra capitals, probably composed around the 5th–6th century. It contains early Tamil depictions of Kṛṣṇa, Murukaṉ and Koṟṟavai worship.

type:LABEL: character
name: Rādhā
summary: The cowherd beloved of Kṛṣṇa. She is not named in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa; the earliest datable literary mentions are scattered Prakrit and Sanskrit verses (Gāhā Sattasaī, 9th-c. poetics), she becomes the heroine of Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda (12th c.), and the supreme goddess of the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa and Gauḍīya theology.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Murukaṉ (Tamil)
summary: The Tamil god of the hills, Cēyōṉ (“the red one”) of the Tolkāppiyam, praised in the Paripāṭal and Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai. From the late Caṅkam period he converges with the northern Skanda-Kārttikeya; the two are kept as separate ids here, joined by an IDENTIFIED_WITH assertion.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Pāñcarātra
summary: The Vaiṣṇava ritual and theological tradition of the Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās, centred on Vāsudeva-Nārāyaṇa and the doctrine of four emanations (vyūha: Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha). It governs worship in many South Indian Vaiṣṇava temples, including Srirangam.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Śaiva Siddhānta
summary: The dualist, Veda-congruent school of the Śaiva Mantramārga, based on the Siddhānta Āgamas (traditionally 28), systematised by Kashmirian exegetes (Sadyojyoti, Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha) and later by Aghoraśiva at Chidambaram. In Tamil it fused with the Tirumurai hymns through Meykaṇṭār’s Civañāṉapōtam (13th c.).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Śrīvaiṣṇava
summary: The South Indian Vaiṣṇava tradition that joins the Tamil hymns of the Āḻvārs (as a “Tamil Veda”) with Sanskrit Vedānta (Viśiṣṭādvaita) and Pāñcarātra temple ritual, centred on Viṣṇu with Śrī (Lakṣmī). Its ācāryas include Nāthamuni, Yāmuna, Rāmānuja and Vedānta Deśika.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava
summary: The Bengal Vaiṣṇava tradition stemming from Caitanya (1486–1534), centred on the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, with a theology elaborated by the Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana and a hagiographic canon including Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja’s Caitanya Caritāmṛta.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Vīraśaiva / Liṅgāyata
summary: The Kannada-speaking Śaiva tradition associated with Basava (12th c.) and the vacana poets (Allama Prabhu, Akka Mahādēvi and others), marked by wearing the personal iṣṭaliṅga, devotion to Śiva alone, and — in the vacanas — criticism of caste, temple ritual and Brahmanical sacrifice.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Kashmir Śaivism (Trika)
summary: The non-dualist Śaiva traditions of Kashmir — Trika, Krama, Spanda and the Pratyabhijñā philosophy of Somānanda and Utpaladeva — culminating in Abhinavagupta (c. 975–1025) and Kṣemarāja.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Jain tradition
summary: The Jain religion, here recorded chiefly as the source of its own Rāma and Kṛṣṇa tellings (Vimalasūri’s Paumacariya, Raviṣeṇa’s Padmapurāṇa, Svayambhū’s Paumacariu, Guṇabhadra’s Uttarapurāṇa, Hemacandra) and of Jain poets in Kannada and Tamil such as Pampa.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Buddhist tradition
summary: The Buddhist religion, here recorded as the source of the Dasaratha Jātaka, of the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra’s frame story with Rāvaṇa, and of the Theravāda-framed Rāma tellings of mainland Southeast Asia (Lao Phra Lak Phra Lam as a jātaka; Khmer Reamker; Thai Ramakien).

type:LABEL: person
name: Kampaṉ (Kambar)
summary: Tamil poet, author of the Irāmāvatāram (Kamba Rāmāyaṇam), patronised by Caṭaiyappa Vaḷḷal of Tiruveṇṇainallūr. His date is disputed between the 9th and the 12th century, with most modern scholars favouring the 12th.

type:LABEL: person
name: Tulsīdās
summary: Awadhi and Braj poet (d. 1623), author of the Rāmcaritmānas (begun 1574), the Vinaya Patrikā, Kavitāvalī and other Rāma-devotional works; he lived in Ayodhyā and above all in Kāśī (Vārāṇasī).

type:LABEL: person
name: Kṛttibās Ojhā
summary: Bengali poet to whom the Śrīrām Pā̃cālī (Kṛttivāsī Rāmāyaṇa) is attributed; tradition places him at Phuliyā on the Bhāgīrathī and in the 15th century, though the identification of the king he mentions is disputed.

type:LABEL: person
name: Jayadeva
summary: Sanskrit poet of the late 12th century, author of the Gītagovinda; tradition makes him a poet at the court of Lakṣmaṇasena of Bengal, and both Bengal and Odisha claim his birthplace “Kindubilva.” Two hymns attributed to him are in the Sikh Ādi Granth.

type:LABEL: person
name: Jñāneśvar
summary: Marathi poet-saint (traditionally 1275–1296), disciple of his elder brother Nivṛttinātha, author of the Jñāneśvarī (1290) and the Amṛtānubhava, and revered as a founder of the Vārkarī tradition of Viṭṭhala devotion.

type:LABEL: person
name: Āṇṭāḷ
summary: The only woman among the twelve Āḻvārs, foster-daughter of Periyāḻvār at Śrīvilliputtūr, author of the Tiruppāvai (30 verses) and Nācciyār Tirumoḻi (143 verses in the standard count); she is usually dated to the 8th–9th century.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nammāḻvār
summary: The foremost Āḻvār (Caṭakōpaṉ, Māṟaṉ) of Kurukūr (Āḻvārtirunagari) in the far south of Tamil Nadu, author of the Tiruvāymoḻi (1,102 verses) and three shorter works; scholars date him to the 8th–9th century.

type:LABEL: person
name: Appar (Tirunāvukkaracar)
summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint of the 7th century, author of Tirumurai books 4–6. The Periya Purāṇam tells that he was first a Jain monk named Dharmasena, returned to Śaivism, and brought the Pallava king Mahendravarman I back to Śiva.

type:LABEL: person
name: Campantar (Tiruñāṉacampantar)
summary: Tamil Śaiva child-poet of Cīrkāḻi (7th c.), author of Tirumurai books 1–3 — the largest share of the Tēvāram. The Periya Purāṇam narrates his contest with Jain monks at Madurai and the return of the Pāṇḍya king to Śaivism.

type:LABEL: person
name: Cuntarar
summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint of the 8th century (Cuntaramūrtti), author of Tirumurai book 7; his Tiruttoṇṭattokai lists the devotees whom the Periya Purāṇam later expanded into the sixty-three Nāyaṉmār. Tradition calls him the “friend of Śiva” and links him to Tiruvārūr.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rāmānuja
summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya and Vedāntin of Śrīperumbudūr, chief exponent of Viśiṣṭādvaita and author of the Śrībhāṣya; he reorganised worship at Srirangam and, during a sojourn in the Hoysala country, at Melkote. Traditional dates are 1017–1137; many scholars prefer 1077–1157.

type:LABEL: person
name: Caitanya
summary: Bengali Vaiṣṇava saint (1486–1534), born at Navadvīpa, who spent his last two decades at Puri; the Gauḍīya tradition regards him as Kṛṣṇa, and as Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in one body. The eight-verse Śikṣāṣṭaka is the only work accepted as his.

type:LABEL: person
name: Basava
summary: Kannada Śaiva poet and minister at the Kalacuri court of Bijjala II at Kalyāṇa (12th c.), whose vacanas, addressed to Kūḍalasaṅgamadēva, are central to the Vīraśaiva / Liṅgāyata tradition.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vimalasūri
summary: Jain (Śvetāmbara) monk-poet, author of the Prakrit Paumacariya, the earliest surviving Jain Rāma narrative. His date depends on the disputed reading of his colophon (530 years after Mahāvīra) and is placed by scholars anywhere from the 1st to the 5th century CE.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bṛhadīśvara temple, Thanjavur
summary: Granite Śiva temple built by the Cōḻa king Rājarāja I at his capital Thanjavur and consecrated in 1010 CE; its c. 60 m vimāna was the tallest of its age and the walls carry a large corpus of Rājarāja’s own Tamil inscriptions.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bṛhadīśvara temple, Gangaikondacholapuram
summary: Śiva temple at the new capital founded by Rājendra I after his northern campaign to the Gaṅgā (c. 1025); its vimāna has a gently concave profile, unlike Thanjavur’s straight-sided pyramid. Part of the Great Living Chola Temples World Heritage property.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Airāvateśvara temple, Darasuram
summary: Twelfth-century Śiva temple near Kumbakonam built under the Cōḻa king Rājarāja II; its maṇḍapa is designed as a stone chariot and its reliefs include narrative friezes of the 63 Nāyaṉmār saints.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Naṭarāja temple, Chidambaram
summary: Temple of Śiva as Naṭarāja, the cosmic dancer, worshipped in the gold-roofed Kaṉakasabhā; it is the “ether” (ākāśa) shrine among the five element liṅgas and one of the most celebrated temples sung in the Tēvāram.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śrī Raṅganāthasvāmī temple, Srirangam
summary: Island temple of Viṣṇu as Raṅganātha reclining on the serpent, set within seven concentric enclosures on an island of the Kāvēri; first among the 108 Divya Deśams of the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mīnākṣī–Sundareśvara temple, Madurai
summary: Twin-shrine temple of the goddess Mīnākṣī and her consort Sundareśvara (Śiva) at the heart of Madurai; its fourteen painted gopuras, the tallest c. 52 m, largely date from Nāyaka rebuilding in the 16th–17th centuries.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Rāmanāthasvāmī temple, Rameswaram
summary: Śiva temple on Pamban (Rameswaram) island where, according to tradition, Rāma worshipped a liṅga; it is counted among the twelve jyotirliṅgas and as the southern dhāma of the Char Dham, and is known for its very long pillared corridors.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Aruṇācaleśvara temple, Tiruvannamalai
summary: Large temple at the foot of Aruṇācala hill, worshipped as the fire (agni) liṅga among the five element shrines; the hill itself is identified in tradition with the column of fire of the Liṅgodbhava story.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Jambukeśvara temple, Thiruvanaikaval
summary: Śiva temple on Srirangam island worshipped as the water (jala) liṅga among the five element shrines; a spring keeps the sanctum floor moist.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Ekāmbareśvara temple, Kanchipuram
summary: Major Śiva temple of Kanchipuram worshipped as the earth (pṛthvī) liṅga among the five element shrines, centred on a sacred mango tree; its southern gopura is among the tallest in South India.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kailāsanātha temple, Kanchipuram
summary: Sandstone Śiva temple built by the Pallava king Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha around 700 CE, with additions by his son Mahendravarman III; one of the earliest large structural temples of Tamil Nadu.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vaikuṇṭha Perumāḷ temple, Kanchipuram
summary: Eighth-century Pallava Viṣṇu temple built by Nandivarman II Pallavamalla, with three superimposed sanctums and a cloister of relief panels that narrate Pallava dynastic history; a Divya Deśam sung by Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Varadarāja Perumāḷ temple, Kanchipuram
summary: Large Viṣṇu temple of Kanchipuram on the Hastigiri mound, a Divya Deśam closely associated with Rāmānuja; renovated under the Cōḻas from 1053 and expanded by later dynasties.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Group of Monuments at Mamallapuram
summary: Seventh- and eighth-century Pallava port with rock-cut cave temples (maṇḍapas), monolithic rathas, open-air reliefs and the structural Shore Temple; a World Heritage property since 1984.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Shore Temple, Mamallapuram
summary: Granite structural temple on the shore at Mamallapuram, built under Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha around 700–728 CE, combining two Śiva shrines with a shrine of the reclining Viṣṇu.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Pañca Rathas, Mamallapuram
summary: Five monolithic shrines carved from a single granite outcrop in the 7th century, popularly named after the Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī; they model the main types of early Drāviḍa shrine and were never consecrated.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Subrahmaṇya temple, Tirupparankundram
summary: Rock-cut and structural temple of Murukaṉ on a hill outside Madurai, counted first of the six abodes; tradition places Murukaṉ’s marriage to Deivayāṉai (Devasenā) here.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Subrahmaṇya temple, Tiruchendur
summary: Seashore temple of Murukaṉ on the Gulf of Mannar, counted second of the six abodes; tradition places here Murukaṉ’s victory over the demon Śūrapadma, re-enacted in the Skanda Ṣaṣṭhī festival.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi temple, Palani
summary: Hilltop temple of Murukaṉ as the renunciant Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi, counted third of the six abodes and one of the most visited temples in Tamil Nadu.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Svāminātha temple, Swamimalai
summary: Temple of Murukaṉ as Svāminātha near Kumbakonam, counted fourth of the six abodes; tradition says the child Murukaṉ taught Śiva the meaning of Om here.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Subrahmaṇya temple, Tiruttani
summary: Hill temple of Murukaṉ in northern Tamil Nadu, traditionally counted fifth of the six abodes, where Murukaṉ married the hunter-maiden Vaḷḷi in local tradition.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Murukaṉ temple, Pazhamudircholai
summary: Forest-hill shrine of Murukaṉ above the Aḻakar Kōvil near Madurai, counted sixth of the six abodes.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Guruvāyūr temple
summary: Kerala temple of Kṛṣṇa as Guruvāyūrappaṉ (a four-armed Viṣṇu image worshipped as the child Kṛṣṇa), one of the most visited temples of South India.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Padmanābhasvāmī temple, Thiruvananthapuram
summary: Temple of Viṣṇu reclining on Ananta at the heart of Thiruvananthapuram, a Divya Deśam and the tutelary shrine of the Travancore royal house; the opening of its vaults in 2011 revealed a very large treasure.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Veṅkaṭeśvara temple, Tirumala
summary: Hill temple of Veṅkaṭeśvara on the Tirumala range above Tirupati, among the most visited and richest religious institutions in the world; a Divya Deśam sung by the Āḻvārs.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mallikārjuna temple, Srisailam
summary: Fortified hilltop temple above the Krishna gorge that is counted both as a jyotirliṅga (Mallikārjuna) and as a Śakti Pīṭha (Bhramarāmbā); it is also sung in the Tēvāram.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śrīkāḷahastīśvara temple, Srikalahasti
summary: Śiva temple on the Svarṇamukhī river worshipped as the air (vāyu) liṅga among the five element shrines and associated with the hunter-saint Kaṇṇappa; it is sung in the Tēvāram.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Paraśurāmeśvara temple, Gudimallam
summary: Village temple near Renigunta whose apsidal sanctum enshrines the Gudimallam liṅga, a realistic liṅga carved with a standing two-armed figure that is among the earliest surviving images connected with Śiva; the liṅga is dated by most scholars between the 2nd/1st c. BCE and the early centuries CE.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Navabrahma temples, Alampur
summary: Group of nine Śiva temples of the Bādāmi Cālukya period (7th–8th c.) near the confluence of the Tuṅgabhadrā and Kṛṣṇā, unusual in the south for their Nāgara (curvilinear) towers; the nearby Jogulāmbā shrine is counted among the eighteen Mahāśakti Pīṭhas.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Rāmappa (Rudreśvara) temple, Palampet
summary: Kākatīya Śiva temple at Palampet commissioned in 1213 by the general Recherla Rudra under king Gaṇapati; inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2021 and popularly named after its sculptor.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bādāmi cave temples
summary: Four rock-cut cave temples (three Hindu, one Jain) in the sandstone cliff of Vātāpi, capital of the early Cālukyas; Cave 3, dedicated to Viṣṇu, carries an inscription of Śaka 500 (578 CE), making it one of the earliest precisely dated Brahmanical cave temples.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Meguti Jain temple, Aihole
