summary: Jain temple on a hill at Aihole whose east wall bears the Aihole praśasti of Pulakeśin II composed by Ravikīrti and dated Śaka 556 (634/635 CE); it is one of the earliest securely dated structural temples in the Deccan.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Durgā temple, Aihole
summary: Apsidal-ended early Cālukya temple at Aihole (late 7th–early 8th c.) surrounded by a colonnaded ambulatory; its name derives from a later fort (durga) built on it, not from the goddess.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Lāḍ Khān temple, Aihole
summary: Flat-roofed early Cālukya Śiva temple at Aihole, named after a later occupant; its date is a classic problem of Indian architectural history, with proposals ranging from the 5th to the early 8th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Virūpākṣa temple, Pattadakal
summary: The largest temple at Pattadakal, built c. 740–745 CE by Queen Lokamahādevī to commemorate her husband Vikramāditya II’s victory over the Pallavas; its Drāviḍa design closely follows the Kailāsanātha temple of Kanchipuram.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Pāpanātha temple, Pattadakal
summary: Mid-8th-century Cālukya Śiva temple at Pattadakal that fuses Nāgara and Drāviḍa elements and is known for its narrative panels from the Rāmāyaṇa and the Kirātārjunīya.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kailāsa temple (Ellora Cave 16)
summary: A complete Drāviḍa temple carved downward and inward from the basalt hillside at Ellora in the 8th century, generally attributed to the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Kṛṣṇa I (r. c. 756–773); its form evokes Mount Kailāsa, Śiva’s abode.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Daśāvatāra cave (Ellora Cave 15)
summary: Two-storeyed rock-cut temple at Ellora whose plan follows the Buddhist vihāras nearby but whose sculpture is Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava; an inscription of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa founder Dantidurga on the back wall of the front maṇḍapa is key to its date.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Elephanta Caves (Cave 1)
summary: Great Śiva cave on Elephanta island in Mumbai harbour, completed in the mid-6th century, whose colossal three-headed Sadāśiva (Maheśamūrti) is among the masterpieces of Indian sculpture.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Virūpākṣa temple, Hampi
summary: Living Śiva temple of Virūpākṣa–Pampāpati on the Tuṅgabhadrā at Hampi, whose small early shrine was enlarged into a vast complex under the Vijayanagara kings; it predates and outlived the imperial city.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Hazāra Rāma temple, Hampi
summary: Royal chapel of the Vijayanagara palace zone dedicated to Rāma, whose outer and inner walls are covered with friezes of the Rāmāyaṇa and of royal processions; it is attributed to Devarāya I in the early 15th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vijaya Viṭṭhala temple, Hampi
summary: Vijayanagara temple of Viṭṭhala (a form of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa worshipped at Pandharpur) at Hampi, famous for its “musical” pillars and the stone chariot that serves as Garuḍa’s shrine; mostly built in the 15th–16th centuries, with major additions under Kṛṣṇadevarāya.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Cennakeśava temple, Belur
summary: Hoysaḷa temple of Viṣṇu as Cennakeśava commissioned by King Viṣṇuvardhana in 1117 CE at his early capital Belur; its bracket figures and lathe-turned pillars are hallmarks of the Hoysaḷa style.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Hoysaḷeśvara temple, Halebidu
summary: Twin-shrined Śiva temple at the Hoysaḷa capital Dvārasamudra (Halebidu), begun c. 1121 under Viṣṇuvardhana by his officer Ketamalla; its friezes carry thousands of sculptures including Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and Bhāgavata scenes.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Keśava temple, Somanathapura
summary: Triple-shrined (trikūṭa) Hoysaḷa Viṣṇu temple on a star-shaped plan, consecrated by Somanātha Daṇḍanāyaka, a general of Narasiṃha III; Wikipedia gives 1258 CE while many guides give 1268.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śiva temple, Ambarnath
summary: Bhūmija-style Śiva temple near Mumbai bearing an inscription of 1060 CE from the Śilāhāra period, one of the best-preserved 11th-century temples of the northern Konkan.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bhīmaśaṅkara temple
summary: Śiva temple in the Sahyādri forest at the source of the Bhīmā river, claimed as the Bhīmaśaṅkara jyotirliṅga (a claim also made for sites in Assam and elsewhere).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Tryambakeśvara temple
summary: Jyotirliṅga temple near the source of the Godāvarī in the Brahmagiri hills, whose liṅga is a hollow with three small lingas (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva); the present temple was built by the Peshwa Bāḷājī Bājīrāv in the mid-18th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Ghṛṣṇeśvara temple
summary: Jyotirliṅga temple near Ellora, restored by Mālojī Bhosale in the 16th century and rebuilt in its present red-stone form in the 18th century under Holkar patronage.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vaijanātha temple, Parli
summary: Śiva temple at Parli in Marathwada, one of the candidates for the Vaidyanātha jyotirliṅga (the other main claimant being Deoghar in Jharkhand).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Nāganātha temple, Aundha
summary: Hemāḍpanthī-style Śiva temple in Marathwada claimed as the Nāgeśvara jyotirliṅga, one of three competing claimants (with Dwarka and Jageshwar).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Udayagiri caves (Vidiśā)
summary: Group of about twenty rock-cut shrines near Vidiśā excavated under the Gupta king Candragupta II, the only cave site securely tied to a Gupta monarch by inscriptions; Cave 5 holds the monumental relief of Varāha raising the Earth.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Daśāvatāra temple, Deogarh
summary: Late Gupta stone temple of Viṣṇu (c. 500–550 CE) on the Betwā, one of the earliest surviving North Indian temples with a tower; its wall panels show Viṣṇu reclining on Śeṣa, Gajendra-mokṣa and Nara-Nārāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Pārvatī temple, Nachna
summary: Early stone temple at Nachna with a sanctum surrounded by a covered ambulatory and an upper chamber, carved with rock-like rustication; dated by style to the 5th or 6th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bhitargaon brick temple
summary: Late 5th-century Gupta-period brick temple near Kanpur, the oldest surviving roofed brick/terracotta Hindu shrine with a high śikhara; its terracotta panels include Viṣṇu and other Purāṇic subjects.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kaṅkālī Devī temple, Tigawa
summary: Small flat-roofed Gupta-period temple (c. 400–425 CE) with a pillared porch, one of the earliest structural Hindu temples to survive; the doorway shows the river goddesses Gaṅgā and Yamunā.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Muṇḍeśvarī temple
summary: Octagonal stone temple on a hill in Kaimur district, Bihar, worshipped for Muṇḍeśvarī and a four-faced liṅga; it is often promoted as the oldest functioning Hindu temple (108 CE), a date most historians of architecture reject.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Lakṣmaṇa temple, Sirpur
summary: Brick temple at Sirpur (Śrīpura) in Chhattisgarh with a well-preserved śikhara and stone doorframe, the earliest dated monument of the Sirpur group (c. 595–605 CE per Wikipedia; other accounts c. 650).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kandarīya Mahādeva temple, Khajuraho
summary: The largest and most elaborate of the Khajuraho temples, a Śiva temple of c. 1025–1050 CE built under the Candela king Vidyādhara, whose clustered śikhara rises like a mountain range.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Lakṣmaṇa temple, Khajuraho
summary: Candela temple of Vaikuṇṭha Viṣṇu completed by Yaśovarman (Lakṣavarman) and dated by an inscription of Vikrama 1011 (953/954 CE), the earliest securely dated of the great Khajuraho temples.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Sun Temple, Konark
summary: Colossal 13th-century temple of Sūrya conceived as the Sun god’s chariot with 24 carved wheels and seven horses, built c. 1250 under the Eastern Gaṅga king Narasiṃhadeva I; the tower collapsed, and the surviving jagamohana is the largest standing part.
earliest_textual: not before the 10th c.; Orissa chapters probably after the 13th c.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Jagannātha temple, Puri
summary: Temple of Jagannātha with Balabhadra and Subhadrā, worshipped in wooden images periodically renewed (Navakalevara), at Puri; the present temple was begun by the Eastern Gaṅga king Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga in the 12th century, and Puri is the eastern dhāma of the Char Dham.
earliest_textual: not before the 10th c.; Orissa chapters probably after the 13th c.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Liṅgarāja temple, Bhubaneswar
summary: The largest temple of Bhubaneswar (Ekāmra Kṣetra), an 11th-century Kaliṅga-style Śiva temple whose deity is worshipped as Harihara (Śiva–Viṣṇu); it is attributed to Somavaṃśī kings with later Gaṅga additions.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mukteśvara temple, Bhubaneswar
summary: Small 10th-century Kaliṅga-style Śiva temple in Bhubaneswar (c. 950–975 CE), celebrated for its arched gateway (toraṇa) and refined carving, marking the transition to the mature Odishan style.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Causaṭh Yoginī temple, Hirapur
summary: Small circular, roofless (hypaethral) sandstone shrine near Bhubaneswar housing images of sixty-four yoginīs around a central Kālī/Mahāmāyā, dated to the 9th century and associated with the Bhauma-Kara queen Hīrādevī.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kāmākhyā temple, Guwahati
summary: Principal temple of the goddess Kāmākhyā on Nīlācala hill, Guwahati, where an aniconic yoni-shaped stone in a cave is worshipped; one of the oldest centres of tantric Śākta practice and a Śakti Pīṭha in all major lists. The present temple was rebuilt in 1565 under the Koch king Naranārāyaṇa by his brother Chilarai.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kālīghāṭ temple, Kolkata
summary: Temple of Kālī on the old course of the Hooghly (Ādi Gaṅgā) in Kolkata, counted as a Śakti Pīṭha where the toes of Satī’s right foot fell; the present building was completed in 1809 under the Sābarṇa Rāy Caudhurī family.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Dakṣiṇeśvar Kālī temple
summary: Navaratna-style temple of Kālī as Bhavatāriṇī on the Hooghly north of Kolkata, founded by Rāṇī Rāsmaṇi and consecrated on 31 May 1855; Rāmakṛṣṇa served as its priest.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Viṣṇupada temple, Gaya
summary: Temple at Gaya enshrining a footprint of Viṣṇu in basalt, central to the śrāddha rites for ancestors performed at Gaya; the present temple was rebuilt in 1787 by Ahilyābāī Holkar.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Baidyanātha temple, Deoghar
summary: Complex of 22 temples at Deoghar in Jharkhand, the most widely accepted claimant to the Vaidyanātha jyotirliṅga and also claimed as a Śakti Pīṭha; the month of Śrāvaṇa brings very large kāṃvaṛ pilgrimages carrying Gaṅgā water.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kāśī Viśvanātha temple, Varanasi
summary: Temple of Śiva as Viśvanātha (Viśveśvara), “Lord of the Universe”, at Varanasi, one of the twelve jyotirliṅgas; the present temple was built in 1780 by Ahilyābāī Holkar on a site adjacent to the earlier temple.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Somanātha temple, Prabhas Patan
summary: Seashore Śiva temple at Prabhāsa Pāṭan, first of the twelve jyotirliṅgas in the Śiva Purāṇa list; repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt, the present temple in Māru-Gurjara (Cālukya) style was completed in 1951.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Dvārakādhīśa temple, Dwarka
summary: Temple of Kṛṣṇa as “King of Dvārakā” at Dwarka on the Gujarat coast, the western dhāma of the Char Dham and a Divya Deśam; the present five-storeyed structure dates from the 15th–16th centuries.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Nāgeśvara temple, Dwarka
summary: Śiva temple between Dwarka and Bet Dwarka promoted as the Nāgeśvara jyotirliṅga, one of three competing claimants (with Aundha in Maharashtra and Jageshwar in Uttarakhand).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Sun temple, Modhera
summary: Caulukya (Solaṅkī) temple of Sūrya at Modhera with a stepped tank (Sūrya Kuṇḍa) and a detached dance hall; its shrine was built in the reign of Bhīma I, shortly after 1026–27 CE.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mahākāleśvara temple, Ujjain
summary: Jyotirliṅga temple of Śiva as Mahākāla in Ujjain, whose south-facing (dakṣiṇāmūrti) liṅga is worshipped with the dawn bhasma-ārati; the present temple is an 18th-century Marāṭhā-period reconstruction.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Oṃkāreśvara temple
summary: Jyotirliṅga temple on the island of Māndhātā in the Narmadā, whose island is said to resemble the syllable Om; the jyotirliṅga is shared in tradition with the Amaleśvara (Mamaleśvara) temple on the south bank.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bhojeśvara temple, Bhojpur
summary: Unfinished 11th-century Śiva temple at Bhojpur near Bhopal attributed to the Paramāra king Bhoja, housing one of the largest liṅgas in India; construction drawings engraved on the surrounding rock show how the temple was to be completed.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Brahmā temple, Pushkar
summary: Temple of Brahmā beside the sacred lake of Puṣkara in Rajasthan, among the very few temples in India dedicated to Brahmā; the present structure dates from the 14th century with later rebuilding.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Rām Mandir, Ayodhya
aliases: Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Mandir|Ram Janmabhoomi temple
summary: Temple of Rāma in Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh, built in the Nāgara (Māru-Gurjara) style after the Supreme Court of India’s judgment of 9 November 2019 and consecrated (prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā) on 22 January 2024; many Hindus regard the site as Rāma’s birthplace (Rāma Janmabhūmi).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kedāranātha temple
summary: High-altitude stone temple of Śiva at about 3,580 m in the Garhwal Himalaya, a jyotirliṅga, one of the Chota Char Dham and the chief of the Pañca Kedāra; it survived the 2013 flash flood that devastated the town.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Badrīnātha temple
summary: Temple of Viṣṇu as Badrīnārāyaṇa at about 3,100 m on the Alaknandā, the northern dhāma of the Char Dham, one of the Chota Char Dham and a Divya Deśam; it was largely rebuilt after the 1803 Garhwal earthquake.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Gaṅgotrī temple
summary: Temple of the goddess Gaṅgā at about 3,100 m on the Bhāgīrathī, one of the Chota Char Dham; the original temple was built in the early 19th century by the Gorkha general Amar Singh Thapa.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Yamunotrī temple
summary: Temple of the river goddess Yamunā near the source of the Yamunā in the Garhwal Himalaya, the westernmost of the Chota Char Dham; built in the 19th century by a ruler of Tehri Garhwal and rebuilt after destruction by snow and floods.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Jageśvara temple group
summary: Group of more than 100 stone temples (7th–14th c.) in a deodar valley near Almora, claimed locally as the Nāgeśa jyotirliṅga “in the Dāruka forest”; ASI-protected.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mārtaṇḍa Sun temple, Kashmir
summary: Ruined 8th-century temple of Sūrya (Mārtaṇḍa) on a plateau near Anantnag, built by the Kārkoṭa king Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa according to Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī and destroyed in the early 15th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Paśupatinātha temple, Kathmandu
summary: Pagoda-roofed temple of Śiva as Paśupati (“Lord of creatures”) on the Bāgmatī at Deopatan, Kathmandu, Nepal’s principal Hindu shrine; worship here is attested from the Licchavi period, and the present building dates from a renovation of 1692.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Changu Narayan temple
summary: Hilltop Viṣṇu temple east of Kathmandu that preserves the pillar inscription of the Licchavi king Mānadeva (Saṃvat 386, 464 CE), the earliest dated inscription of Nepal; the two-tiered pagoda itself is a later rebuilding, heavily damaged in 2015 and restored.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Jānakī Mandir, Janakpur
summary: White marble-and-stone temple of Sītā (Jānakī) at Janakpur, Nepal, built in 1910 by Queen Vṛṣabhānu of Tikamgarh (Orchha) in a Hindu–Rajput (Mughal-influenced) style; Janakpur is identified by tradition with Mithilā, Sītā’s city.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Muktinātha temple
summary: High-altitude pagoda shrine (c. 3,700 m) in Mustang, Nepal, sacred to Hindus as Viṣṇu Muktinārāyaṇa — a Divya Deśam (Sāḷagrāmam) — and to Tibetan Buddhists as Chumig Gyatsa, an abode of Avalokiteśvara.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kōṇēsvaram temple, Trincomalee
aliases: Thirukonamalai Konesar|Temple of a Thousand Pillars
summary: Śiva temple on Swami Rock above Trincomalee bay, Sri Lanka, praised in the Tēvāram hymns of Campantar and Cuntarar; the medieval complex was destroyed by the Portuguese in 1622–1624 and a fort built from its stones, and the temple was rebuilt in 1952.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Muṉṉēsvaram temple, Chilaw
summary: Śiva temple near Chilaw on Sri Lanka’s west coast, in existence since at least c. 1000 CE; tradition holds that Rāma worshipped Śiva here after the war with Rāvaṇa. It was destroyed twice by the Portuguese and rebuilt in 1753.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Katās Rāj temples
summary: Group of Hindu temples (6th century onward) around a sacred pond in the Salt Range of Punjab, Pakistan; tradition holds that the pond formed from Śiva’s tears after Satī’s death and that the Pāṇḍavas met the Yakṣa here.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Hiṅglāj Mātā cave shrine
summary: Natural cave shrine of the goddess Hiṅgulā in the Hingol valley of Balochistan, Pakistan, counted as a Śakti Pīṭha where part of Satī’s head fell; the spring Hinglaj Yātrā draws very large numbers of pilgrims and is also revered by local Muslims as “Nani”.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Prambanan (Candi Rara Jonggrang)
summary: Ninth-century Hindu temple compound in Central Java with towering shrines to Śiva, Brahmā and Viṣṇu; it is identified with the Śiva temple whose inauguration on 12 November 856 is recorded in the Śivagṛha inscription, and its balustrade reliefs tell the Rāmāyaṇa and the Kṛṣṇa story.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Arjuna temple group, Dieng Plateau
summary: Small Śaiva stone temples on the volcanic Dieng Plateau of Central Java (mid-7th to late 8th c.), among the oldest standing stone structures in Java; their Mahābhārata names (Arjuna, Semar, Srikandi, Puntadewa) were given much later by local people.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Angkor Wat
summary: State temple of the Khmer king Sūryavarman II (r. 1113–c. 1150), built as a temple-mountain to Viṣṇu at Yaśodharapura (Angkor); its galleries carry vast bas-reliefs of the churning of the ocean, the Kurukṣetra battle and the war in Laṅkā. From the late 13th century it became a Theravāda Buddhist monastery.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Banteay Srei
summary: Small, exquisitely carved red-sandstone Śiva temple near Angkor consecrated on 22 April 967 CE, unusual in having been built not by a king but by the court official Yajñavarāha; its pediments include Rāvaṇa shaking Mount Kailāsa.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Preah Vihear temple
summary: Khmer Śiva temple stretched along a north–south axis on a cliff of the Dângrêk escarpment, built mainly in the 11th–12th centuries under Sūryavarman I and Sūryavarman II; the International Court of Justice ruled in 1962 that it lies in Cambodia, and it was inscribed as a World Heritage property in 2008.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vat Phou
summary: Khmer-period Śiva sanctuary at the foot of Mount Phou Kao (Liṅgaparvata, named for its liṅga-shaped summit) in southern Laos, with structures from the 5th to the 13th century; now a Theravāda Buddhist site and a World Heritage property (2001).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mỹ Sơn sanctuary
summary: Valley of Cham brick temple-towers in central Vietnam, the principal religious centre of the kings of Champa from the 4th to the 13th century, dedicated chiefly to Śiva as Bhadreśvara; inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1999.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Pura Besakih
summary: The “mother temple” of Balinese Hinduism, a complex of more than twenty temples terraced on the slopes of Mount Agung; in use as a Hindu sanctuary at least since the 14th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Batu Caves temple
summary: Murukaṉ shrine in limestone caves north of Kuala Lumpur, completed in 1891 and the focus since 1892 of one of the largest Thaipūsam festivals outside India; a very tall gilded statue of Murukaṉ was unveiled beside the steps in January 2006.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Naṭarāja (Śiva as lord of dance)
summary: Śiva as the king of dancers, above all in the South Indian ānanda-tāṇḍava form standardised in Cōḻa bronzes: four-armed, dancing within a ring of flames on the dwarf Apasmāra, worshipped above all at Chidambaram.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Jagannātha
summary: “Lord of the world”, the deity of Puri worshipped in a stylised wooden image with large round eyes and stump arms, together with Balabhadra and Subhadrā; Vaiṣṇavas regard him as Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa, while scholars debate the cult’s tribal, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist and Jain antecedents.
earliest_material: begun under Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga, early–mid 12th c.; completion given as 1161 in Wikipedia’s infobox

type:LABEL: claim
name: The tribal (Śabara) origin hypothesis for Jagannātha
summary: The scholarly hypothesis that Jagannātha began as a wooden deity of tribal (Śabara) communities of Odisha and was progressively integrated into Brahmanical Vaiṣṇavism and royal cult, culminating under the Eastern Gaṅgas.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The claim that the Muṇḍeśvarī temple dates to 108 CE
summary: The claim, displayed by the ASI and the Bihar State Religious Trust Board, that the Muṇḍeśvarī temple was built in 108 CE and is the oldest functioning Hindu temple in the world.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Veṅkaṭeśvara
summary: Viṣṇu as Lord of the Vēṅkaṭa hill, worshipped at Tirumala in a standing four-armed image; one of the most widely worshipped forms of Viṣṇu in South India and the diaspora.
earliest_material: 966 CE gift of a silver image by the Pallava queen Sāmavai (earliest dated gift commonly cited)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Mīnākṣī
summary: The “fish-eyed” goddess of Madurai, who in the temple’s myth is born as a three-breasted Pāṇḍya princess, conquers the world and marries Śiva as Sundareśvara; she is identified with Pārvatī.
earliest_material: 14th c. CE restoration after Sultanate-period destruction

type:LABEL: deity
name: Raṅganātha
summary: Viṣṇu reclining on the serpent Ādiśeṣa, “lord of the stage (raṅga)”, worshipped above all at Srirangam on the Kāvēri.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Yamunā
summary: The river Yamunā personified as a goddess, daughter of Sūrya and sister of Yama, worshipped at her Himalayan source at Yamunotri and along the river, notably at Mathurā and Vṛndāvana.
earliest_material: 19th c. CE (Mahārāja Pratāp Śāh of Tehri Garhwal per Wikipedia), rebuilt since

type:LABEL: place
name: Hampi
summary: Ruined capital of the Vijayanagara empire on the Tuṅgabhadrā in Karnataka, a pilgrimage centre of Virūpākṣa–Pampā and, in local tradition, the Kiṣkindhā of the Rāmāyaṇa; the Group of Monuments at Hampi was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1986.

type:LABEL: place
name: Adam’s Bridge (Rāma Setu)
summary: Chain of limestone shoals and sandbanks, about 48 km long, between Pamban (Rameswaram) Island in India and Mannar Island in Sri Lanka; Hindu tradition identifies it with the causeway built by Rāma’s army to reach Laṅkā.

type:LABEL: place
name: Rameswaram (Pamban island)
summary: Island in the Gulf of Mannar off Tamil Nadu, linked to the mainland by the Pamban bridges, home of the Rāmanāthasvāmī temple and of Dhanushkodi at its south-eastern tip, where pilgrimage tradition places the start of Rāma’s bridge.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rājarāja I
summary: Cōḻa king (r. 985–1014) whose conquests made the Cōḻas the leading power of South India; builder of the Bṛhadīśvara temple at Thanjavur.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rājendra I
summary: Cōḻa king (r. 1014–1044), son of Rājarāja I, whose northern expedition reached the Gaṅgā and whose navy raided Śrīvijaya; founder of Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rājarāja II
summary: Later Cōḻa king (r. c. 1146–1173) under whom the Airāvateśvara temple at Darasuram was built.

type:LABEL: person
name: Parāntaka I
summary: Early Cōḻa king (r. c. 907–955) credited in copper-plate inscriptions with covering the roof of Naṭarāja’s hall at Chidambaram with gold.

type:LABEL: person
name: Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha
summary: Pallava king (r. c. 690–728) who built the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram and the Kailāsanātha temple at Kanchipuram, the first large structural temples of Tamil Nadu.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nandivarman II Pallavamalla
summary: Pallava king (r. c. 731–796) who built the Vaikuṇṭha Perumāḷ temple at Kanchipuram; a contemporary of Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vikramāditya II
summary: Cālukya king of Bādāmi (r. c. 733–746) who captured Kanchipuram from the Pallavas; his queens commissioned temples at Pattadakal to commemorate the victory.

type:LABEL: person
name: Lokamahādevī
summary: Queen of the Cālukya king Vikramāditya II who commissioned the Virūpākṣa (Lokeśvara) temple at Pattadakal c. 740–745.

type:LABEL: person
name: Dantidurga
summary: Founder of Rāṣṭrakūṭa imperial power (r. c. 735–756), who overthrew the Cālukyas of Bādāmi; his inscription is carved in Ellora Cave 15.

type:LABEL: person
name: Yaśovarman (Candela)
summary: Candela king (r. c. 925–950) who built the Lakṣmaṇa temple at Khajuraho for an image of Vaikuṇṭha Viṣṇu, as recorded in the inscription of 953/954 CE.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vidyādhara (Candela)
summary: Candela king (r. c. 1003–1035) in whose reign the Kandarīya Mahādeva temple at Khajuraho was begun; he resisted Mahmud of Ghazni.

type:LABEL: person
name: Narasiṃhadeva I
summary: Eastern Gaṅga king of Odisha (r. 1238–1264) who built the Sun temple at Konark and campaigned against the Bengal sultanate.

type:LABEL: person
name: Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga
summary: Eastern Gaṅga king (r. c. 1078–1147/50) who united Kaliṅga and Utkala and began the present Jagannātha temple at Puri.

type:LABEL: person
name: Ahilyābāī Holkar
summary: Marāṭhā queen and ruler of Indore (r. 1767–1795) who rebuilt or endowed temples, ghāṭs and rest houses across India, including the present Kāśī Viśvanātha temple (1780) and the Viṣṇupada temple at Gaya (1787).

type:LABEL: person
name: Naranārāyaṇa
summary: King of the Koch kingdom (r. 1540–1587) in whose reign the Kāmākhyā temple was rebuilt in 1565.

type:LABEL: person
name: Chilarai
summary: Koch general and brother of King Naranārāyaṇa who, according to an inscription in the temple, rebuilt the Kāmākhyā temple in 1565.

type:LABEL: person
name: Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa
summary: Kārkoṭa king of Kashmir (r. c. 724–760) whom Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī credits with the Mārtaṇḍa Sun temple and far-reaching conquests.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bhīma I (Caulukya)
summary: Caulukya (Solaṅkī) king of Gujarat (r. c. 1022–1064) during whose reign Mahmud of Ghazni raided Somanātha (1026) and the Modhera Sun temple was built.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bhoja (Paramāra)
summary: Paramāra king of Mālava (r. c. 1010–1055), patron and author of works on poetics and architecture, to whom the unfinished Bhojeśvara temple is attributed.

type:LABEL: person
name: Sūryavarman II
summary: Khmer king (r. 1113–c. 1150) who built Angkor Wat as his Vaiṣṇava state temple.

type:LABEL: person
name: Yajñavarāha
summary: Brahmin counsellor at the Khmer court (10th c.), tutor of Jayavarman V, credited with founding Banteay Srei (consecrated 967).

type:LABEL: person
name: Rakai Pikatan
summary: Ruler of the Medang (Mataram) kingdom in Central Java in the mid-9th century, whose name painted on a finial of the Śiva temple suggests he began Prambanan.

type:LABEL: person
name: Viṣṇuvardhana (Hoysaḷa)
summary: Hoysaḷa king (r. c. 1108–1152) who commissioned the Cennakeśava temple at Belur in 1117 and under whom the Hoysaḷeśvara temple at Halebidu was begun.

type:LABEL: person
name: Ketamalla
summary: Officer of the Hoysaḷa king Viṣṇuvardhana credited by an inscription with building the Hoysaḷeśvara temple at Halebidu.

type:LABEL: person
name: Somanātha Daṇḍanāyaka
summary: Hoysaḷa general of Narasiṃha III who founded Somanathapura and its Keśava temple in the mid-13th century.

type:LABEL: person
name: Recherla Rudra
summary: Kākatīya general who in 1213 commissioned the Rudreśvara (Rāmappa) temple at Palampet during the reign of Gaṇapati.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kṛṣṇadevarāya
summary: Tuḷuva emperor of Vijayanagara (r. 1509–1529), a major patron of temples including Tirumala, Hampi’s Virūpākṣa and Viṭṭhala temples and Srikalahasti.

type:LABEL: person
name: Devarāya I
summary: Saṅgama king of Vijayanagara (r. c. 1406–1422) to whom the Rāmacandra (Hazāra Rāma) temple in the royal centre is attributed.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rāṇī Rāsmaṇi
summary: Kolkata zamindar and philanthropist (1793–1861) who founded the Dakṣiṇeśvar Kālī temple, consecrated in 1855.

type:LABEL: person
name: Mārtāṇḍa Varma
summary: King of Travancore (r. 1729–1758) who rebuilt the Padmanābhasvāmī temple and in 1750 dedicated his kingdom to Padmanābha.

type:LABEL: person
name: Queen Vṛṣabhānu of Tikamgarh
summary: Queen of the Bundela state of Orchha (Tikamgarh) who built the Jānakī Mandir at Janakpur, completed in 1910.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bāḷājī Bājīrāv (Nānāsāheb Peshwa)
summary: Peshwa of the Marāṭhā state (r. 1740–1761) who built the present Tryambakeśvara temple.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Pāṇḍya dynasty
summary: Tamil dynasty centred on Madurai, attested from the early historic period and powerful again in the 7th–10th and 13th centuries; patrons of rock-cut and structural temples in southern Tamil Nadu.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Nāyakas of Madurai
summary: Telugu-speaking governors of Vijayanagara who became independent rulers of Madurai (c. 1529–1736) and rebuilt the Mīnākṣī temple on a monumental scale.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Hoysaḷa dynasty
summary: Karnataka dynasty (c. 10th–14th c.) whose capitals Belur and Dvārasamudra (Halebidu) gave their name to the ornate Hoysaḷa temple style.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Kākatīya dynasty
summary: Telugu dynasty ruling from Warangal (c. 1163–1323), patrons of the Rāmappa and Thousand Pillar temples.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Caulukya (Solaṅkī) dynasty of Gujarat
summary: Dynasty ruling Gujarat from Aṇahilapāṭaka (c. 940–1244), patrons of the Māru-Gurjara temple style including Modhera and the medieval Somanātha.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Paramāra dynasty
summary: Dynasty of Mālava (c. 9th–14th c.) ruling from Dhārā, best known for King Bhoja.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Kārkoṭa dynasty
summary: Dynasty of Kashmir (c. 625–855) whose greatest king, Lalitāditya, is credited with the Mārtaṇḍa temple.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Koch kingdom
summary: Kingdom in western Assam and northern Bengal founded by Viśva Siṃha in the early 16th century; it rebuilt the Kāmākhyā temple in 1565.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Somavaṃśī dynasty of Odisha
summary: Dynasty of Dakṣiṇa Kosala and Odisha (c. 9th–12th c.) credited with early Bhubaneswar temples including the Mukteśvara and Liṅgarāja.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Holkar state of Indore
summary: Marāṭhā ruling house of Indore (18th c. – 1948), best known for Ahilyābāī Holkar’s temple patronage.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Malla dynasty of Nepal
summary: Rulers of the Kathmandu Valley (c. 1200–1769) under whom much of the valley’s surviving temple architecture was built or rebuilt.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Champa
summary: Cham kingdoms of central and southern Vietnam (c. 2nd–17th c.) whose royal sanctuary at Mỹ Sơn was dedicated to Śiva Bhadreśvara.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Kingdom of Travancore
summary: Kerala kingdom (1729–1949) whose rulers styled themselves servants of Padmanābha (Padmanābhadāsa).

type:LABEL: polity
name: Śilāhāra dynasty (northern Konkan)
summary: Dynasty of the northern Konkan (c. 800–1265) during whose rule the Ambarnath Śiva temple was built.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Pāṇḍuvaṃśīs of Dakṣiṇa Kosala
summary: Dynasty ruling from Śrīpura (Sirpur) in Chhattisgarh in the 6th–7th centuries, patrons of the brick Lakṣmaṇa temple.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Divya Deśams (the 108)
summary: The 108 abodes of Viṣṇu sung by the twelve Āḻvār poet-saints in the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham; 105 are in India, one in Nepal (Muktinath/Sāḷagrāmam), and two (Tiruppāṟkaṭal, the milk ocean, and Paramapadam) are beyond the earth.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pāṭal Peṟṟa Talaṅkaḷ (the 276 Tēvāram shrines)
summary: The 276 Śiva temples praised in the Tēvāram hymns of the three Nāyaṉmār Appar, Campantar (Sambandar) and Cuntarar (Sundarar), 7th–9th c.; most are in the Kāvēri delta, with a few in Sri Lanka, northern India and the Himalaya.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Char Dham (the four dhāmas)
summary: Four pilgrimage “abodes” at the corners of India — Badrinath (north), Dwarka (west), Puri (east) and Rameswaram (south) — associated in tradition with Ādi Śaṅkara.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Chota Char Dham (Uttarakhand)
summary: Circuit of four Himalayan shrines in Garhwal — Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath and Badrinath — that became a mass pilgrimage after road access in the second half of the 20th century.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pañca Bhūta Sthalas (five element liṅgas)
summary: Five South Indian Śiva temples each identified with one of the five elements: earth (Kanchipuram Ekāmbareśvara), water (Tiruvanaikaval Jambukeśvara), fire (Tiruvannamalai Aruṇācaleśvara), air (Srikalahasti) and space/ether (Chidambaram).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Āṟupaṭai Vīṭu (six abodes of Murukaṉ)
summary: Six Tamil Nadu shrines of Murukaṉ — Tirupparankundram, Tiruchendur, Palani, Swamimalai, Tiruttani and Pazhamudircholai — traditionally identified with the places named in Nakkīrar’s Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai, a guide-poem of the Pattuppāṭṭu.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Rival identifications of jyotirliṅga sites
summary: The question of which modern temple corresponds to several of the twelve jyotirliṅgas named in the Śiva Purāṇa list, where the text gives only a region or an ambiguous name: Vaidyanātha, Nāgeśa, Bhīmaśaṅkara and Oṃkāra/Amaleśvara.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Vedic Saṃhitās
summary: The four mantra collections — Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, Yajurveda (Śukla and Kṛṣṇa) and Atharvaveda — that form the base of the Vedic canon and were transmitted orally by recitation schools (śākhās).

type:LABEL: collection
name: Brāhmaṇas
summary: Prose texts attached to each Vedic school that explain the meaning, origin and correct performance of the śrauta rites, often through myths (ākhyāna) and identifications (bandhu).

type:LABEL: collection
name: Āraṇyakas
summary: Late Vedic texts, studied apart from the village, that treat esoteric or dangerous rites (e.g. the Pravargya) and contain or shade into the oldest Upaniṣads.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Upaniṣads
summary: Texts at the end of the Vedic corpus (hence “Vedānta”) that discuss the self (ātman), brahman, death and rebirth, and liberation; the principal (“early”) Upaniṣads number about thirteen.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Vedāṅgas
summary: The six “limbs of the Veda” — phonetics (śikṣā), ritual (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), metre (chandas) and astronomy/calendar (jyotiṣa) — developed to preserve, understand and apply the Vedic texts.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Kalpa Sūtras
aliases: Śrauta, Gṛhya and Dharma Sūtras|Śrauta Sūtras|Gṛhya Sūtras|Dharma Sūtras|Śulba Sūtras
summary: Aphoristic manuals of each Vedic school that codify the solemn (śrauta) rites, domestic (gṛhya) rites, rules of conduct (dharma) and altar geometry (śulba).

type:LABEL: text
name: Rigveda
summary: The oldest Vedic collection: 1,028 hymns in ten books (maṇḍalas) addressed chiefly to Indra, Agni and Soma, composed by hereditary poet families and transmitted orally with exceptional fidelity.

type:LABEL: text
name: Samaveda
summary: The Veda of chants (sāman): verses, almost all drawn from the Ṛgveda, arranged for singing by the udgātṛ priests in the soma rites, with separate song-books (gāna) recording the melodies.

type:LABEL: text
name: Yajurveda
summary: The Veda of sacrificial formulas (yajus) recited by the adhvaryu priest who performs the manual acts of the rite; it exists in a “Black” (Kṛṣṇa) branch mixing mantra and explanatory prose and a “White” (Śukla) branch with mantras alone.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śukla Yajurveda (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā)
summary: The “White” Yajurveda, the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā in forty chapters (Mādhyandina and Kāṇva recensions), whose mantras are separated from the explanatory prose collected in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Taittirīya Saṃhitā (Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda)
summary: The principal Saṃhitā of the Black Yajurveda, in seven books (kāṇḍas) mixing ritual formulas with Brāhmaṇa-style prose explanation; it contains the Śatarudrīya litany to Rudra (TS 4.5).

type:LABEL: text
name: Atharvaveda
summary: The fourth Veda, a collection of hymns and spells for healing, protection, prosperity, love, kingship and domestic life, alongside speculative cosmological hymns; preserved in the Śaunaka and Paippalāda recensions.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa
summary: The Brāhmaṇa of the White Yajurveda, the largest and most systematic Brāhmaṇa (“of a hundred paths”), and a source of many narratives later retold in the epics and Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: text
name: Aitareya Brāhmaṇa
summary: A Ṛgvedic Brāhmaṇa for the hotṛ priest in forty adhyāyas (eight pañcikās), best known for the royal consecration (rājasūya) material and the story of Śunaḥśepa (AB 7.13–18).

type:LABEL: text
name: Taittirīya Āraṇyaka
summary: The Āraṇyaka of the Taittirīya school in ten prapāṭhakas; books 7–9 are the Taittirīya Upaniṣad and book 10 the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
summary: The largest and, with the Chāndogya, the oldest Upaniṣad, forming the end of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; it presents Yājñavalkya’s teachings at Janaka’s court, his dialogues with Maitreyī and Gārgī, and the earliest explicit doctrine of karma and rebirth.

type:LABEL: text
name: Chāndogya Upaniṣad
summary: An early prose Upaniṣad of the Kauthuma Sāmaveda school, in eight prapāṭhakas, containing Uddālaka Āruṇi’s instruction of Śvetaketu (“tat tvam asi”), the “five fires” doctrine of rebirth, and the only Vedic mention of a Kṛṣṇa son of Devakī (3.17.6).

type:LABEL: text
name: Taittirīya Upaniṣad
summary: Books 7–9 of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, in three vallīs (Śikṣā, Brahmānanda, Bhṛgu), known for the five sheaths of the self and Varuṇa’s instruction of his son Bhṛgu on brahman.

type:LABEL: text
name: Aitareya Upaniṣad
summary: A short Ṛgvedic Upaniṣad (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.4–6) describing creation by the self (“ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt”) and ending with the equation “prajñānaṃ brahma” (3.3).

type:LABEL: text
name: Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad
summary: A Ṛgvedic Upaniṣad in four chapters, part of the Kauṣītaki (Śāṅkhāyana) Āraṇyaka, in which kṣatriya teachers instruct brahmins: Citra Gāṅgyāyani teaches Āruṇi, Indra teaches Pratardana, and Ajātaśatru teaches Bālāki.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kena Upaniṣad
summary: A short Upaniṣad of the Jaiminīya Sāmaveda school: two verse sections on the unknowable brahman, followed by the prose parable in which Agni, Vāyu and Indra fail to recognise a mysterious being until Umā Haimavatī reveals that it is brahman.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kaṭha Upaniṣad
summary: A verse Upaniṣad in six vallīs framed by the story of the boy Naciketas, who receives three boons from Yama, the third being the teaching about what happens after death and the imperishable self.

type:LABEL: text
name: Īśā Upaniṣad
summary: A brief verse Upaniṣad forming the final chapter (40) of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, opening “īśā vāsyam idaṃ sarvaṃ” — all this is to be dwelt in by the Lord.

type:LABEL: text
name: Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad
summary: A verse Upaniṣad of the Atharvaveda in three muṇḍakas that distinguishes the “lower” knowledge (the four Vedas and six Vedāṅgas) from the “higher” knowledge of the imperishable, taught by Aṅgiras to Śaunaka.

type:LABEL: text
name: Praśna Upaniṣad
summary: A prose Upaniṣad of the Atharvaveda in which six students — among them Sukeśā Bhāradvāja, Satyakāma Śaibya and Kausalya Āśvalāyana — put six questions to the sage Pippalāda.

type:LABEL: text
name: Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad
summary: The shortest principal Upaniṣad (twelve verses), which identifies the syllable Om with all that is, past, present and future, and the self (ātman) with brahman, analysed into four states (waking, dream, deep sleep and the “fourth”).

type:LABEL: text
name: Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad
summary: A theistic verse Upaniṣad in six chapters that proclaims one Rudra, called Śiva and Maheśvara, as creator and lord, using Sāṃkhya and Yoga vocabulary; it is the earliest text to make Rudra–Śiva the supreme god and closes with the word bhakti.

type:LABEL: text
name: Aṣṭādhyāyī of Pāṇini
summary: Pāṇini’s grammar of Sanskrit in nearly 4,000 sūtras arranged in eight chapters, describing both the spoken language of his time and Vedic usage; it is an external, datable witness to names and cults of its period, including Vāsudeva and Arjuna (4.3.98).

type:LABEL: text
name: Mahābhāṣya of Patañjali
summary: Patañjali’s “Great Commentary” on Pāṇini and Kātyāyana’s vārttikas (c. mid-2nd c. BCE), whose example sentences incidentally attest the Kṛṣṇa–Kaṃsa story, its performance by actors (śobhikas), devotees of Vāsudeva, and contemporary events.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nirukta of Yāska
summary: Yāska’s explanatory commentary on the Nighaṇṭu word-lists, the oldest surviving work of Vedic exegesis, which records rival schools of interpretation — the etymologists (nairuktas) and the “historians” (aitihāsikas).

type:LABEL: deity
name: Indra
summary: The most frequently praised god of the Ṛgveda (about 250 hymns, roughly a quarter), the soma-drinking warrior who wields the vajra and slays Vṛtra to release the waters; in the Upaniṣads, epics and Purāṇas he remains king of the gods but loses supremacy and is often humbled.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Agni
summary: The sacrificial fire as god — messenger between gods and humans, divine hotṛ and purohita — praised in about 200 Ṛgvedic hymns, including the first (RV 1.1); central to all Vedic ritual and still present in every Hindu rite.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Soma
summary: The pressed ritual drink and its god, praised in about 120 Ṛgvedic hymns, including all 114 hymns of maṇḍala 9 to Soma Pavamāna (“self-purifying”); in later tradition Soma is identified with the Moon and becomes ancestor of the Lunar dynasty.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Varuṇa
summary: The sovereign Āditya of the Ṛgveda who guards cosmic and moral order (ṛta), sees all and binds wrongdoers with his fetters; praised alone in about a dozen hymns and often with Mitra. Later he declines to lord of the waters and guardian of the west.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Mitra
summary: An Āditya personifying alliance and contract, almost always paired with Varuṇa; only one Ṛgvedic hymn (RV 3.59) is addressed to him alone. He is cognate with Iranian Mithra.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Sūrya
summary: The Sun as god, praised in about ten Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.50, 1.115); closely related solar deities include Savitṛ, addressed in the Gāyatrī (RV 3.62.10). Sūrya later becomes the focus of Saura worship and of great temples such as Konark.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Uṣas
summary: The goddess Dawn, daughter of heaven, celebrated in about twenty of the most admired Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.113); she has little independent cult in later Hinduism.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Rudra
summary: A fierce Ṛgvedic archer-god of storms, disease and healing, addressed in only about three hymns (RV 1.114, 2.33, 7.46), who through the Yajurvedic Śatarudrīya and the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad becomes the supreme god Śiva.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Prajāpati
summary: “Lord of creatures”, named as creator in the last verse of RV 10.121 and the central creator-god of the Brāhmaṇas, whose dismembered body is restored in the fire-altar ritual; his role passes to Brahmā in the epics and Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Yama
summary: Son of Vivasvat and, in the Ṛgveda, the first mortal who found the path to the world of the fathers and rules there (RV 10.14); he is the teacher of Naciketas in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad and later the god of death and judge of the dead (Dharmarāja).

type:LABEL: deity
name: Vāyu
summary: The Wind, first to drink the soma, often paired with Indra (Indra–Vāyu); praised in a few Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.134–135, 7.90) and, as Vāta, in RV 10.168. Later he is the father of Hanumān and Bhīma.
earliest_material: c. 127–230 CE (Kaniṣka I to Vāsudeva I)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Aśvins
summary: Twin horsemen gods of the dawn, healers and rescuers who appear in more than fifty Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.116–120); in the Mahābhārata they are the fathers of Nakula and Sahadeva.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Aditi
summary: “Boundlessness”, mother of the Ādityas (Mitra, Varuṇa and others), who has no Ṛgvedic hymn of her own but is praised as all things (RV 1.89.10); later the wife of Kaśyapa, mother of the gods and of Vāmana.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Sarasvatī
summary: In the Ṛgveda both a mighty river and its goddess, praised in three hymns (RV 6.61, 7.95, 7.96); identified with Vāc (speech) in the Brāhmaṇas, she becomes the goddess of learning, music and speech and consort of Brahmā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vasiṣṭha
summary: Ṛgvedic poet-priest to whose family maṇḍala 7 is attributed; priest of the Bharata king Sudās in the Battle of the Ten Kings, and in the Rāmāyaṇa the family priest of Daśaratha and rival of Viśvāmitra.

type:LABEL: character
name: Viśvāmitra
summary: Ṛgvedic poet of the Kuśika clan to whom maṇḍala 3 — including the Gāyatrī (RV 3.62.10) — is attributed; he adopts Śunaḥśepa in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa and, in the Rāmāyaṇa, takes the young Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa to protect his sacrifice.

type:LABEL: character
name: Agastya
summary: Ṛgvedic poet to whom RV 1.165–191 are attributed, husband of Lopāmudrā (RV 1.179), who becomes in the Rāmāyaṇa the forest sage who arms Rāma, and in Tamil tradition (as Akattiyar) the founder of Tamil grammar and a culture-hero of the south.

type:LABEL: character
name: Aṅgiras
summary: Primeval seer and eponym of the Āṅgirasa priestly clan; in the Ṛgveda the Aṅgirases are ancestral “fathers” who with Indra or Bṛhaspati opened the Vala cave and found the cows, and in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad Aṅgiras teaches the higher knowledge to Śaunaka.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bhṛgu
summary: Ancestor of the Bhārgava priestly clan; in the Ṛgveda the Bhṛgus establish Agni among men, and in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and Taittirīya Upaniṣad Bhṛgu Vāruṇi is the son and pupil of Varuṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Atri
summary: Ṛgvedic seer whose family (the Ātreyas) is credited with maṇḍala 5; RV 5.40 tells how Atri found the Sun hidden by Svarbhānu’s darkness. In the Rāmāyaṇa Rāma visits Atri and his wife Anasūyā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Yājñavalkya
summary: The pre-eminent teacher of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad and an authority of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, who wins the debate at Janaka’s sacrifice, teaches Janaka and his wife Maitreyī, and to whom the “white” formulas of the Śukla Yajurveda are attributed.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: character
name: Gārgī Vācaknavī
summary: A woman philosopher who twice questions Yājñavalkya at Janaka’s court (BU 3.6, 3.8), pressing him on what the worlds are “woven upon” until he warns her not to ask too much; her second questioning elicits the teaching of the imperishable (akṣara).
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: character
name: Maitreyī
summary: One of Yājñavalkya’s two wives, described as a discourser on brahman (brahmavādinī), who on his departure asks for the teaching of immortality instead of wealth (BU 2.4; 4.5).
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: character
name: Uddālaka Āruṇi
summary: A leading Kuru-Pañcāla teacher of the early Upaniṣads who instructs his son Śvetaketu with the refrain “tat tvam asi” (CU 6), questions Yājñavalkya at Janaka’s court (BU 3.7) and, by the lineage in BU 6.3.7, was Yājñavalkya’s own teacher.
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: character
name: Śvetaketu
summary: Son and pupil of Uddālaka Āruṇi who returns proud from twelve years of Vedic study and is taught by his father that the self is the subtle essence of all (“tat tvam asi, śvetaketo”, CU 6); in CU 5.3 and BU 6.2 he cannot answer Pravāhaṇa Jaivali’s questions on the afterlife.
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: character
name: Satyakāma Jābāla
summary: The boy of the Chāndogya (4.4) who, not knowing his father, truthfully reports his mother Jabālā’s words and is accepted as a pupil by Hāridrumata Gautama for that truthfulness; he later teaches Upakosala (CU 4.10–15).
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: character
name: Janaka of Videha (Upaniṣadic king)
summary: The king of Videha in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad who holds a sacrifice with lavish gifts, sets a prize of a thousand cows for the most learned brahmin, and becomes Yājñavalkya’s student.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: character
name: Naciketas
summary: The boy of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad whose father, angered by his questioning, gives him to Death; waiting three nights at Yama’s house, he receives three boons and refuses all worldly gifts in favour of the knowledge of what lies beyond death.
earliest_textual: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

type:LABEL: character
name: Ghora Āṅgirasa
summary: A teacher of the Āṅgirasa clan who, according to Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.17.6, taught Kṛṣṇa son of Devakī a doctrine likening a man’s life to a soma sacrifice, after which Kṛṣṇa “became free from thirst”.
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: character
name: Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra (Chāndogya)
summary: The pupil of Ghora Āṅgirasa named in a single sentence of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (3.17.6) — “Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī” — the only Vedic occurrence of that name-pair; whether he is the epic and Purāṇic Kṛṣṇa is disputed.
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: character
name: Purūravas
summary: A mortal king, called “son of Iḍā” (aiḍa), who loses his apsaras wife Urvaśī; their dialogue is RV 10.95 and the full story ŚB 11.5.1. In Purāṇic genealogy he is the first king of the Lunar dynasty.

type:LABEL: character
name: Urvaśī
summary: An apsaras who lives with the mortal Purūravas on conditions he breaks, then leaves him (RV 10.95; ŚB 11.5.1); RV 7.33.11 also links her with Vasiṣṭha’s birth. She is a celebrated heroine of later literature, notably Kālidāsa’s Vikramorvaśīya.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vṛtra
summary: The serpent (ahi) or “obstruction” who encloses the waters and is slain by Indra (RV 1.32). Yāska records two readings — a cloud (nairuktas) or an asura son of Tvaṣṭṛ (aitihāsikas); later texts make Vṛtra a brahmin-born asura whose killing brings Indra guilt, and the Bhāgavata a devotee of Viṣṇu.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śunaḥśepa
summary: Son of the brahmin Ajīgarta, sold to prince Rohita as a substitute victim for Varuṇa; bound to the stake at Hariścandra’s rājasūya, he is freed by praising the gods and adopted by Viśvāmitra as Devarāta (AB 7.13–18).

type:LABEL: character
name: Saramā
summary: Indra’s messenger who tracks the cows stolen by the Paṇis and demands them back in the dialogue hymn RV 10.108; later tradition makes her the bitch of the gods, mother of Yama’s two dogs (Sārameya, RV 10.14.10).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Brahman
summary: In the Ṛgveda (neuter bráhman) the potent sacred formulation of the poet-priest; in the Upaniṣads the ultimate reality, the ground from which beings arise and into which they return, often identified with the self (ātman).
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Ātman
summary: The self — originally the body or breath, then the inner essence of a person — which the early Upaniṣads make the object of liberating knowledge and identify with brahman.
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Ṛta
summary: The Ṛgvedic principle of cosmic, ritual and moral order and truth, guarded above all by Varuṇa and Mitra; in later thought its role is largely taken over by dharma.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Yajña
summary: Vedic sacrifice — offerings into the fire with recitation, chant and formula — the central religious act of the Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas, which the Brāhmaṇas identify with Prajāpati and with Viṣṇu (“yajño vai viṣṇuḥ”).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Om
summary: The sacred syllable recited at the beginning and end of Vedic recitation; the Upaniṣads make it an object of meditation and a symbol of brahman (CU 1.1.1; Kaṭha 2.15–17; the whole Māṇḍūkya).
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Karma
summary: Action — first, in the Brāhmaṇas, ritual action — which the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad makes the determinant of one’s future: “as one acts, so one becomes” (BU 4.4.5); the earliest explicit statements of the doctrine of moral retribution in Indian texts.
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Saṃsāra
summary: The cycle of death and rebirth. The early prose Upaniṣads describe the cycle (the “five fires” and the two paths, BU 6.2; CU 5.3–10) before the word saṃsāra itself appears in the verse Upaniṣads (Kaṭha 3.7; Śvetāśvatara 6.16).
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Mokṣa
summary: Liberation from the cycle of rebirth. The early Upaniṣads speak of immortality and of the desireless knower who, being brahman, goes to brahman (BU 4.4.6); the noun mokṣa itself appears in the Śvetāśvatara (6.16).
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Indra slays Vṛtra
summary: The central Ṛgvedic combat myth: fortified with soma and armed with the vajra fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ, Indra kills the serpent Vṛtra who lies on the mountain enclosing the waters, and the waters flow to the sea (RV 1.32).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The three strides of Vishnu
summary: Viṣṇu measures out the earthly realms in three wide strides, his highest step holding a spring of honey (RV 1.154; 1.22.16–21); the Brāhmaṇas re-enact the strides in ritual and identify Viṣṇu with the sacrifice. The motif is the Vedic root of the later Vāmana–Bali story.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The sacrifice of Puruṣa
summary: RV 10.90: the gods sacrifice the thousand-headed cosmic Man (Puruṣa), and from his dismembered body come the verses, the animals, the four social classes, the moon, sun, Indra and Agni, and the worlds.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The Nāsadīya creation hymn
summary: RV 10.129, a speculative cosmogony: in the beginning there was neither non-being nor being; the One breathed windlessly; desire (kāma) arose as the first seed of mind — and perhaps even the overseer in the highest heaven does not know how creation came about.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Manu and the fish (the flood)
summary: The earliest Indian flood story (ŚB 1.8.1.1–11): a small fish caught in Manu’s washing water asks for protection, grows, warns of a flood, and tows Manu’s ship by a rope tied to its horn to the northern mountain; alone surviving, Manu sacrifices and obtains a daughter, Iḍā, through whom he generates humankind.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Purūravas and Urvaśī
summary: The apsaras Urvaśī lives with king Purūravas on condition she never sees him naked; tricked by the gandharvas, she vanishes, and the grieving king finds her among the apsarases, who appear as birds; she foretells their son and the gandharvas’ gift of a fire by which he becomes one of them (RV 10.95; ŚB 11.5.1).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Saramā and the Paṇis
summary: Indra’s messenger Saramā crosses the Rasā river to the Paṇis, who have hidden cows in a cave; she refuses their bribe and warns that Indra, Bṛhaspati, Soma and the Aṅgirases will recover the cows (RV 10.108) — a form of the Vala myth.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The story of Śunaḥśepa
summary: King Hariścandra, sonless, is advised by Nārada to vow a son to Varuṇa; when Rohita is born the king delays the sacrifice, Varuṇa afflicts him, and Rohita buys Śunaḥśepa from his father Ajīgarta as a substitute; bound to the stake, Śunaḥśepa praises a sequence of gods until his bonds fall away at the verses to Uṣas, and Viśvāmitra adopts him as Devarāta (AB 7.13–18).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Naciketas and Yama
summary: Vājaśravasa gives away his worthless cows; his son Naciketas asks repeatedly “to whom will you give me?” and is told “to Death”; after three nights unfed at Yama’s house he receives three boons — his father’s calm, the fire-altar that leads to heaven (named after him), and the truth about what happens after death.
earliest_textual: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Uddālaka teaches Śvetaketu: “tat tvam asi”
summary: Uddālaka Āruṇi teaches his son Śvetaketu through examples — clay, the banyan seed, salt dissolved in water — that the subtle essence of everything is the self, ending each lesson “tat tvam asi, Śvetaketu” (CU 6.8.7–6.16.3).
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Umā Haimavatī reveals Brahman to the gods
summary: After a victory the gods take pride; a mysterious being (yakṣa) appears; Agni cannot burn and Vāyu cannot lift a straw before it; when Indra approaches it vanishes, and in its place he meets a radiant woman, Umā Haimavatī, who tells him it was brahman (Kena 3–4).
earliest_textual: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The debates at Janaka’s court
summary: At a sacrifice of king Janaka of Videha attended by brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas, a thousand cows with gold on their horns are offered to the most learned; Yājñavalkya drives them off and defeats in turn Aśvala, Ārtabhāga, Bhujyu, Uṣasta, Kahoḍa, Gārgī, Uddālaka Āruṇi and Vidagdha Śākalya (BU 3.1–9).
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Vedic Śrauta ritual tradition
summary: The tradition of the solemn public Vedic rites performed with three fires by specialist priests (hotṛ, adhvaryu, udgātṛ, brahman) according to the Brāhmaṇas and Śrauta Sūtras; it survives in a few lineages, e.g. among Nambudiri brahmins of Kerala.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Advaita Vedānta
summary: The non-dualist school of Vedānta, systematised by Gauḍapāda and Śaṅkara, which reads the Upaniṣads, the Bhagavad Gītā and the Brahma Sūtra as teaching that the self (ātman) is identical with brahman and that the world of plurality is not ultimately real.

type:LABEL: person
name: Pāṇini
summary: The grammarian of Gandhāra (traditionally of Śalātura) who composed the Aṣṭādhyāyī, the foundational grammar of Sanskrit, probably in the 5th–4th c. BCE (disputed).

type:LABEL: person
name: Patañjali (grammarian)
summary: Author of the Mahābhāṣya on Pāṇini and Kātyāyana, generally placed in the mid-2nd c. BCE from his references to Puṣyamitra’s sacrifice and Yavana attacks. Whether he is the same person as the author of the Yoga Sūtra is disputed and not assumed here.

type:LABEL: person
name: Yāska
summary: Author of the Nirukta, the earliest surviving Vedic exegesis and etymology, usually placed before Pāṇini (c. 6th–5th c. BCE; disputed).

type:LABEL: person
name: Sāyaṇa
summary: Fourteenth-century scholar and minister at the Vijayanagara court under Bukka I and Harihara II whose commentaries (Vedārthaprakāśa) on the Ṛgveda and much of the Vedic corpus are the fullest traditional exegesis; he died in 1387.

type:LABEL: person
name: Ādi Śaṅkara
summary: The Advaita Vedānta philosopher whose commentaries on the Brahma Sūtra, the principal Upaniṣads and the Bhagavad Gītā define the school; modern scholarship dates him c. 700–750 CE, though older scholarship gave 788–820 and maṭha traditions much earlier dates.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 1
summary: A later composite book of 191 hymns by many poets (including Agastya’s group 1.165–191 and the riddle hymn 1.164); it and maṇḍala 10 frame the older family books.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 2 (Gṛtsamada family book)
summary: Family book of 43 hymns attributed to the Gṛtsamadas; includes the Rudra hymn 2.33.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 3 (Viśvāmitra family book)
summary: Family book of 62 hymns attributed to Viśvāmitra and the Kuśikas; includes the river dialogue 3.33, the Bharata hymn 3.53 and the Gāyatrī 3.62.10.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 4 (Vāmadeva family book)
summary: Family book of 58 hymns attributed to Vāmadeva Gautama; RV 4.26.1 (“aham manur abhavaṃ sūryaś ca”) is quoted in BU 1.4.10.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 5 (Atri family book)
summary: Family book of 87 hymns attributed to the Ātreyas; RV 5.40 tells how Atri recovered the hidden Sun.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 6 (Bharadvāja family book)
summary: Family book of 75 hymns attributed to the Bhāradvājas; includes the Sarasvatī hymn 6.61 and the Indra–Viṣṇu hymn 6.69.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 7 (Vasiṣṭha family book)
summary: Family book of 104 hymns attributed to Vasiṣṭha and his descendants; includes the Ten Kings hymns 7.18 and 7.33, the Varuṇa hymns 7.86–89 and the Sarasvatī hymns 7.95–96.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 9 (Soma Pavamāna)
summary: All 114 hymns to Soma Pavamāna, gathered from the poet families into one book arranged by metre.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 10
summary: The youngest book (191 hymns), with the cosmogonies (10.90, 10.121, 10.129), funeral and Yama hymns (10.14–18), the river hymn (10.75), Vāc (10.125) and dialogue hymns (10.10, 10.95, 10.108).

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 1.24 (Śunaḥśepa’s plea to Varuṇa)
summary: A hymn attributed to Śunaḥśepa Ājīgarti in which the bound Śunaḥśepa calls on King Varuṇa to release him (1.24.12–13).

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 1.32 (Indra slays Vṛtra)
summary: The classic hymn of Indra’s victory over Vṛtra: “I shall now proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra …” (1.32.1); the waters released run to the sea.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 1.154 (Viṣṇu’s three strides)
summary: Hymn to Viṣṇu who measured the earthly realms in three strides; in his highest step is a spring of honey (1.154.5).

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 1.164.46 (“ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti”)
summary: Verse of the riddle hymn 1.164: “They call it Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni … the inspired speak of the one that is in many ways”.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 1.165–191 (hymns of Agastya)
summary: The group of hymns closing maṇḍala 1 that the Anukramaṇī attributes to Agastya Maitrāvaruṇi, including the Indra–Maruts–Agastya dialogue (1.165, 1.170) and the dialogue of Agastya and Lopāmudrā (1.179).

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 2.33 (hymn to Rudra)
summary: The longest Ṛgvedic hymn to Rudra, father of the Maruts, asking the fearsome, tawny, many-formed lord to spare and heal; “from Rudra, lord of this world, lordship does not depart” (2.33.9).

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 3.53 (Viśvāmitra and the Bharatas)
summary: Hymn of Viśvāmitra in which the great seer conveys king Sudās (3.53.9) and declares that his formulation protects the Bharata people (3.53.12); tradition reads verses 21–24 as imprecations against Vasiṣṭha.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 3.62.10 (the Gāyatrī / Sāvitrī)
summary: The verse to Savitṛ in gāyatrī metre — “tat savitur vareṇyam …” — recited daily by twice-born Hindus and taught at initiation.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 7.18 (the Battle of the Ten Kings)
summary: Vasiṣṭha’s hymn celebrating Indra’s help to king Sudās of the Tṛtsus/Bharatas against a coalition of ten kings on the Paruṣṇī river.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 7.33 (Vasiṣṭha’s birth and the Ten Kings)
summary: Hymn of the Vasiṣṭhas recalling how their prayer won Indra’s aid for Sudās (7.33.3–5) and telling of Vasiṣṭha’s birth from Mitra and Varuṇa, “from the mind of Urvaśī”, and Māna’s (Agastya’s) birth from a jar (7.33.10–13).

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 7.59.12 (the Tryambaka verse)
summary: The verse “tryambakaṃ yajāmahe …” (we worship the three-mothered/three-eyed one … may I be released from death like a cucumber from its stalk), appended to a Marut hymn; recited later as the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya mantra to Śiva.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 10.14 (Yama, king of the dead)
summary: Funeral hymn honouring Yama Vaivasvata, who first found the path for many, and sending the dead past Yama’s two four-eyed dogs, the Sārameyas.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 10.75 (Nadīstuti, praise of rivers)
summary: Hymn praising the Sindhu (Indus) and naming the rivers from the Gaṅgā and Yamunā in the east to the Kubhā and Gomatī in the west (10.75.5–6); besides this verse the Ṛgveda has only the adjective gāṅgya (RV 6.45.31), so the Gaṅgā is marginal in the oldest text.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 10.90 (Puruṣasūkta)
summary: The hymn of the cosmic Man sacrificed by the gods, from whose body the world and the four varṇas arise.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 10.95 (Purūravas and Urvaśī)
summary: Dialogue hymn in which Purūravas begs the departing Urvaśī to return; she refuses: “Go home again, Purūravas; I am hard to catch, like the wind” (10.95.2).

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 10.108 (Saramā and the Paṇis)
summary: Dialogue between Indra’s messenger Saramā and the Paṇis who hold the stolen cows.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 10.121 (Hiraṇyagarbha)
summary: Hymn to the Golden Embryo who arose in the beginning as lord of all, with the refrain “to which god shall we offer?”; the last verse names Prajāpati.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 10.125 (Vāc hymn; Devīsūkta)
summary: Speech (Vāc) speaks in the first person as the power moving with the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas and all gods and supporting Mitra–Varuṇa, Indra–Agni and the Aśvins; later recited as the Devīsūkta in goddess worship.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 10.129 (Nāsadīyasūkta)
summary: The hymn of creation “Then there was neither non-being nor being …”, ending in doubt whether even the overseer knows.

type:LABEL: passage
name: ŚB 1.2.5 (the dwarf Viṣṇu wins the earth)
summary: The asuras divide the earth; the gods, putting Viṣṇu — the sacrifice — at their head, ask for a share “as much as this Viṣṇu lies upon”; Viṣṇu was a dwarf (vāmano ha viṣṇur āsa), but enclosed by the metres he gains the whole earth for the gods.

type:LABEL: passage
name: ŚB 1.4.1.10–17 (Videgha Māthava and Agni Vaiśvānara)
summary: King Videgha Māthava, then on the Sarasvatī, follows Agni Vaiśvānara burning eastward across the rivers to the Sadānīrā, which Agni did not burn; east of it the land of Videha is settled.

type:LABEL: passage
name: ŚB 1.7.3.1–8 (Rudra left behind; Vāstavya)
summary: When the gods went to heaven by sacrifice, the god who rules over cattle (Rudra) was left behind, hence called Vāstavya; he claims a share of the offering, and the rite of the Sviṣṭakṛt is explained.

type:LABEL: passage
name: ŚB 1.8.1.1–11 (Manu and the fish)
summary: The flood story of the Śatapatha: the fish, the ship tied to its horn, the northern mountain (“Manu’s descent”), and Manu’s daughter Iḍā born of his offerings.

type:LABEL: passage
name: ŚB 6.1.3.7–18 (Kumāra receives eight names)
summary: A boy (kumāra) born of Uṣas from the seed of the Year cries and asks Prajāpati for names; he receives eight — Rudra, Sarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Aśani, Bhava, Mahān Deva, Īśāna — each a form of Agni.

type:LABEL: passage
name: ŚB 11.5.1 (Purūravas and Urvaśī)
summary: The prose narrative of the apsaras Urvaśī and Purūravas Aiḍa, framing the verses of RV 10.95 and explaining the origin of a fire rite; the king wanders around Kurukṣetra searching for her (11.5.1.4).

type:LABEL: passage
name: ŚB 13.5.4 (kings who performed the horse sacrifice)
summary: A list of aśvamedha performers with commemorative verses (gāthās), beginning with Janamejaya Pārikṣita and his brothers Bhīmasena, Ugrasena and Śrutasena, and including Bharata Dauḥṣanti, whom “the apsaras Śakuntalā Nāḍapitī bore” (13.5.4.13).

type:LABEL: passage
name: ŚB 14.1.1 (Viṣṇu best of the gods; his head severed)
summary: The gods hold a session at Kurukṣetra; Viṣṇu reaches the goal first and becomes the best of the gods (14.1.1.5); being the sacrifice and the sun, he cannot contain his glory, and ants gnaw his bowstring so that the bow-end cuts off his head — the origin of the Pravargya.

type:LABEL: passage
name: AB 7.13–18 (the Śunaḥśepa story)
summary: The Śunaḥśepa narrative recited at the royal consecration (pañcikā 7, khaṇḍas 13–18; adhyāya 33 in continuous numbering).

type:LABEL: passage
name: TS 4.5 (Śatarudrīya / Śrī Rudram)
summary: Eleven anuvākas of homage to Rudra in his hundred forms — benign and terrible, lord of cattle, of thieves, of mountains — beginning “namas te rudra manyave” and including “namaḥ śivāya ca śivatarāya ca” (4.5.8.1); used in the agnicayana to pacify Rudra (cf. ŚB 9.1.1) and recited in Śaiva worship as the Śrī Rudram.

type:LABEL: passage
name: BU 1.4 (the self in the beginning; “ahaṃ brahmāsmi”)
summary: Creation from the self alone in the form of a person, who says “I am”, fears, desires a second, splits into husband and wife and produces all pairs (1.4.1–5); whoever knows “I am brahman” (ahaṃ brahmāsmi, 1.4.10) becomes the whole world — as the seer Vāmadeva realised, “I was Manu and the Sun”.

type:LABEL: passage
name: BU 2.4 (Yājñavalkya and Maitreyī, first version)
summary: About to leave home, Yājñavalkya offers to divide his property between Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī; Maitreyī asks for what makes one immortal and is taught that all is dear for the sake of the self.

type:LABEL: passage
name: BU 3.6 (Gārgī’s first questions)
summary: Gārgī Vācaknavī asks Yājñavalkya on what each world is woven, back to the worlds of brahman, until he warns: “Gārgī, do not ask too much, or your head will shatter.”

type:LABEL: passage
name: BU 3.8 (Gārgī’s second questions; the imperishable)
summary: Gārgī returns with two questions “like arrows”; Yājñavalkya answers that all is woven on space, and space on the imperishable (akṣara), at whose command sun and moon stand apart.

type:LABEL: passage
name: BU 4.4.5–6 (karma and rebirth)
summary: Yājñavalkya to Janaka: “as one acts, as one behaves, so one becomes”; the desiring man returns to this world for further action, while the desireless, being brahman, goes to brahman.

type:LABEL: passage
name: BU 4.5 (Yājñavalkya and Maitreyī, second version)
summary: The longer version of the Maitreyī dialogue, introducing Maitreyī as a brahmavādinī and Kātyāyanī as knowing only what women know.

type:LABEL: passage
name: BU 6.2 (Pravāhaṇa Jaivali: the five fires and two paths)
summary: Śvetaketu Āruṇeya cannot answer the Pañcāla king Pravāhaṇa Jaivali’s five questions about the dead; the king teaches his father Gautama the five fires and the paths of the gods and of the fathers (6.2.1–16).

type:LABEL: passage
name: CU 3.17.6 (Ghora Āṅgirasa and Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra)
summary: Having explained man’s life as a soma sacrifice (3.17.1–5), “Ghora Āṅgirasa told this to Kṛṣṇa son of Devakī, and he became free from thirst”, with three formulas for the time of death.

type:LABEL: passage
name: CU 4.4 (Satyakāma Jābāla)
summary: Satyakāma asks his mother Jabālā his lineage; she does not know; he repeats her words truthfully to Hāridrumata Gautama, who accepts him as a true brahmin for his truthfulness.

type:LABEL: passage
name: CU 5.3–10 (the five fires)
summary: Pravāhaṇa Jaivali’s questions to Śvetaketu and teaching to Gautama: the dead pass through five sacrificial fires (heaven, rain-cloud, earth, man, woman) to rebirth; the knowers go by the path of the gods, others by the path of the fathers, and rebirth follows conduct (5.10.7).

type:LABEL: passage
name: CU 6.8.7 and CU 6 (“tat tvam asi”)
summary: Uddālaka’s teaching of his son (CU 6.1–16), from the sat that alone existed in the beginning (6.2.1) to the refrain first given at 6.8.7: “that is the self; tat tvam asi, Śvetaketu”.

type:LABEL: passage
name: CU 8.7–12 (Indra and Virocana with Prajāpati)
summary: Indra for the gods and Virocana for the asuras live as students with Prajāpati; Virocana leaves content with the body as self, while Indra returns again and again over 101 years until taught the bodiless self.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Kaṭha Up. vallī 1 (Naciketas and the three boons)
summary: The frame story: Vājaśravasa’s gift, Naciketas sent to Death, three nights’ wait and Yama’s three boons (KaU 1.1–29).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Kaṭha Up. 2.18–19 (the self neither born nor slain)
summary: “The wise one is not born and does not die … unborn, eternal … it is not killed when the body is killed” (2.18); “If the killer thinks he kills … neither understands” (2.19) — verses reused in Bhagavad Gītā 2.19–20.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Kaṭha Up. 3.9 (“that highest step of Viṣṇu”)
summary: The man whose charioteer is understanding and whose reins are the mind “reaches the end of the road — that highest step of Viṣṇu” (tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam), echoing RV 1.22.20.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Kena Up. 3–4 (the yakṣa and Umā Haimavatī)
summary: The prose parable of the gods’ pride, the yakṣa, the failure of Agni, Vāyu and Indra, and Umā Haimavatī’s revelation that it was brahman.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Śvetāśvatara Up. 3–4 (the one Rudra)
summary: Chapters proclaiming the one Rudra who rules the worlds (3.2), source and origin of the gods (3.4), whose “auspicious form” (śivā tanūḥ) is invoked with Śatarudriya mantras (3.5–6), the all-pervading Śiva (3.11) and the māyin Maheśvara (4.10).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Śvetāśvatara Up. 6.23 (bhakti to god and teacher)
summary: The closing verse: these teachings shine forth for the great-souled one “who has the highest devotion (bhakti) to god, and as to god, so to the teacher”.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Taittirīya Up. 3.1–6 (Bhṛgu and Varuṇa)
summary: Bhṛgu Vāruṇi asks his father Varuṇa to teach him brahman; through repeated austerity he comes to know brahman as food, breath, mind, understanding and finally bliss (ānanda).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Muṇḍaka Up. 1.1 (lineage; lower and higher knowledge)
summary: Brahmā teaches brahman-knowledge to Atharvan, who passes it via Aṅgir and Satyavāha Bhāradvāja to Aṅgiras; Śaunaka asks Aṅgiras, who distinguishes the lower knowledge (four Vedas, six Vedāṅgas) from the higher.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Māṇḍūkya Up. 1–12 (Om and the four states)
summary: Om is all this; this self is brahman (verse 2) and has four quarters — waking, dream, deep sleep and the fourth — mapped onto a, u, m and the soundless syllable.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.3.98 (vāsudevārjunābhyāṃ vun)
summary: Sūtra prescribing the suffix -aka after Vāsudeva and Arjuna in the sense “one whose object of bhakti is …” (heading 4.3.95 bhaktiḥ), giving vāsudevaka, “devotee of Vāsudeva”.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Mahābhāṣya on Pāṇini 3.1.26 (Kaṃsa-vadha and Bali-bandha)
summary: Patañjali’s discussion of causatives used of narration: “kaṃsavadham ācaṣṭe kaṃsaṃ ghātayati, balibandham ācaṣṭe baliṃ bandhayati”; śobhikas (performers) enact these before one’s eyes, paintings show the blows, and the reciters (granthikas) are seen divided into partisans of Kaṃsa and of Vāsudeva, some with red faces and some with black.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Nirukta 2.16 (who is Vṛtra?)
summary: Yāska’s gloss on RV 1.32.10: “Who then is Vṛtra? A cloud, say the etymologists; an asura son of Tvaṣṭṛ, say the historians.” Battle imagery, he explains, is metaphor for the mingling of waters and light that produces rain.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
summary: The commentary on the Kāṇva Bṛhadāraṇyaka ascribed to Śaṅkara, one of the two Upaniṣad commentaries (with the Taittirīya) whose authenticity is most widely accepted; a principal source for Advaita readings of “ahaṃ brahmāsmi” and “neti neti”.

type:LABEL: text
name: Brahma Sūtra
summary: Aphorisms attributed to Bādarāyaṇa that systematise the teaching of the Upaniṣads; with the Upaniṣads and the Bhagavad Gītā it is one of the three foundations (prasthānatrayī) on which every Vedānta school, beginning with Śaṅkara, wrote commentaries.

type:LABEL: text
name: Sāyaṇa’s commentary on the Ṛgveda (Vedārthaprakāśa)
summary: The comprehensive 14th-century commentary on the whole Ṛgveda produced at Vijayanagara under Sāyaṇa’s direction at the request of Bukka I; it was the basis of Max Müller’s edition and remains the standard traditional interpretation.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vikramorvaśīya of Kālidāsa
summary: Kālidāsa’s five-act Sanskrit play on the love of king Purūravas and the apsaras Urvaśī, the best-known classical retelling of the Vedic story with a happy ending in place of the Vedic separation.

type:LABEL: character
name: Lopāmudrā
summary: Wife of Agastya who, in the dialogue hymn RV 1.179, urges her ascetic husband to love; the Anukramaṇī counts her among the women seers, and the Mahābhārata tells her story at length.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sudās
summary: Ṛgvedic king of the Tṛtsu–Bharatas, patron of Vasiṣṭha (RV 7.18, 7.33) and of Viśvāmitra (RV 3.53), victor with Indra’s help in the Battle of the Ten Kings.

type:LABEL: character
name: Pravāhaṇa Jaivali
summary: A Pañcāla king who teaches the brahmin Gautama (Uddālaka Āruṇi) the doctrine of the five fires and the two paths of the dead, remarking that this knowledge had never before gone to brahmins (CU 5.3–10; BU 6.2).
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: character
name: Vāmadeva
summary: Ṛgvedic poet of maṇḍala 4 whose first-person verse “I was Manu and the Sun” (RV 4.26.1) the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.4.10) cites as the realisation of one who knows “I am brahman”.
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: character
name: Iḍā
summary: The woman born from Manu’s post-flood offering of ghee, curds, whey and curd (ŚB 1.8.1.7–11), through whom Manu generates his progeny; Purūravas is called her son (aiḍa). Purāṇic genealogies make Iḷā/Ila the parent of Purūravas with Budha, son of Soma.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The dwarf Viṣṇu wins the earth for the gods
summary: In ŚB 1.2.5 the asuras agree to give the gods as much of the earth as the dwarf Viṣṇu lies upon; Viṣṇu, who is the sacrifice, is enclosed by the metres and so obtains the whole earth — an early prose form of the later Vāmana–Bali story, without Bali.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The Battle of the Ten Kings
summary: The Ṛgvedic battle on the Paruṣṇī (Ravi) in which king Sudās of the Tṛtsu–Bharatas, aided by Indra through Vasiṣṭha’s prayers, defeats a coalition of ten kings (RV 7.18; 7.33.3–5; 7.83).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Pravāhaṇa Jaivali teaches the five fires
summary: The episode in which Śvetaketu fails the Pañcāla king’s questions about the fate of the dead and the king teaches Śvetaketu’s father the five fires and two paths — the earliest systematic account of rebirth, told in two versions (CU 5.3–10; BU 6.2).
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Videgha Māthava and the eastward course of Agni
summary: King Videgha Māthava and his priest Gotama Rāhūgaṇa follow Agni Vaiśvānara as it burns eastward from the Sarasvatī across the rivers to the Sadānīrā; the land beyond, once marshy, becomes Videha (ŚB 1.4.1.10–17).
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: place
name: Videha
summary: The late Vedic land east of the Sadānīrā (usually identified with the Gaṇḍak) in present north Bihar and the Nepal Tarai, ruled in the Brāhmaṇas and Upaniṣads by kings called Janaka; the Rāmāyaṇa’s Mithilā is its capital.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Upaniṣadic Janaka of Videha is Sītā’s father
summary: A popular conflation of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka/Śatapatha king Janaka Vaideha, patron of Yājñavalkya, with Janaka of Mithilā, Sītā’s father in the Rāmāyaṇa; the Vedic texts never mention Sītā, and later tradition treats “Janaka” as a title borne by many Videha kings.
